teile.einleitung: Drizzle is rain with very fine droplets. You can hardly feel them one by one, but after a while you get wet anyway. Here it often drizzles on grey days with low clouds.
wichtigste: Drizzle is made of very fine droplets.
The droplets are smaller than half a millimetre.
It usually falls from low, grey layer clouds.
The droplets fall slowly, almost floating.
Drizzle is also called spray rain in German.
It usually brings only a little water.

abschnitte.text: In **drizzle**, a great many tiny droplets fall. Each is smaller than half a millimetre. Normal raindrops are usually much bigger. Because the droplets are so light, the air slows them down a lot. They fall **slowly** and almost float down. On your skin, drizzle feels like a damp breath.

Drizzle usually falls from a flat, grey layer of cloud lying low over the land. Such clouds are called **layer clouds** or stratus. There is hardly any updraught in them, so the droplets cannot grow into big drops. In autumn and winter there is often **low cloud** over the Swiss Plateau. A light drizzle can fall from it too.

In German, drizzle is also called **Sprühregen**, which means “spray rain”. The fine droplets come down as if from a spray bottle. Because they are so small, usually only **a little water** adds up. Even so, it can sometimes drizzle all day long. Then everything slowly gets wet, although it never really rains. An umbrella helps less, because the droplets come from the side with the wind.

When it is colder than 0 degrees, drizzle can become very dangerous. The droplets are still liquid, but they freeze immediately when they hit the cold ground. This creates **black ice**. Roads and paths become as slippery as glass. That is why the weather service warns of **freezing drizzle**, and the roads are salted.

gewusst: A normal raindrop contains as much water as thousands of drizzle droplets.
Freezing drizzle can make roads as slippery as glass in a short time.
Drizzle can last for hours without much water falling.

teile.einleitung: Nagra is looking for a safe place in Switzerland for radioactive waste. This waste comes mainly from nuclear power stations, but also from medicine, industry and research. It is to be sealed deep in the rock for a very long time.
wichtigste: Nagra stands for National Cooperative for the Disposal of Radioactive Waste.
It was founded in 1972 and is based in Wettingen in Aargau.
In September 2022 it proposed the Nördlich Lägern site.
A combined repository for all types of waste is planned.
In November 2024 it submitted the applications to the federal government.
A referendum can be called against the decision.

abschnitte.text: **Nagra** in full is the **National Cooperative for the Disposal of Radioactive Waste** (the abbreviation comes from its German name). It was founded in 1972 by the operators of the nuclear power stations and the federal government. It is based in **Wettingen** in the canton of Aargau. By law, those who produce the waste must make sure it is disposed of safely. For this, Nagra is planning a **deep geological repository**.

Since 1984, Nagra has run the **Grimsel Test Site** in the Bernese Oberland. It lies in granite. There scientists study, for example, how substances move in fine cracks and how well artificial barriers seal. At the **Mont Terri** rock laboratory in the canton of Jura, **Opalinus Clay** is also studied. This rock is meant to seal in the waste in the deep repository.

In the **Sectoral Plan for Deep Geological Repositories**, the federal government set out how the search should work. In the last stage, Nagra studied three areas in northern Switzerland: **Jura Ost**, **Nördlich Lägern** and **Zürich Nordost**. There the Opalinus Clay lies at a suitable depth. The areas were compared using boreholes and measurements. In September 2022, Nagra proposed **Nördlich Lägern** in the cantons of Zurich and Aargau, saying it had the greatest safety margins.

Nagra is planning a **combined repository**. This means that high-level waste as well as low- and intermediate-level waste go to the same site, but into separate parts of the repository. Spent fuel elements are first to go to a **packaging plant** at the existing interim storage facility **Zwilag** in Würenlingen, Aargau. There they will be packed into final disposal containers. The waste is already being stored temporarily in Würenlingen today.

In November 2024, Nagra submitted the **general licence applications** to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy. The authorities are now checking them. After that the **Federal Council** grants the general licence, and **Parliament** has to approve it. An **optional referendum** can be called against this decision. Then the voters would have the last word. Such a vote would be possible around 2031 at the earliest.

gewusst: Radioactive waste has to stay safely sealed in for hundreds of thousands of years.
The Grimsel Test Site lies in the middle of the granite of the Aar Massif.
Part of the waste comes from hospitals and research.

teile.einleitung: Pack ice is sea ice that has been pushed together by wind and currents. It can pile up into high ridges and trap ships. For polar bears and seals, sea ice is an important habitat.
wichtigste: Pack ice is ice on the sea that has been pushed together.
A single drifting plate of ice is called an ice floe.
Icebreakers drive up onto the ice and break it with their weight.
Polar bears hunt mainly seals on the pack ice.
From 1893, Nansen let the Fram drift in the ice on purpose.
Today there is less sea ice in the Arctic than 50 years ago.

abschnitte.text: In the polar seas, the seawater freezes into **sea ice** in winter. Flat pieces of it that drift on the water are called **ice floes**. Wind and ocean currents push the floes together. They slide over each other and pile up into ridges. This creates **pack ice**. It is often much thicker than the flat ice next to it and hard to cross.

Thick ice is dangerous for normal ships. **Icebreakers** have an especially strong, rounded hull. They drive their bows up onto the ice and break it with their **weight**. Behind them a channel forms through which other ships can sail. Icebreakers are used in the Arctic, in the Antarctic and also in the Baltic Sea.

Sea ice is important for many animals. **Seals** like to rest on ice floes and breathe through holes in the ice. The **polar bear** lies in wait at these breathing holes and hunts mainly seals. Without sea ice it finds much less food. In summer part of the sea ice melts, and in winter it freezes again. But satellite images show that the Arctic sea ice in summer is much **smaller** today than 50 years ago. This is linked to warming.

The Norwegian explorer **Fridtjof Nansen** had a daring idea. From 1893, he let his ship, the **Fram**, freeze into the pack ice on purpose. The Fram was built so that the ice pushed it upwards instead of crushing it. The ship drifted with the ice across the **Arctic Ocean**. In this way Nansen was able to show that the ice there is floating on a sea. The Fram is now in a museum in Oslo.

The polar explorer **Ernest Shackleton** was less lucky. His ship, the **Endurance**, got stuck in the pack ice of the Weddell Sea in Antarctica. In 1915 it was crushed by the ice and sank. The men lived on the ice for months and then saved themselves in lifeboats. All the members of the crew survived. In 2022 the wreck was found at a depth of around 3,000 metres.

gewusst: The wreck of the Endurance was only discovered in 2022.
The Fram was built so round that the ice pushed it upwards.
Sea ice is much less salty than the seawater it freezes from.

teile.einleitung: In the climate system, many things are connected: if the temperature changes, ice, water vapour, clouds and the carbon cycle change too. These changes then act back on the temperature. This is called **feedback**.
wichtigste: A feedback is an effect that acts back on its own cause.
Positive feedbacks strengthen a change, negative ones weaken it.
The Planck feedback is the most important brake: a warmer Earth gives off more heat.
The water vapour feedback is the strongest amplifier of warming.
The cloud feedback is seen as the greatest uncertainty in climate calculations.
A warmer ocean can dissolve less CO2, so more of it stays in the air.

abschnitte.text: In a **feedback**, a change influences itself. If it gets warmer and this leads to even more warmth, this is called a **positive feedback**. If the result works against the change, it is a **negative feedback**. “Positive” and “negative” are not judgements here; they only describe the direction. Negative feedbacks act like a brake and stabilise the climate.

Every warm body gives off heat. According to the **Stefan-Boltzmann law**, this radiation grows with the fourth power of the absolute temperature. Even a small warming makes the radiation rise clearly. This **Planck feedback** makes sure that a new balance is reached after a disturbance. The **lapse rate feedback** also has a damping effect: in the tropics, the upper troposphere warms more than the ground and gives off more heat into space from there.

Warmer air can hold more **water vapour**, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas. This feedback roughly doubles the direct warming caused by CO2. Another amplifier is the **ice-albedo feedback**: when snow and ice melt, dark ground or dark water appears. This reflects less sunlight and warms up more. You can see this in the shrinking glaciers of the Alps too.

**Clouds** can warm or cool, depending on their height, thickness and position. Low, dense clouds reflect a lot of sunlight, while high, thin clouds tend to hold heat in. The **IPCC** considers the overall effect of clouds probably to be amplifying, but with great uncertainty. The **ocean** plays a part too: gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm water. That is why a warmer ocean takes up less CO2.

Researchers sum up feedbacks with a **feedback factor** f. The warming without feedback is divided by 1 minus f. If, for example, it is 1.0 °C and f is 0.6, this gives 1.0 divided by 0.4, which is 2.5 °C. In this way amplifying feedbacks multiply an initial warming. How much the Earth warms when CO2 doubles is called **climate sensitivity**.

gewusst: Without the Planck feedback there would be no stable climate: the Earth would keep warming or cooling with every disturbance.
Water vapour is the most common greenhouse gas on Earth, but its amount depends mainly on the temperature.

teile.einleitung: A rainbow is a colourful arc of light in the sky that forms when sunlight meets raindrops. It shows that white sunlight really contains many colours. Because it appears and disappears so suddenly, many people see it as a small miracle.
wichtigste: For a rainbow you need sun and rain at the same time.
The sun must be behind you when you see a rainbow.
The raindrops split white sunlight into its colours.
In the main rainbow, red is on the very outside and violet on the very inside.
A rainbow is shaped like an arc; actually it is even a whole circle.
Brown does not appear in a rainbow.
Sometimes you can see a fainter secondary rainbow above the main one, with the colours the other way round.

abschnitte.text: A rainbow forms when the sun is shining and it is raining at the same time. Sunlight enters the raindrops and is bent as it does so; this is called **refraction**. Inside the drop, the light is reflected at the back and then comes out again. Because each colour is bent a little differently, the white light fans out into its colours. This fanning out is called **dispersion**.

In a rainbow you see, from the outside in, red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Indigo is often added, and then people speak of seven colours. In reality the colours blend smoothly into each other; there are no sharp borders. Brown, pink, grey and black do not appear, because they are not pure **spectral colours**. The colours in a rainbow are the same as in light that passes through a glass prism.

You can only see a rainbow when the sun is behind you and rain is falling in front of you. Its centre is exactly opposite the sun, at what is called the **antisolar point**. The arc appears at an angle of about 42 degrees around this point. That is why rainbows are most likely to be seen in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low. If the sun is higher than 42 degrees, the whole arc is below the horizon.

Sometimes a second, fainter arc appears above the main rainbow. This **secondary rainbow** forms when the light is reflected twice inside the drop. Its colours are the other way round, so red is on the inside. Between the two arcs the sky is noticeably dark. This strip is called **Alexander's dark band**, after a scholar of ancient times.

In ancient times, scholars such as Aristotle were already thinking about the rainbow. In 1637 the French scientist René Descartes used experiments with a glass ball filled with water to explain how light is refracted and reflected in the drop. Isaac Newton later showed with a **prism** that white light is made of all the colours. That made it clear where the colours of the rainbow come from.

On a sunny day you can make your own rainbow with a garden hose. Stand with your back to the sun and spray a fine mist of water in front of you. At waterfalls such as the **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen or the Staubbach Falls in Lauterbrunnen you can also often see rainbows in the spray. With a glass of water on a sunny windowsill you can make little stripes of colour appear on the wall.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ray of light changes direction when it passes from air into water or glass.
The pure colours that white light is made of.
A see-through glass object that splits light into its colours.
A second, fainter rainbow above the main arc, with the colours the other way round.

gewusst: From an aeroplane you can sometimes see a rainbow as a whole circle.
Every person sees their own rainbow, because different drops light up for each eye.
A rainbow can also form in moonlight, but to our eyes it looks almost white.

teile.einleitung: A bog is a very wet area with soft ground. Special plants grow here, and over thousands of years peat forms. In Switzerland, bogs have been specially protected since a popular vote.
wichtigste: In a bog, the ground is full of water and very soft.
Peat slowly forms from dead plants.
In a raised bog, peat moss makes up a large part of the ground.
Peat moss soaks up water like a sponge.
The sundew is a small carnivorous bog plant.
In 1987, voters said yes to protecting bogs.

abschnitte.text: In a bog, the water reaches almost to the surface. That is why the ground is as soft as a wet sponge, and you can sink into it. Because there is little air in the water, dead plants rot only very slowly. They pile up and over a long time turn into **peat**. A layer of peat usually grows only about one millimetre a year.

A **fen** is kept wet by groundwater or streams. Many grasses and sedges grow there. A **raised bog** gets its water almost only from rain. Here **peat moss** keeps growing upwards while it dies off underneath. Peat moss can take up many times its own weight in water. Substances come out of the dead plants and colour the water **brown like tea**.

The ground in a bog is wet, acidic and poor in nutrients. Only a few plants can cope with this. The **sundew** gets extra food: on its leaves there are sticky drops to which small insects stick and are digested. Cotton grass, dragonflies and rare butterflies also live in bogs. Many of these species are found almost nowhere else.

In the past, many bogs were drained to cut peat as fuel or to gain farmland. That is why most Swiss bogs have disappeared. In 1987, voters approved the **Rothenthurm initiative**. Since then, the protection of bogs has been written into the **Federal Constitution**. If you visit a bog, you stay on the paths, because the ground will not hold you everywhere, and rare plants are easily damaged.

Bogs hold back a lot of **water** and release it slowly. In this way they help against flooding when there is heavy rain. The peat also stores a great deal of **carbon** from ancient plants. If a bog is drained, the peat breaks down and carbon dioxide is produced. That is why a healthy bog is also good for the climate.

gewusst: Plant remains can survive in peat for thousands of years.
The sundew is a plant that catches small insects.
The Rothenthurm initiative is named after a bog in the canton of Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: Raindrops are small drops of water that fall from clouds to the Earth. They look different from what many people think, and they form from countless tiny cloud droplets. Rain brings water to plants, animals and people.
wichtigste: Very small raindrops are perfectly round.
Large falling drops look like a bread roll: flat at the bottom, round at the top.
If drops get too big, they burst into smaller drops.
A drop two millimetres across falls at about 20 km/h.
One raindrop forms from around a million cloud droplets.
1 millimetre of rain means one litre of water on one square metre.
Most of the water for rain evaporates over the seas.

abschnitte.titel: From the sea to the cloud
abschnitte.text: The sun warms water, and it **evaporates**. Most water evaporates over the **seas**, because they are so big. The water vapour rises and cools down. There it forms small **cloud droplets** on tiny specks of dust. We see many of them together as a cloud.

Cloud droplets are so tiny and light that they float in the air. Only when they bump into each other and join together do they get heavier. A single **raindrop** needs around **a million** cloud droplets. When the drop is heavy enough, it falls out of the cloud. In cold clouds, rain often also forms from snowflakes that melt as they fall.

In pictures, raindrops are often drawn like a tear with a point. In reality, very small drops are **perfectly round**. As large drops fall, the air flattens them at the bottom. They then look like a **bread roll**, flat at the bottom and round at the top. If they get even bigger, they change shape a lot and **burst** into smaller drops.

Large drops fall faster than small ones. A drop two millimetres across falls at about **20 km/h**. That is about as fast as a bike. Very fine drizzle, on the other hand, falls much more slowly. The air slows the drops down, so they do not keep getting faster.

Weather services such as **MeteoSwiss** measure how much rain falls. It is given in **millimetres**. **1 millimetre of rain** means that one **litre of water** has fallen on one square metre. If the water did not soak away, it would stand one millimetre deep there. It is measured with a container that catches the rain.

gewusst: The smell after rain has its own name: petrichor.
Raindrops rarely get bigger than about 5 millimetres; otherwise they burst.

teile.einleitung: **Sedimentology** is the science of deposits. It studies how sediments are carried and deposited. From grains, layers and patterns in the rock, researchers can read what a landscape used to look like.
wichtigste: Sedimentology studies how sediments form, travel and are deposited.
By the usual classification, sand has a grain size of 0.063 to 2 millimetres.
The Hjulström diagram shows at what current speed grains are eroded, carried or deposited.
Turbidites show graded bedding, with grains getting finer towards the top.
Cross-bedding reveals the former direction of the current.
The Molasse of the Swiss Plateau is made mainly of eroded debris from the Alps.

abschnitte.text: Sediments are classified by their **grain size**. By the usual classification, **sand** has grains of **0.063 to 2 millimetres**. Finer particles are called **silt** and **clay**, coarser ones **gravel**. **Roundness** is important too: well-rounded pebbles have usually been carried a long way, because their edges were worn away on the journey.

The **Hjulström diagram** shows at what flow speed grains of a certain size are **eroded**, **carried** or **deposited**. What is surprising is that fine clay needs quite a strong current to be torn loose, because the particles stick together. But once it is in the water, it only sinks in very calm water.

**Cross-bedding** in a sandstone shows the former **direction of the current** of water or wind. **Ripple marks** are small waves in the sand. Symmetrical ripples point to a **wave movement** swinging back and forth, for example on a beach. A **turbidite** is formed by a turbidity current under water. It shows **graded bedding**: coarse grains lie at the bottom, and they get finer and finer towards the top.

**Facies** are the features of a deposit that reveal where it formed, for example a beach, a lagoon or the deep sea. **Walther's law of facies** says: only facies that once lay **side by side** follow each other vertically. If sea level rises, for example, the beach moves inland, and marine deposits are laid down on top of beach sand.

A large part of the **Swiss Plateau** is made of **Molasse**. It is mainly **eroded debris from the Alps**. As the Alps rose, rivers carried gravel, sand and mud into the foreland. This turned into Nagelfluh, sandstone and marl. Sedimentologists read the history of the Alps in these layers.

gewusst: Sedimentologists also use their knowledge to find groundwater, oil or building materials such as gravel.
Ripple marks that formed millions of years ago often look almost exactly the same as the ripples on a beach today.

teile.einleitung: **Slate** is a rock that can be split into thin slabs. In the past, schoolchildren wrote on it, and houses got roofs made of it. In the Glarus region you can even find fossilised fish in slate.
wichtigste: Slate can be split into thin slabs.
Slate forms from mudstone.
In the past, schoolchildren wrote on slates with a slate pencil.
The former slate mine Landesplattenberg is in Engi in the canton of Glarus.
Fossilised fish are found in Glarus slate.
In the Grisons, Bündner schist is widespread.

abschnitte.text: Slate is a **metamorphic rock**. This means it formed from another rock that was changed deep inside the Earth by **pressure** and **heat**. **Slate** forms, for example, from **mudstone**. As it does, the tiny flakes of mineral all line up in the same way. That is why slate can be split into **thin slabs**.

Before paper and exercise books became cheap, schoolchildren wrote on a **slate**. They wrote with a **slate pencil**, a stick made of soft slate. The writing could be wiped off again with a damp sponge. In this way the slate could be used again and again. Slabs of slate were also used to make **roofs**, floors and tables.

In **Engi** in the canton of **Glarus** lies the former slate mine **Landesplattenberg**. Slate was quarried there for centuries, and today you can visit it. **Glarus slate** is famous for its **fossilised fish**. They lived in a sea many millions of years ago and were trapped in the mud.

In the **Grisons**, **Bündner schist** is widespread. It often contains lime and forms whole mountainsides. **Mica schist** glitters in the light because it contains many small **flakes of mica**. They reflect the light like tiny mirrors. (In German, both slate and schist are called “Schiefer”.)

gewusst: The fish in Glarus slate are so well preserved that you can often still see fins and fine bones.
The pencils for writing slates were themselves made of slate, only of a softer kind.

teile.einleitung: A lava flow is liquid, glowing rock that comes out of the Earth during a volcanic eruption and flows down the slope. It is fascinatingly beautiful, but also very dangerous, because it destroys everything in its path.
wichtigste: Deep inside the Earth, the molten rock is called **magma**; at the surface it is called **lava**.
Depending on the type, lava is about 700 to 1,200 degrees hot.
Fresh lava glows red to orange.
Many lava flows move slowly, often about as fast as a person walking.
When lava cools, it turns into hard rock, for example basalt.
In Hawaii you can often see long lava flows.

abschnitte.text: Deep below the Earth's surface it is so hot that rock can melt. This liquid rock is called **magma**. In a volcanic eruption it rises upwards and comes out of the crater or out of cracks. As soon as it is at the surface, it is called **lava**. When the lava flows down the mountain in a long tongue, it is called a **lava flow**.

Lava is about 700 to 1,200 degrees hot. For comparison: water boils at just 100 degrees. Very hot, fresh lava glows **red to orange**, like the embers in a fireplace. When it gets a bit cooler, its surface turns dark and forms a crust. Trees that a lava flow reaches catch fire immediately and burn.

Many lava flows move slowly, often about as fast as a person walks. That is why people can usually get to safety in time. But houses, roads and fields cannot be carried away. A lava flow can hardly be stopped and buries everything under it. Runny lava flows faster and further than thick, sticky lava.

In **Hawaii** in the Pacific there are volcanoes that often pour out runny lava. It sometimes flows in long streams all the way into the sea. There it hisses and steams tremendously, because the seawater instantly turns to steam on the hot lava. Huge clouds of steam rise up. The lava cools quickly in the water, and in this way the island can even grow a little.

Volcanologists study lava flows to understand volcanoes better. When they go close, they wear a silvery **heat protection suit**. It reflects the heat. When lava cools, it turns into hard rock. Often dark **basalt** forms, one of the most common rocks on Earth.

gewusst: A large part of the sea floor is made of solidified lava, especially basalt.
The islands of Hawaii formed from lava that piled up over a very long time.

teile.einleitung: The Mohs scale of hardness arranges minerals by their hardness. It was presented by Friedrich Mohs in 1812 and is still used today in schools and by rock collectors. Its principle is very simple: the harder one scratches the softer one.
wichtigste: The scale comes from **Friedrich Mohs** in **1812**.
It has **10 levels**, from 1 (softest) to 10 (hardest reference mineral).
The harder mineral **scratches** the softer one.
Fluorite has hardness 4, topaz hardness 8, corundum hardness 9.
A penknife blade has a hardness of about 5.5.
The gaps between the levels are **not equal**.

abschnitte.text: **Friedrich Mohs** was a German mineralogist. He taught in **Graz** and **Vienna**, among other places. In **1812** he presented his scale of hardness. So it is more than 200 years old. Because it is so simple, it is still used today in schools and by rock collectors.

The scale works on a simple principle: **the harder mineral scratches the softer one**. So you test which mineral can scratch which. A mineral scratches all minerals with a lower hardness and is scratched by harder ones. Each of the **10 levels** has its own reference mineral. If an unknown stone does not scratch quartz but is itself scratched by quartz, it is softer than 7.

The order is: 1 **talc**, 2 **gypsum**, 3 **calcite**, 4 **fluorite**, 5 **apatite**, 6 **orthoclase**, 7 **quartz**, 8 **topaz**, 9 **corundum** and 10 **diamond**. Fluorite is also called fluorspar and can still be scratched easily with a knife. Topaz is harder than quartz and a popular gemstone. The coloured varieties of corundum are known as **ruby** and **sapphire**.

When you are out and about, you do not need all ten minerals. The steel blade of a **penknife** has a hardness of about **5.5**. It scratches minerals up to about hardness 5, but none from hardness 6. Your fingernail helps too: it scratches talc and gypsum. In this way you can already roughly place a stone.

The Mohs scale only gives an **order**. The gaps between the levels are **not equal**. The step from 9 to 10, for example, is much bigger than the one from 1 to 2. **Diamond** is many times harder than corundum. That is why experts use other methods for exact measurements.

gewusst: Diamond is so hard that it can only be cut and polished with diamond.
Talc, with hardness 1, is so soft that you can scratch it with your fingernail.

teile.einleitung: A valley is a long hollow in the landscape that lies between mountains or hills. Usually a stream or river flows through the bottom. In Switzerland, many people live in valleys, and every valley has its own history.
wichtigste: A valley is a long hollow between mountains or hills.
A stream or river often flows along the bottom of the valley.
A river carves a valley with a V-shaped cross-section.
A glacier grinds out a valley with a U-shaped cross-section.
The Rhône flows through Valais.
The valley floor is the lowest and usually flattest part of a valley.
Many Swiss valleys contain villages, roads and railway lines.

abschnitte.text: A valley is a long dip in the Earth's surface that is bordered by higher ground on at least two sides. The lowest part is called the **valley floor**, and the sloping sides are called the **valley slopes** or valley sides. Usually a stream or river flows through the valley and has helped to shape it over a very long time. The upper end of a valley, where it leads up into the mountains, is called the valley head.

With its water and the stones and sand it carries along, a river slowly digs its way into the ground. The slopes keep slipping down, and a valley with a V-shaped cross-section forms: the **V-shaped valley**. If a river cuts especially quickly into hard rock, a narrow **gorge** forms. Well-known gorges in Switzerland are the Aare Gorge near Meiringen and the Viamala in the Grisons.

During the ice ages, large parts of Switzerland were covered by glaciers. The mighty streams of ice ground the valleys wider and deeper. This created valleys with steep walls and a wide, flat floor, with a U-shaped cross-section: the **U-shaped valleys**, or glacial troughs. A famous example is the Lauterbrunnen Valley in the Bernese Oberland, with its almost vertical rock walls. Side valleys that end high above the main valley are called hanging valleys, and waterfalls such as the Staubbach Falls often plunge down from them.

The **Rhône Valley** in Valais is one of the largest valleys in Switzerland; the Rhône flows through it from the Rhône Glacier to Lake Geneva. Other well-known valleys are the Engadine with the Inn, the Rhine Valley, the Hasli Valley and, in Ticino, the Verzasca Valley and the Maggia Valley. Many valleys are so remote that their own dialects and customs developed there. In the past, the people of a valley often formed their own community, called a **Talschaft**.

In the valleys it is flatter, warmer and more sheltered than on the mountains. That is why many villages and towns, fields and orchards lie there. Roads and railway lines also run through the valleys, often up to a pass or tunnel. In Valais, vines even grow on the sunny valley slopes. One disadvantage is natural hazards such as floods, avalanches and debris flows.

Valleys often have their own weather. During the day the wind usually blows up the valley, and at night down the valley. In winter, cold air collects on the valley floor and fog forms, while it is sunny on the mountains. In some Alpine valleys the **foehn** blows, a warm, dry wind coming down from the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest, usually flat part of a valley.
A valley carved by a river, with a V-shaped cross-section.
A valley ground out by a glacier, with a U-shaped cross-section.
A side valley that ends high above the main valley.
A warm, dry wind that blows down from the mountains in the Alps.

gewusst: There are 72 waterfalls in the Lauterbrunnen Valley.
At the bottom of many large Alpine valleys lies a layer of debris many hundreds of metres thick, deposited by rivers and glaciers.
Some valleys are not in the mountains at all but deep under the sea, like huge underwater canyons.

teile.einleitung: Volcanic ash is very different from the ash in a fireplace. It is made of tiny pieces of rock and glass that a volcano hurls into the air during an eruption. The wind can carry it a very long way.
wichtigste: Volcanic ash is made of tiny pieces of rock and glass.
It is usually grey to dark grey.
Ash can damage the engines of aeroplanes.
In 2010 an ash cloud from Iceland partly brought air traffic in Europe to a halt.
In the year 79 Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii.
The wind carries fine ash for thousands of kilometres.
When there is a lot of ash in the air, a dust mask protects your lungs.

abschnitte.text: In an explosive eruption, molten rock is torn apart with great force. In the air it hardens into tiny grains of **rock and glass**. These grains are smaller than two millimetres and are called **volcanic ash**. It is usually **grey** to dark grey and very hard. When a lot of it falls, it covers cars, roads and roofs like grey snow.

Fine ash rises many kilometres up into the sky. There the wind carries it for **thousands of kilometres**. A thick ash cloud blocks the sunlight, and it can become almost **dark** in the middle of the day. If a great many particles reach high altitudes, it can become a little cooler all over the Earth for a while.

Volcanic ash is dangerous for aeroplanes. In the hot **engines** it melts and can clog them. That is why aeroplanes do not fly through ash clouds. In **2010** the volcano **Eyjafjallajökull** in **Iceland** erupted. Its ash drifted as far as Central Europe and over Switzerland too. As a result, aeroplanes stayed on the ground for days in many countries.

In the year **79** **Vesuvius** in Italy erupted. Ash and rock buried the Roman town of **Pompeii**. Under the thick layer, houses, streets and objects were preserved. The town has been excavated since the 18th century. Today you can walk through its streets and see how people lived almost 2000 years ago.

The fine grains of ash irritate the eyes and **lungs**. When there is a lot of ash in the air, people therefore wear a **dust mask** and stay indoors as much as possible. Ash on roofs is heavy and has to be cleared away. Over time, though, the ash weathers into very **fertile soil**. That is why people farm on many volcanoes despite the danger.

gewusst: Wet volcanic ash can conduct electricity and can therefore disrupt power lines.
Even in Swiss lakes you can find thin layers of ash from eruptions of faraway volcanoes.

teile.einleitung: The Paris Agreement is a treaty with which almost all the countries of the world want to act together against global warming. It was adopted in December 2015 at the climate conference in Paris. Switzerland takes part too.
wichtigste: The Paris Agreement was adopted in December 2015.
It was agreed at the UN climate conference COP21 in Paris.
Warming should stay well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C.
The comparison is with the time before industrialisation.
Every five years the countries submit new national climate targets.
Its predecessor was the Kyoto Protocol of 1997.
Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990.

abschnitte.titel: A treaty for the whole world
abschnitte.text: Greenhouse gases such as **carbon dioxide** are produced mainly when coal, oil and natural gas are burned. They hold back heat in the atmosphere, and the Earth gets warmer. In December 2015 representatives of almost all countries met at the UN climate conference **COP21** in Paris. There they agreed on a new treaty. It is the first in which all participating countries, rich and poorer, commit themselves to protecting the climate. It came into force in November 2016.

Global warming should stay **well below 2 °C**. In addition, the countries want to try to limit it to **1.5 °C**. It is measured in comparison with the **pre-industrial period**, usually the years 1850 to 1900, before factories and engines used a lot of coal and oil. Since then the Earth has already become well over 1 °C warmer. In the long term, no more greenhouse gases should be emitted than nature or technology can take back up.

The agreement does not lay down how much each country must save. Each country sets its own **national climate targets**. These must be submitted again every five years and should be more ambitious each time. The countries report regularly on what they have achieved. Richer countries should also support poorer countries with money for climate protection and for adapting to climate change.

Before the Paris Agreement there was the **Kyoto Protocol** of 1997. In it, mainly industrialised countries committed themselves to lower emissions. Under President Donald Trump the **United States** withdrew from the Paris Agreement. Under his successor Joe Biden it rejoined in 2021. After Trump returned to office, the government announced its withdrawal again in early 2025. Such decisions are judged differently in politics.

Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017, that is, it officially accepted it. It wants to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by **50 per cent** compared with 1990 by 2030. By 2050 Switzerland should reach **net zero**: then it should emit no more greenhouse gases than are removed again. This target is set out in the Climate and Innovation Act, which voters approved in June 2023.

gewusst: Almost all the countries in the world take part in the Paris Agreement.
When the agreement was adopted, there was loud cheering in the hall and many delegates hugged each other.

teile.einleitung: In rockfall, stones break loose from a slope or rock face and fall or bounce down. In the mountains of Switzerland, rockfall is a common danger for hikers, roads and railway lines.
wichtigste: Rockfall means that stones fall down from a slope or rock face.
Rockfall is especially common when ice in the rock thaws.
Climbers and mountaineers wear a helmet for protection.
Strong steel nets and galleries protect roads and railway lines.
Anyone who kicks a stone loose shouts “Rock!” loudly.
In danger zones you keep walking briskly and do not stop.

abschnitte.text: In **rockfall**, single stones or smaller blocks break loose from a slope. They fall down, bounce over the ground or roll down the valley. As they do so, they become very fast and can cause great damage. If huge amounts of rock break loose at once, it is called a **rock avalanche** or **landslide**.

Water gets into cracks in the rock. When it freezes, it expands and pushes the cracks apart. As long as the ice is there, it holds loose stones in place like **glue**. When it thaws, the stones lose their hold and fall down. That is why rockfall is especially common in spring, on warm afternoons and when the **permafrost** in high mountains thaws.

Along mountain roads and railway lines, strong steel **protective nets** are put up. They catch falling stones. In especially dangerous places, a **gallery** is built. This is a strong concrete roof over the road, closed on the mountain side. Stones and avalanches slide over it. A **warning sign** with falling stones shows where there is danger. You should not stop there.

Climbers and mountaineers wear a hard **helmet** that catches falling stones. If you kick a stone loose yourself, shout **“Rock!”** loudly. In German people shout “Stein!”. This lets people further down protect themselves. On a path where there is a danger of rockfall, you do not stop or take a break. You keep walking **briskly** until you are out of the danger zone. Early in the morning it is usually safer, because the rock is still frozen.

gewusst: A stone the size of a fist falling down a high wall can become as fast as a car on the motorway.
In Switzerland there are hazard maps that show where rockfall threatens.

teile.einleitung: Methane is a colourless gas and the main part of natural gas. It also forms when bacteria break down plant remains without oxygen, for example in bogs, rice fields or in the stomachs of cattle. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.
wichtigste: Methane has the formula **CH4** and is the simplest hydrocarbon.
**Natural gas** is usually 80 to 99 per cent methane.
**Cattle** release a lot of methane during digestion.
Methane also forms in **flooded rice farming** and in bogs.
Over 100 years, methane warms about 28 times more strongly than the same amount of CO2.
On average it stays in the atmosphere for about **12 years**.

abschnitte.text: A **methane molecule** is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. That is why its formula is **CH4**. It is the simplest **hydrocarbon**. Methane is colourless and flammable, and pure methane is **odourless**. So that a leak is noticed at once, a strong-smelling substance is added to natural gas.

**Natural gas** is a fossil fuel and is usually 80 to 99 per cent methane. It is burnt for heating, cooking and producing electricity. This produces carbon dioxide. But if natural gas escapes **unburnt** from pipes or boreholes, it acts directly as a powerful greenhouse gas. In Switzerland too, many houses are still heated with natural gas.

**Cattle** are ruminants. In their first stomach, the **rumen**, tiny living things break down grass and produce methane as they do so. The animals mainly burp it out. **Rice fields** that stand under water also release a lot of methane. In the mud, which has little oxygen, bacteria break down plant remains. The same happens in swamps and bogs. There, methane rises in bubbles, which is why it is also called **marsh gas**.

Per kilogram, methane holds back much more heat than **carbon dioxide**. Calculated over 100 years, according to the **IPCC** it is about 27 to 30 times as effective, so around **28 times**. But methane does not stay in the air as long. On average it is broken down into carbon dioxide and water in about **12 years**.

Because methane is broken down fairly quickly, cutting emissions also has a **quick** effect. That is why less methane is seen as a good way to slow down warming over the next few decades. For example, leaks in gas pipes can be sealed, gas from rubbish dumps can be collected, or the feed of cattle can be changed. **Biogas** can also be produced from slurry and waste and used.

gewusst: On Saturn's moon Titan there are lakes of liquid methane.
The smell of natural gas does not come from the methane but from a scent added on purpose.

teile.einleitung: Dew is the small drops of water that glitter on grass and leaves in the morning. They form during the night from the invisible water vapour in the air.
wichtigste: The water in dewdrops comes from the water vapour in the air.
There is especially a lot of dew on clear, calm nights.
It is usually coolest around sunrise.
There is less dew under trees, because the ground there cools down less.
When the sun shines in the morning, the dew evaporates.
A cold pair of glasses steams up in a warm room in a similar way.

abschnitte.text: There is always some **water vapour** in the air, which you cannot see. Warm air can hold a lot of it, cold air less. When the air cools down, part of the vapour turns back into liquid water. This is called **condensation**. On cold surfaces such as blades of grass, small drops then form: the **dew**.

There is most dew on **clear, calm nights**. Without clouds, the ground gives off a lot of heat into the sky and cools down strongly. Without wind, the cold air stays lying on the ground, and the water can settle well. It keeps cooling down all night. That is why it is usually coldest around **sunrise**.

In the morning there is often **less dew** under a tree. The treetop works like a **blanket** and holds back some warmth. The ground underneath gets less cold. That is why less dew forms there. The grass also often stays dry under a porch roof or a car.

Dew glitters especially beautifully on **spiders' webs**. Many small drops hang on the fine threads and shine like pearls in the morning light. When the sun warms the grass and the air, the drops **evaporate**. They turn back into water vapour. After a short time everything is dry.

If you come into a warm room in winter wearing cold **glasses**, they steam up. The warm air contains water vapour, which turns into tiny drops on the cold lenses. Dew forms in exactly the same way. A cold glass with a drink in it also gets wet on the outside, even though nothing is leaking.

gewusst: If it is colder than zero degrees at night, frost made of ice crystals forms instead of dew.
Some animals and plants in dry regions use dew as a source of water.

teile.einleitung: Nagelfluh is a rock made of many round stones that look as if they were set in concrete. It is found on many mountains of the Prealps, for example on the Napf and the Rigi. Its name describes what it looks like.
wichtigste: Nagelfluh is a conglomerate, a sedimentary rock made of pebbles.
The stones look like nail heads in a rock face.
In Switzerland, “Fluh” means rock.
The pebbles come from the Alps, which were forming at the time.
A cement of lime and sand holds the stones together.
In popular speech, Nagelfluh is also called “the Lord's concrete”.

abschnitte.text: If you look at a wall of Nagelfluh, you see many round stones sticking out of the rock. They look like the heads of nails. In Switzerland, the word **Fluh** means rock. That is how the name **Nagelfluh** came about (“Nagel” means “nail”). Because the rock looks like concrete with gravel, it is jokingly also called **Herrgottsbeton**, “the Lord's concrete”, meaning concrete made by nature.

Nagelfluh is one of the **conglomerates**. These are sedimentary rocks made of rounded stones cemented together by a **binding material**. Fine sand and lime settled between the pebbles. Over time this mass hardened and held the stones firmly together. The pebbles can be very different: limestone, granite, sandstone and other rocks from the Alps.

While the **Alps** were rising, large ancient rivers carried huge amounts of debris into the foreland. During transport, the stones knocked against each other and lost their edges. In this way they became round **pebbles**. Where the rivers came out of the mountains, they deposited the material in large **debris fans**. These debris fans belong to the Molasse and turned into Nagelfluh over millions of years.

Many mountains on the edge of the Alps are made of Nagelfluh. The **Napf**, on the border between the cantons of Bern and Lucerne, is a large former debris fan. Its deeply cut gullies and ridges are typical of this rock. The **Rigi** and the **Speer** in the canton of St Gallen are also built of Nagelfluh. On their slopes you can often see the tilted layers clearly.

Nagelfluh often lies in layers above soft **marl**. When the marl gets wet, it can become slippery. On 2 September 1806, after a long period of rain, large layers of Nagelfluh slid down from the **Rossberg** in the canton of Schwyz. The **Goldau landslide** destroyed the village and killed around 450 people. It is one of the worst natural disasters in Switzerland. The place where the rock broke away is still clearly visible today.

gewusst: In popular speech, Nagelfluh is called “the Lord's concrete”.
Nagelfluh contains stones from Alpine areas that have long since been worn away.
Today there is a wildlife park on the rubble field of the Goldau landslide.

teile.einleitung: Stromatolites are layered bodies of lime built by tiny microbes. They are among the oldest traces of life on Earth and still grow in a few places today.
wichtigste: Stromatolites form from microbial mats, mainly of cyanobacteria.
They grow upwards layer by layer, towards the light.
The oldest accepted stromatolites are around 3.5 billion years old.
They were most widespread in the Proterozoic.
Today, well-known living stromatolites grow in Shark Bay in Western Australia.
“Lithos” is Greek and means stone.

abschnitte.text: A **stromatolite** is a lumpy or column-shaped body of lime. It is built by **microbial mats**, thin layers of tiny living things. **Cyanobacteria** are the main builders. The mats trap fine sediment and make lime settle out. The name comes from Greek: “stroma” means cover or layer, and “lithos” means **stone**. So a stromatolite is a “layer stone”.

Cyanobacteria carry out **photosynthesis** and therefore need light. When a mat is covered by sediment, the bacteria move upwards. There they form a new mat. In this way a layered body forms, layer after layer. Microbial bodies of lime without layering, with a clotted texture, are called **thrombolites**.

The oldest widely accepted stromatolites come from the **Pilbara region** in Western Australia. They are around **3.5 billion years** old. In the **Proterozoic**, stromatolites covered wide shallow seas. Their bacteria gave off oxygen and so changed the atmosphere over a very long time. Towards the end of this eon, their variety fell sharply.

When **animals** appeared, stromatolites became rare. Snails and other animals grazed on the microbial mats and disturbed them. Today they only grow in special places. The best known is **Hamelin Pool** in **Shark Bay** in Western Australia. There the water is very salty, and many animals that eat mats are missing.

gewusst: Stromatolites grow extremely slowly, often only a fraction of a millimetre a year.
Shark Bay is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: With radiometric dating, researchers find out the age of rocks, fossils and finds. They use radioactive substances that decay at a fixed rate. This is how we know today that the Earth is around 4.55 billion years old.
wichtigste: Radioactive isotopes decay with a fixed half-life.
After three half-lives, only an eighth of the original amount is left.
The radiocarbon method goes back to about 50,000 years.
Uranium-238 has a half-life of around 4.5 billion years.
Zircon is especially well suited to uranium-lead dating.
In 1956, Clair Patterson worked out the age of the Earth as around 4.55 billion years.

abschnitte.text: Some atoms are **radioactive**. They decay by themselves into other atoms, which are called **daughter isotopes**. The time in which half of an amount has decayed is called the **half-life**. It is fixed for each isotope and does not depend on heat or pressure. After one half-life, half is left; after two, a quarter; after **three, an eighth**. If you measure how much is still there, you can work out the age.

Living things take in carbon, including a little radioactive **carbon-14**. After death no new carbon is added, and the carbon-14 that is there decays. Its half-life is around 5,730 years. That is why the **radiocarbon method** only goes back to about 50,000 years. It is suitable for bones, wood or fabrics from prehistoric times. In Switzerland there is a laboratory at ETH Zurich that does such measurements.

For very old rocks, **uranium-238** is used, which decays into lead with a half-life of around 4.5 billion years. The mineral **zircon** is especially suitable. As it grows, it takes in uranium but hardly any lead, and it is very tough. The oldest dated mineral grains on Earth are zircons from the **Jack Hills** in Western Australia. They are around 4.4 billion years old.

In the **potassium-argon method**, potassium decays into the noble gas **argon**. In a hot melt, the argon escapes. Only when the rock solidifies is new argon trapped, so the clock starts at zero. That is why the method is well suited to **volcanic rocks**. In the **isochron method**, for example with rubidium and strontium, several samples are measured. This means you do not need to know how much of the daughter isotope was there at the start.

The American scientist **Clair Patterson** studied lead from **meteorites**. Meteorites are remains from the time when the Solar System formed. In 1956 he used them to work out the age of the Earth as around **4.55 billion years**. This value is still basically accepted today. During his work he noticed how much lead from petrol was in the environment, and he campaigned against leaded petrol.

gewusst: The chemist Willard Libby received the Nobel Prize in 1960 for the radiocarbon method.
In Switzerland, leaded petrol has been banned since 2000.

teile.einleitung: A rockfall net is a protective steel barrier that catches falling stones. In Switzerland such nets can often be seen above roads and railway lines in mountain valleys.
wichtigste: Rockfall nets catch falling stones before they hit roads or houses.
They are usually made of high-strength steel wire.
Braking elements in the cables absorb the force of the impact.
Anchors in the rock or ground hold the posts and cables in place.
How much energy a net can absorb is given in kilojoules.
After a rockfall, the net has to be emptied and checked.

abschnitte.text: In the mountains, the **freezing and thawing** of water in cracks in the rock loosens stones again and again. Water expands when it freezes and breaks the cracks open. When it thaws, the stones fall out. Along roads and railway lines in mountain valleys, this is dangerous. **Rockfall nets** are stretched between posts and the rock and catch the stones.

Modern nets are made of **high-strength steel wire** woven into rings or meshes. The net hangs from **posts** and long **support cables**. These are fixed with **anchors** drilled deep into the rock or ground. The anchors pass the forces of the impact into the ground. In this way the whole system can withstand enormous loads.

A falling stone has a lot of **kinetic energy**. It depends on its mass and its speed and is given in **joules** or **kilojoules**. So that the net does not tear, **braking elements** are built into the cables. They deform on impact and absorb the energy slowly. The net gives way like a safety net in a circus.

After a rockfall, the caught stones lie in the net. They put further strain on it, and it could fail at the next impact. That is why **experts** have to empty and check the net. Damaged parts and deformed braking elements are replaced. Even when nothing has happened, the nets are checked regularly.

gewusst: Rockfall nets are tested before they are used by dropping heavy concrete blocks into them on purpose.
Swiss companies are among the well-known makers of such protective nets.

teile.einleitung: An index fossil is a fossilised living thing that can be used to find out the age of rock layers. If the same index fossil is found in two places, the layers are about the same age. This method is called **biostratigraphy**.
wichtigste: A good index fossil comes from a species that lived only for a **short** time but was **widespread** and common.
Index fossils give a **relative age**: older, younger or the same age.
Around 1800, **William Smith** realised that layers can be compared by their fossils.
Important index fossils are graptolites, conodonts, belemnites and nummulites.
To get numbers in years, radiometric dating is needed as well.

abschnitte.text: Not every fossil is suitable as an index fossil. The species must have existed for only a **short time**, so that it marks a narrow period. It must also have been **widespread** and **common**, so that it can be found in places far apart. It also helps if it is easy to recognise. Sea creatures are especially suitable, because they could spread widely in the oceans.

Around 1800, the English geologist **William Smith** noticed that every rock layer has its typical fossils. The order of the fossils is the same everywhere. This principle is called **faunal succession**. In 1815 Smith published a geological map of the whole of England and Wales. **Biostratigraphy**, which divides layers into zones using fossils, is built on his idea.

**Graptolites** were colony-forming sea creatures that drifted in the plankton. They are important index fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian. **Conodonts** are tiny tooth-like parts of eel-like animals, useful from the Cambrian to the Triassic. **Belemnites** were cephalopods from the Jurassic and Cretaceous. Usually only their pointed rostrum made of calcite remains, popularly called a **thunderbolt**.

**Nummulites** are large single-celled organisms from the group of foraminifera. Their shell is shaped like a lens or a coin. The name comes from the Latin “nummulus”, meaning little coin. They are index fossils of the **Eocene** and are also found in limestones of the Swiss Alps. Sometimes whole rock layers are made almost entirely of them.

An index fossil alone does not tell you how many years old a layer is. It only shows whether it is **older, younger or the same age** as another layer. This is called a **relative age**. To get numbers in years, the decay of radioactive substances is also measured: this is called **radiometric dating**. Only together do they give an accurate timescale of Earth's history.

gewusst: Many boundaries between periods of Earth's history are defined by the first appearance of certain index fossils.
Conodonts were a mystery for a long time, until imprints of the whole eel-like animals were found.

teile.einleitung: A puddle is a small pool of water on the ground. It forms after rain and often disappears again after a few hours. Even so, a puddle is an important place for some animals.
wichtigste: Puddles form when rain collects in hollows.
On tarmac they stay for a long time because no water soaks away.
On sunny days a puddle evaporates.
In frost it freezes into ice.
In a calm puddle you can see your reflection.
Swallows, mosquitoes and yellow-bellied toads use puddles.

abschnitte.text: When it rains, the water flows into small dips in the ground. If it cannot **soak away** quickly there, a **puddle** is left. On meadows and forest floors the water usually disappears into the ground soon. **Tarmac** and concrete, on the other hand, are sealed. There the water stays until it runs off or evaporates. That is why there are especially many puddles on roads and squares after rain.

On a sunny day, a puddle gets smaller and smaller. The warmth of the sun makes the water **evaporate**. It becomes invisible **water vapour** in the air. On a frosty night something else happens: below 0 degrees, water turns into **ice**. In the morning the puddle is then often covered with a thin layer of ice. Be careful, it is easy to slip on it.

If you look into a calm puddle, you see your **reflection** and the sky. The smooth surface of the water reflects the light like a mirror. Sometimes a little oil floats on a puddle at the side of the road. This very thin layer makes the light shimmer in colourful **rainbow colours**. It looks pretty, but it shows that oil has got into the water.

**Swallows** collect wet mud from puddles. They shape it into small balls and use them to stick their nests, for example under a roof. **Mosquitoes** like to lay their eggs in still water; even a small puddle or water butt can be enough. In Switzerland, the rare **yellow-bellied toad** likes to lay its eggs in small, warm puddles, for example in tyre tracks on forest paths. It has a grey back and a belly with yellow spots.

gewusst: The yellow-bellied toad needs small puddles where no fish live.
Swallows build their nests from hundreds of little balls of mud.
Jumping in puddles is fun, best of all in wellies.

teile.einleitung: A **snowfield** is a large area of lying snow. In the high mountains of Switzerland, snowfields can often be found well into summer. They are beautiful, but also dangerous when hiking.
wichtigste: A snowfield is a large area of lying snow.
In high mountains, snow stays on the ground in summer because it is colder there.
It is easy to slip on steep snowfields.
Old, grainy snow that has survived a summer is called firn.
A glacier can form from snowfields over many years.
The bright snow reflects sunlight, so you need sunglasses and sun cream.

abschnitte.text: The higher you climb, the **colder** the air becomes. That is why in high mountains it is so cold that not all the snow melts in summer. **Snowfields** stay for a long time especially in shady hollows and on north-facing slopes. Their **meltwater** fills streams and rivers in summer. In this way snowfields supply water for plants, animals and people in the valley.

Snow that has survived at least one summer becomes grainy and firmer. It is called **firn**. If more and more snow stays on the ground over many years, the firn is pressed together by the weight. In the end this turns into **glacier ice**. In this way a **glacier** can form from snowfields over a long time.

A **steep snowfield** is dangerous. The snow can be slippery or frozen hard. Anyone who slips can slide down quickly and a long way, often onto rocks. Especially in the morning, after a cold night, the snow is often hard. That is why it is better to go around steep snowfields, or only cross them with good equipment and an experienced companion.

Snow is bright and **reflects sunlight**. That is why on a snowfield the sun hits you twice over: from above and from below. At altitude the sun's radiation is also stronger. So you get **sunburn** quickly. **Sunglasses** protect your eyes, and sun cream protects your skin.

gewusst: Without sunglasses, the glaring light on snow can irritate your eyes so much that you cannot see well for a while. This is called snow blindness.
Tiny algae sometimes grow on old snowfields and turn the snow reddish.

teile.einleitung: The Ticino is the most important river in the canton of Ticino, which is named after it. It rises near the Nufenen Pass, flows through Lake Maggiore and joins the Po in Italy.
wichtigste: The Ticino rises near the Nufenen Pass.
The canton of Ticino is named after the river.
Between Airolo and Biasca it flows through the Leventina.
It flows through Bellinzona, the capital of the canton.
It flows into Lake Maggiore between Locarno and Bellinzona.
Near Pavia it joins the Po, the longest river in Italy.

abschnitte.text: The **Ticino** rises near the **Nufenen Pass** in the north of Ticino. First it flows east through the **Bedretto Valley**. At **Airolo**, at the foot of the Gotthard, it turns south. The canton of **Ticino** bears the name of this river. In German the river is also called Tessin, just like the canton.

Between Airolo and **Biasca** the Ticino flows through the **Leventina**. This is the main valley of upper Ticino. The **Gotthard motorway** and the **Gotthard railway** also run through this long valley. In several places the river drops over steep valley steps. At Biasca the Brenno joins it from the Blenio Valley.

Further south the Ticino flows through **Bellinzona**, the **capital** of the canton of Ticino. The town lies at a narrow point in the valley. Its **three castles** once guarded the route over the Alpine passes. They are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Below Bellinzona the valley becomes wide and flat; this plain is called the Magadino Plain.

Between **Locarno** and Bellinzona the Ticino flows into **Lake Maggiore**. At **Sesto Calende** in Italy it leaves the lake again. After that it flows through the Po Valley and joins the **Po** near **Pavia**. The Po is the longest river in Italy and flows into the Adriatic Sea. In this way water from the Swiss Alps reaches the Mediterranean.

gewusst: The water of the Ticino ends up in the Adriatic, while the Rhine flows into the North Sea and the Rhône into the Mediterranean in France.
In the Bedretto Valley the Ticino is only a few kilometres away from the source areas of the Rhône and the Reuss.

teile.einleitung: The **Swiss Seismological Service**, or SED for short, monitors all earthquakes in Switzerland and the neighbouring countries. It is part of ETH Zurich and informs the authorities and the public when the ground shakes.
wichtigste: The SED grew out of the Earthquake Commission, which was founded in 1878.
Since 1914, earthquake monitoring has been set out in a federal law.
The SED runs more than 200 seismic measuring stations.
On average, 10 to 20 earthquakes a year can be felt in Switzerland.
The first automatic information about a quake appears within about 90 seconds.
Reports from magnitude 2.5 appear in the MeteoSwiss app.

abschnitte.text: As early as 1878, an **Earthquake Commission** was founded in Switzerland. Today's **Swiss Seismological Service** grew out of it. Since **1914**, earthquake monitoring has been set out in a **federal law**. Today the service is part of **ETH Zurich**. It is the federal government's specialist office for earthquakes. (The abbreviation SED comes from its German name.)

The SED runs **more than 200 seismic measuring stations**. They are spread all over Switzerland, often in tunnels or remote places. The instruments also record very weak quakes that nobody feels. On average only **10 to 20 earthquakes** a year in Switzerland can be **felt** by people. Quakes are especially common in Valais, the Grisons and the Basel area.

After a quake, the SED publishes the first automatic information **within about 90 seconds**: where the quake was and how strong it was. Then experts check the data. Reports from **magnitude 2.5** also appear in the **MeteoSwiss app**. In this way the authorities and the public quickly find out what has happened.

When large damaging earthquakes happen abroad, the SED also informs the **Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit**. This lets Switzerland send help more quickly. In the **Dischma Valley** near Davos, the SED runs a special measuring station. It is used to monitor the **nuclear test ban**: it can also detect underground nuclear tests anywhere in the world.

The SED also studies how great the **earthquake hazard** is in Switzerland. This produces maps that show where strong quakes are more likely. They help with **earthquake-proof building**. The strongest known earthquake in Switzerland destroyed large parts of **Basel** in 1356.

gewusst: Every year, the SED's instruments record well over a thousand earthquakes in Switzerland and the border area; nobody feels most of them.
On the SED website, anyone can report whether they felt an earthquake and how strongly.

teile.einleitung: A **Rüfe** is a debris flow: a fast stream of mud, rubble and water that shoots down a steep stream. The word is used mainly in the Grisons and in Liechtenstein.
wichtigste: A Rüfe is a debris flow of mud, stones and water.
The word is especially common in Liechtenstein and the Grisons.
Rüfen happen mainly in summer after strong thunderstorms.
Debris basins catch stones and rubble.
Torrent barriers reduce the slope and slow the Rüfe down.
A dense forest protects steep slopes best.

abschnitte.text: In a **Rüfe**, it is not just water that slides down the valley, but a thick mush of mud, sand, stones and sometimes whole boulders. Experts call this a **debris flow**. A Rüfe can be very fast and have great force. It can bury roads, damage bridges and threaten houses. That is why it is one of the most important natural hazards in the mountains.

Rüfen (the plural) are especially common in the Alps in **summer**. Strong thunderstorms bring a lot of rain in a short time. Snowmelt can also soak the ground. If there is then a lot of loose rubble in a steep stream bed, the water can sweep it away. In this way a small stream turns into a dangerous torrent within a few minutes.

In **Liechtenstein**, the word “Rüfe” is especially well known. Many small streams flow down the steep slopes into the Rhine Valley there. All these **Rüfe streams** belong to the catchment area of the **Rhine**. Because villages lie right at the foot of the slopes, protective structures have been built on many streams.

A **debris basin** is a large basin in which stones and rubble are left behind while the water flows on. **Torrent barriers** are structures across the stream bed: they reduce the slope and so slow down the Rüfe. Through villages, Rüfe streams are often led in **concrete channels**, so that the rubble flows away quickly and in a controlled way. A **dense forest** is also very important: the roots of the trees hold the soil in place.

gewusst: A debris flow can carry boulders as big as a car.
After big storms, debris basins often have to be emptied with diggers so that they have room again next time.

teile.einleitung: The polarising microscope is a special microscope that experts use to study minerals and rocks. It works with polarised light. In it, many minerals show bright colours by which they can be recognised.
wichtigste: The microscope has two polarising filters: the polariser below and the analyser above.
With crossed polarisers, the two filters are at right angles to each other.
Isotropic minerals such as garnet stay dark all the time between crossed polarisers.
The double refraction of anisotropic minerals produces the interference colours.
An anisotropic mineral goes dark four times during one full turn.
The Michel-Lévy chart links double refraction, section thickness and interference colour.
Interference figures are viewed with the Bertrand lens.

abschnitte.text: What is studied is usually **thin sections**: wafer-thin slices of rock that light can pass through. Under the rotating stage sits the **polariser**. It only lets through light that vibrates in one direction. Above it is a second filter, the **analyser**. When the two are at right angles to each other, they are called **crossed polarisers**. Without a sample, the picture then stays black.

Many minerals are **anisotropic**: light behaves differently in them depending on the direction. They split the light into two rays; this is called **double refraction**. Between crossed polarisers this produces **interference colours**. The **Michel-Lévy chart** shows how double refraction, section thickness and colour are connected. **Calcite** has a very high double refraction and shows pale, creamy colours of high order.

**Isotropic** minerals such as **garnet** bend light in the same way in all directions. Between crossed polarisers they stay dark all the time as the stage is turned. Anisotropic minerals go dark **four times** during one full turn; this is called **extinction**. The type of extinction also helps to identify a mineral.

Some minerals change colour when turned even under just one polariser. This is called **pleochroism**; a typical example is the dark mica **biotite**. **Plagioclase** often shows fine, parallel stripes between crossed polarisers. These are twin stripes, caused by crystal parts grown together. In this way common minerals can be recognised quickly.

In **conoscopic** viewing, a strongly focused beam of light is sent through the crystal. With an extra lens, the **Bertrand lens**, you then see **interference figures**. These patterns of crosses and coloured rings show how the optical axes lie in the crystal. They make it possible to tell apart even minerals that look alike. Polarising microscopes are part of the basic equipment in geology and mineralogy.

gewusst: A thin section is usually only about 0.03 millimetres thick, thinner than a hair.
Plastics and glass also show colourful patterns in polarised light when they are under strain.

teile.einleitung: A cliff coast is a coast where the land drops into the sea in a steep rock face. The waves constantly gnaw at the rock and so change the coast bit by bit.
wichtigste: A steep rock face by the sea is also called a cliff.
Cliff coasts form because the waves hollow out the rock at the bottom until it breaks off.
The white chalk cliffs of Dover in England and on the island of Rügen are famous.
Arches and sea stacks can form from rocky headlands.
Many seabirds, such as puffins, nest on cliff coasts.
It is dangerous at the edge of a cliff, because the edge can break off.

abschnitte.text: On a cliff coast, the waves crash against the rock again and again. With water, sand and stones they hollow out the bottom of the wall. This creates a **wave-cut notch**, a groove at the foot of the wall. At some point the upper part has nothing left to hold it, and it breaks off. Then everything starts again, and the coast slowly moves inland. Such a steep wall is called a **cliff**.

Some cliff coasts are made of **chalk**, a soft, white limestone. It formed from the tiny chalky shells of sea creatures. The white cliffs of **Dover** in England are very famous. You can see them from far away from a ship. On the German island of **Rügen** in the Baltic Sea, pale chalk cliffs also rise steeply above the sea. Because chalk is soft, it breaks off especially easily.

When a rocky headland sticks out into the sea, the waves attack it from both sides. Over time they wash a hole right through it, and an arch forms. It is called a **sea arch**. If the roof of the arch collapses, a single column of rock is left standing in the sea. It is called a **sea stack**. In this way cliff coasts show how the sea shapes the landscape.

Cliff coasts are important nesting places for **seabirds**. In the rocks they are safe from many enemies. In the north, for example in Iceland, **puffins** nest, with their colourful, orange-striped beaks. They dig burrows in the soil at the top of the cliffs. For people, on the other hand, the edge is dangerous, because the sea hollows out the rocks from below and the edge can suddenly **break off**.

gewusst: Switzerland has no sea, but rivers and lakes can also wash out steep walls along their banks.
Some cliffs move back by a few tens of centimetres every year, because pieces keep breaking off.

teile.einleitung: **Sandstone** is a rock made of grains of sand that have been stuck together over a long time. In Switzerland it is especially well known from the old town of Bern, much of which is built of it.
wichtigste: Sandstone is made of grains of sand stuck together.
It formed from the sand of beaches, rivers or deserts.
Much of Bern's old town is built of sandstone.
Sandstone is easy to work, which is why sculptors like it.
Wind and rain wear it down, so that it crumbles over time.
Sandstone can be yellow, red or grey.

abschnitte.text: A very long time ago, a lot of sand was deposited on **beaches**, in **rivers** or in **deserts**. New layers kept coming on top. The weight pressed the sand together. Substances dissolved in the water acted like **glue** and stuck the grains together. In this way loose sand turned into solid stone. Sandstone is a **sedimentary rock**.

Sandstone can be **yellow**, **red**, **grey** or greenish. The colour depends on which substances are between the grains. Iron compounds often colour it red or brown. The famous rock **Uluru** in Australia is made of sandstone and glows especially red at sunset. Bernese sandstone, on the other hand, is mostly grey to greenish.

Much of the **old town of Bern** is built of sandstone, including **Bern Minster**. The stone comes from the surrounding area and is easy to cut. **Sculptors** have also liked working with it, because it is easy to shape. Many figures on churches and fountains are carved from sandstone.

Sandstone is not particularly hard. Over time, **wind and rain** wear it down, and frost can also break it apart. If you rub your finger hard over old sandstone, single **grains of sand** often come loose. That is why old sandstone buildings have to be repaired again and again. Stonemasons then replace damaged stones with new ones.

gewusst: Uluru in Australia is a sacred place for the country's Aboriginal people.
Work goes on almost all the time on Bern Minster, because the sandstone keeps needing repairs.

teile.einleitung: The water in the sea is salty; the water in Swiss lakes and rivers is not. A litre of seawater contains about 35 grams of salt. This has exciting effects when swimming and when drinking.
wichtigste: A litre of seawater contains about 35 grams of salt.
You must not drink seawater; it makes you even thirstier.
It is easier to swim in salt water than in fresh water.
In the Dead Sea you float on top almost by yourself.
Sea salt is obtained by letting seawater evaporate in the sun.
Water with very little salt is called fresh water.

abschnitte.text: About **35 grams of salt** are dissolved in a litre of **seawater**. That is about seven teaspoons. The water in **lakes and rivers**, on the other hand, contains only very little salt. It is called **fresh water**; in German it is called “Süsswasser”, meaning “sweet water”, even though it does not taste sweet. The word simply means not salty.

If you are thirsty, you must not drink seawater. It contains so much salt that the body needs extra water to get rid of the salt again. So you become even **thirstier**. That is why sailors on ships always take drinking water with them or make it from seawater with machines.

Salt water is heavier than fresh water. That is why it **holds you up** better. So it is easier to swim in the sea than in a Swiss lake. In the **Dead Sea** between Israel and Jordan, the water is so salty that you float on top almost by yourself. You can even lie on your back there and read a newspaper.

**Sea salt** is obtained in shallow basins: seawater is left to **evaporate** in the sun, and the salt stays behind. There is no sea in Switzerland. Here the salt comes from the **ground**. It formed from an **ancient sea** that dried out many millions of years ago. Today it is brought up from the depths, for example on the Rhine and at Bex.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea, the water is almost ten times as salty as in the ocean.
The salt in Switzerland is many millions of years old.

teile.einleitung: The Tethys was a prehistoric ocean between the great land masses of Eurasia and Gondwana. Its deposits are found today high up in the Alps and the Himalayas.
wichtigste: The Tethys is named after a Greek sea goddess.
Eduard Suess coined the name in 1893.
It lay as a bay open to the east in the supercontinent Pangaea.
Before it there was the Palaeo-Tethys, and later the Neo-Tethys.
In the Jurassic, the Alpine Tethys opened together with the Central Atlantic.
Radiolarite and ophiolites in the Grisons are remains of the Tethys Ocean.

abschnitte.text: In Greek mythology, **Tethys** was a Titan and a **sea goddess**. In **1893**, the geologist **Eduard Suess** gave her name to a prehistoric sea. He had realised that marine deposits in the Alps and the Himalayas pointed to a large ocean. It lay between **Eurasia** in the north and **Gondwana** in the south.

Around 250 million years ago, the continents were joined in the supercontinent **Pangaea**. It was roughly shaped like a **C**, with its opening facing east. The sea in this bay was the Tethys. Around Pangaea lay the great world ocean **Panthalassa**. First there was the **Palaeo-Tethys**. It closed while the **Neo-Tethys** opened further south.

In the **Jurassic**, another ocean tore open between Europe and the Adriatic Plate. It is called the **Alpine Tethys** or **Piedmont-Liguria Ocean**. It opened at the same time as the **Central Atlantic** and was, in a way, its eastern continuation. Later it closed again as Africa and Europe came closer. This is how the Alps formed.

In the Alps there are rocks from the former sea floor. **Radiolarite** is made of the silica shells of tiny plankton creatures, the radiolarians. It was deposited at great depth. **Ophiolites** are remains of ocean crust. The **Platta nappe** in the Oberhalbstein in the Grisons contains serpentinite and pillow lavas from the floor of the Alpine Tethys.

In the warm, shallow Tethys, large limestone reefs grew in the **Triassic**. Organisms built them up over a long time. By taking in magnesium, they later turned into **dolomite**. This rock gave its name to the **Dolomites** in Italy. So their striking rocky mountains are former reefs.

gewusst: Today's Mediterranean is often seen as a small remnant of the great Tethys.
In the Swiss Alps you can find fossilised sea creatures from the Tethys, for example ammonites.
