teile.einleitung: An omega block is a special weather pattern in which a strong high stays in the same place for a long time. On the weather map, the air flow then looks like the Greek letter omega. It can bring weeks of heat, but continuous rain in other places.
wichtigste: The upper-level flow looks like the Greek capital letter Ω.
A high lies between two lows.
The omega block is one of the blocking weather patterns.
In the high, it stays dry and hot for a long time in summer.
Under the lows on its flanks, it often rains for days.
The heatwaves of 2003 in Europe and 2010 in Russia were linked to blocks.

abschnitte.titel: A letter on the weather map
abschnitte.text: On the **upper-air weather map**, lines show how the air flows a few kilometres up. In an omega block, the flow goes around a strong **high** in a wide arc to the north. To the left and right of it, it bends southwards. Together this looks like the Greek capital letter **omega** (Ω). That is how the weather pattern got its name.

In the centre is a strong high, with a **low** on each side, one to the west and one to the east. This arrangement is very stable. Normally lows travel from the Atlantic to Europe with the **westerly flow**. The omega block blocks this flow, and the lows are steered around the high. That is why it is counted among the **blocking weather patterns**. It can last for a week or longer.

abschnitte.titel: Heat in the high, rain at the edge
abschnitte.text: In the high, air sinks, and clouds dissolve as it does so. In summer, **heat** and drought can build up in this way over many days. The two lows on the flanks also stay in the same place for a long time. That is why it often rains for days under them, which can cause **flooding**. So an omega block brings very different weather depending on where you are.

In **August 2003**, a stationary high lay over central Europe. It brought weeks of heat and drought, in Switzerland too. At that time new temperature records were measured in Switzerland, and many glaciers lost a lot of ice. In summer **2010**, a high over western Russia blocked the westerly flow. Around **Moscow** there was record heat and large forest and peat fires.

Omega blocks are a challenge for weather services. Weather models find it hard to get the timing right for when a block forms and especially when it **breaks down**. That is why the uncertainty is higher than with ordinary westerly patterns. Often the block lasts longer than the models first calculate.

gewusst: An omega block can bring heat to one country and floods to the neighbouring country at the same time.
The name simply comes from the shape of the lines on the weather map.
Blocking highs steer lows from the Atlantic far to the north or south.

teile.einleitung: Vulcano is a small volcanic island in the Mediterranean north of Sicily. It belongs to Italy and is one of the Aeolian Islands. Our word volcano comes from its name.
wichtigste: Vulcano belongs to Italy and lies north of Sicily.
The island is one of the Aeolian Islands, the largest of which is called Lipari.
It is named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
The word volcano comes from the island’s name.
The last eruption lasted from 1888 to 1890.
Many visitors bathe in warm mud on the island.
You reach Vulcano by boat.

abschnitte.titel: The workshop of the fire god
abschnitte.text: The ancient Romans worshipped **Vulcan**, the god of fire and of blacksmiths. They believed his forge lay under the island. They thought the smoke and fire from the mountain were the fire of his forge. That is why they called the island Vulcano. Later this name gave us the word **volcano** for all fire-spitting mountains.

Vulcano is one of the **Lipari Islands**, which are also called the Aeolian Islands. They lie in the Mediterranean north of **Sicily** and belong to **Italy**. The largest island in the group is called **Lipari**. The island of Stromboli with its very active volcano also belongs to it. Vulcano is the southernmost of the islands and lies closest to Sicily.

The last eruption on Vulcano lasted from **1888 to 1890**. At that time many lumps of rock flew through the air. Since then the volcano has been quiet. But it is not extinct and is closely **monitored** by experts. Gases rise from the ground and from the large crater, the **Gran Cratere**.

In many places on Vulcano it smells of **rotten eggs**. This comes from **sulphur gases** rising from the ground. Near the harbour there is a pool of warm **mud** in which many people bathe. In the sea next to it, gas bubbles up from the bottom in some places. There is no bridge to the mainland, so you get to the island by **ferry** or hydrofoil.

gewusst: A certain type of explosive eruption is named after the island in scientific language: a Vulcanian eruption.
The Aeolian Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: A roche moutonnée is a hump of rock that a glacier has ground down. Such rocks are found wherever there used to be ice, in the Swiss Alps too. They reveal the direction in which the ice flowed.
wichtigste: A roche moutonnée is a hump of rock ground down by a glacier.
The side the glacier came from is gently sloping and ground smooth.
The sheltered side facing away is steep, rough and stepped.
Glacial striations show in which direction the ice flowed.
On the sheltered side, ice frozen to the rock tears out blocks.
In German a roche moutonnée is called a “Rundhöcker”.
Small islands of roches moutonnées off Scandinavia are called skerries.

abschnitte.text: Glaciers are heavy and move slowly down the valley. Sand and stones are stuck in their underside. Like sandpaper, they rub over the rock beneath. If a hump of rock sticks up there, it is ground round. This creates a **roche moutonnée** (in German “Rundhöcker”, round hump). When the glacier later melts, the shaped rock comes to light.

A roche moutonnée has two very different sides. The side the glacier came from is called the **stoss side**. It is **gently sloping and ground smooth**. The other side, which faced away from the glacier, is called the **lee side**. It is **steep, rough and stepped**. Even thousands of years later, this shows where the ice came from.

Something different happens on the lee side from the stoss side. Meltwater gets into cracks in the rock and freezes there again. The **ice frozen to the rock** holds pieces of it tight. When the glacier moves on, it **tears out blocks**. This creates the rough, stepped breaks. Experts call this process **plucking**.

On many roches moutonnées you can see fine scratches, the **glacial striations**. They were made when stones in the ice scraped over the rock. All the striations run in roughly the same direction. That is why they reveal **in which direction the ice flowed**. In this way researchers can reconstruct the movement of glaciers that disappeared long ago.

In the Alps there are especially many roches moutonnées in **cirques** and on **passes**. A cirque is a hollow on a mountainside where a small glacier used to lie. In Switzerland, fine examples can be seen at the Grimsel, for example. The French name is **roche moutonnée**. Off the coasts of Scandinavia, many small roches moutonnées stick out of the sea as islands. They are called **skerries**.

gewusst: The term “roche moutonnée” goes back to the Geneva naturalist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure.
From a distance, groups of roches moutonnées look like a flock of sheep lying down.

teile.einleitung: A tornado is a violent whirlwind that reaches from a thundercloud to the ground as a rotating tube of air. It is often only a few hundred metres wide, but it can reach wind speeds of more than 400 kilometres per hour. This makes it one of the most destructive weather events on Earth.
wichtigste: A tornado is a rotating column of air between a thundercloud and the ground.
Tornadoes form from cumulonimbus clouds, that is, large thunderclouds.
The strength of a tornado is given on the Fujita scale.
In Tornado Alley in the USA there are especially many tornadoes.
A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a waterspout.
Tornadoes usually last only a few minutes.
Tornadoes also occur in Europe and in Switzerland, but much less often.

abschnitte.text: A tornado is a small but very violent **whirlwind**. It looks like a trunk or funnel reaching down from a dark thundercloud to the ground. You can see the funnel because water vapour condenses into droplets inside it and because dust and debris are whirled up. A tornado usually lasts only a few minutes, rarely more than an hour. In German it is also called a **Windhose**.

Tornadoes form from **cumulonimbus clouds**, that is, from huge thunderclouds. **Supercells** are especially dangerous: long-lasting thunderstorms with a rotating updraft. This needs warm, moist air near the ground, cooler air higher up and winds that change direction and strength with height. Then the air can draw together into a narrow whirl that reaches the ground. Meteorologists are still researching exactly how this happens.

Most of the world’s tornadoes occur in the USA, about 1000 to 1200 a year. Especially many occur in **Tornado Alley** in the middle of the country, for example in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas. There warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico meets dry, cool air from the north and west. That is why many houses have a storm cellar. Weather services issue tornado warnings by radio, mobile phone and sirens.

The strength of a tornado is given on the **Fujita scale**, which the Japanese-American researcher Tetsuya Theodore Fujita developed in 1971. It ranges from F0 for light damage to F5 for devastating destruction. Because wind speed can rarely be measured directly, it is estimated from the damage. Since 2007 an improved version, the Enhanced Fujita scale, has been used in the USA. Strong tornadoes can destroy houses and hurl cars through the air.

A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a **waterspout**. Water is whirled up as spray, and a tube of water droplets becomes visible. Waterspouts are usually weaker than tornadoes over land. They can occasionally be seen on Swiss lakes too, for example on Lake Constance or Lake Maggiore. If a waterspout moves onto land, it becomes a tornado.

In Europe too there are hundreds of tornadoes every year, but most are weak. In Switzerland tornadoes are rare. The strongest known Swiss tornado swept through the **Vallée de Joux** in the Vaud Jura on 19 August 1926 and destroyed houses and large areas of forest. If you see a tornado, you should immediately seek shelter in a cellar or a windowless room on the ground floor.

begriffe.erklaerung: Huge thundercloud that towers high into the sky.
Especially strong, long-lasting thunderstorm with a rotating updraft.
Scale from F0 to F5 used to give the strength of a tornado.
Tornado over a lake or the sea.

gewusst: The highest wind speed ever measured in a tornado was almost 500 kilometres per hour, measured by radar in Oklahoma in 1999.
In the northern hemisphere tornadoes usually turn anticlockwise.
A tornado can completely destroy one house and leave the house next door almost undamaged.

teile.einleitung: Oceans are the huge seas that cover most of the Earth. They affect the weather, the climate and life all over the world. Switzerland has no coast, but its rivers connect it with several seas.
wichtigste: Oceans cover about seven tenths of the Earth's surface.
The Pacific is the largest ocean, and the Arctic Ocean the smallest.
The Indian Ocean lies between Africa and Australia.
Pacific means “the peaceful one”.
The sea closest to Switzerland is the Mediterranean.
Seawater is salty.

abschnitte.text: About **seven tenths** of the Earth's surface is covered by sea. That is why the Earth looks blue from space. Usually five oceans are counted: the **Pacific**, the **Atlantic**, the **Indian Ocean**, the **Arctic Ocean** and the **Southern Ocean** around Antarctica. They are all connected. The water in the sea is **salty**, because rivers have been carrying dissolved minerals into it for millions of years.

The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean. It lies between America, Asia and Australia. The seafarer **Magellan** found calm weather there and so called it the **peaceful** ocean. The **Atlantic** separates Europe and Africa from America. The **Indian Ocean** lies south of India and stretches from Africa to Australia. Around the North Pole lies the **Arctic Ocean**, the smallest ocean, which is often covered with ice.

On average the oceans are almost four kilometres deep. The deepest point is in the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific, almost 11 kilometres below the surface. There it is completely dark and icy cold, and the water pressure is enormous. Even so, animals live there. Large parts of the sea floor are still less accurately explored than the surface of the Moon.

Switzerland has no sea coast. The nearest sea is the **Mediterranean**: from Ticino to the coast at Genoa in Italy is only about 150 kilometres. But Switzerland is connected with several seas through its rivers. The **Rhine** flows into the North Sea, which belongs to the Atlantic. The **Rhône** flows into the Mediterranean. The **Inn** flows into the Danube and so into the Black Sea, and the **Ticino** flows via the Po into the Adriatic.

Countless living things live in the ocean, from tiny **plankton** to the **blue whale**, the largest animal on Earth. Tiny algae in the sea produce a large share of the oxygen we breathe. The oceans also store a lot of heat and so affect the climate. Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream bring warm water to Europe.

gewusst: Water from Switzerland flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic and the Black Sea.
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is high.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake, different waves spread through the Earth. The **S-wave** is one of them: it shakes the rock at right angles to the direction it travels and arrives after the P-wave.
wichtigste: The S stands for “secondary”, because the S-wave arrives second.
In an S-wave, the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel.
S-waves cannot travel through liquids, because the shear modulus there is zero.
In typical rock, P-waves are about 1.7 times as fast as S-waves.
If the particles vibrate horizontally, they are called SH-waves.
S-waves often cause more damage to buildings than P-waves.

abschnitte.text: The S-wave is also called a **shear wave** or **transverse wave**. The particles of the rock move **at right angles** to the direction in which the wave travels. You can imagine it like a rope that you shake up and down. If the particles vibrate horizontally, they are called **SH-waves**; if they vibrate in a vertical plane, they are called **SV-waves**. The S stands for **secondary**: this wave is the second to arrive at the measuring station.

An S-wave needs a material that resists being sheared. This property is called the **shear modulus**. In liquids and gases the shear modulus is zero, which is why there are no S-waves there. This fact helped researchers to realise that the **outer core is liquid**: S-waves do not get through it.

In typical rock, **P-waves** are about 1.7 times as fast as S-waves. That is why in an earthquake the P-waves arrive first and the S-waves afterwards. From the time difference between the two, experts can calculate how far away the focus of the earthquake is. When a P-wave hits a boundary between layers at a slant, **reflected and refracted S-waves** can also form.

S-waves often have **bigger swings** than P-waves and shake the ground sideways. Many buildings cope well with vertical forces, but less well with sideways shaking. That is why S-waves often cause more damage. In earthquake-proof building, people try to strengthen houses against such sideways forces.

Sometimes an S-wave splits into two waves in the rock that travel at different speeds. This is called **shear wave splitting**. It shows that the **minerals in the rock are lined up**. In this way researchers learn something about how the rock deep inside the Earth has moved or been deformed.

gewusst: The fact that S-waves do not cross the Earth's core is one of the most important clues that the outer core is liquid.
When you feel an earthquake, you often notice a short jolt first and then a stronger shaking: these are the P-wave and the S-wave.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is a star, and in fact the star that is closest to us. It gives the Earth light and warmth and so makes life possible at all. Without the Sun, our planet would be a dark, icy-cold ball.
wichtigste: The Sun is a star made of hot gas, mainly hydrogen and helium.
It is around 150 million kilometres from the Earth.
The Sun gives us light and warmth.
In the morning it rises in the east, and in the evening it sets in the west.
Day and night happen because the Earth spins once around itself every day.
You must never look straight at the Sun, because it damages your eyes.
In summer, sun cream protects your skin from sunburn.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a **star**, a huge ball of glowing gas. Its diameter is about 109 times that of the Earth, and more than a million Earths would fit inside it. It stands at the centre of our **Solar System**, and all the planets travel around it. The Sun is around 4.6 billion years old. It will keep shining like this for about another 5 billion years.

Inside the Sun it is around 15 million degrees Celsius hot. There, hydrogen particles fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. This releases an enormous amount of energy, which shines out into space as light and heat. At its surface the Sun is about 5,500 degrees hot. Darker, slightly cooler spots on the surface are called **sunspots**.

Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel the roughly 150 million kilometres to the Earth. Because the Earth spins once around itself every day, the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west. The Earth takes a year to go once around the Sun. Because the Earth's axis is tilted, Switzerland gets more sunlight, falling more steeply, in summer than in winter. This is how the **seasons** come about.

Plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from water and carbon dioxide; this is called **photosynthesis**. Almost all animals, and we humans too, live on this directly or indirectly. The Sun also drives the weather and the water cycle. In our skin, sunlight helps to make vitamin D, which is important for healthy bones.

With **solar cells**, sunlight can be turned directly into electricity. In Switzerland you see more and more solar panels on house roofs, barns and even on dam walls. Solar collectors use the Sun's rays to heat water for showers and heating. Solar energy is renewable, because it will not run out for billions of years.

The Sun also sends out invisible **UV rays**, which can cause sunburn. Sun cream, a hat, a T-shirt and shade protect your skin. In the mountains, UV radiation is especially strong, even when it is cool. Never look straight at the Sun, not even with sunglasses, because this can damage your eyes permanently. A solar eclipse should only be watched with special protective glasses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge ball of hot gas that gives off its own light.
A process in which light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones, releasing energy.
Plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from water and carbon dioxide.
Invisible sunlight that can cause sunburn.

gewusst: When you see the Sun, you see it as it was about 8 minutes ago.
The Sun contains more than 99 per cent of the total mass of our Solar System.
In a total solar eclipse, the Moon moves exactly in front of the Sun, and it gets dark in the middle of the day.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect makes sure that the Earth is a pleasantly warm planet. Certain gases in the air hold on to heat, similar to the glass roof of a greenhouse. Because people are releasing more and more of these gases, the effect is getting stronger and the Earth is warming up.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases hold back the Earth’s heat radiation in the atmosphere.
Without the natural greenhouse effect it would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius on Earth on average.
With it the average temperature is about plus 15 degrees Celsius.
Carbon dioxide is the greenhouse gas that people release in the largest amounts.
Methane is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows.
The extra greenhouse effect caused by people leads to climate change.
The Paris climate agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground and the seas. The warm Earth gives off this energy again as invisible **heat radiation**. Part of it is absorbed by **greenhouse gases** in the air and radiated back towards the Earth. So more heat stays near the Earth’s surface. This is similar to a greenhouse, where it is warmer than outside, or to a blanket that keeps you warm.

The natural greenhouse effect is very important for life on Earth. Without it the average temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius, and the Earth would be an ice planet. Thanks to it, the average is about plus 15 degrees. The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**. Carbon dioxide also occurs naturally in the air, for example from volcanoes and the breathing of living things.

Since industrialisation, people have been burning large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas. This mainly produces **carbon dioxide**, CO2 for short, the greenhouse gas that people release in the largest amounts. Its share in the air has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to more than 420 ppm (as of 2024). **Methane** is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows, in rice fields and at rubbish tips. Cutting down forests also strengthens the greenhouse effect, because trees store CO2.

The French researcher Joseph Fourier suspected as early as 1824 that the atmosphere warms the Earth. Around 1859 the Irishman John Tyndall proved in the laboratory that gases such as water vapour and CO2 absorb heat radiation. In 1896 the Swede **Svante Arrhenius** was the first to calculate that more CO2 would warm the Earth. Today thousands of researchers in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the **IPCC**, sum up what is known about the climate.

On average the Earth is clearly warmer today than before industrialisation. In Switzerland the temperature has even risen about twice as much as the global average since measurements began in 1864. The glaciers in the Alps are melting, and heatwaves and heavy rain are becoming more frequent. Sea level is rising because ice melts and warm water expands. Many animal and plant species have to move to higher or cooler areas.

In the **Paris climate agreement** of 2015, almost all countries committed to keeping warming well below 2 degrees and, if possible, limiting it to 1.5 degrees. In 2023 Swiss voters approved a law under which Switzerland should emit no more greenhouse gases on balance by 2050. This needs renewable energy such as solar, wind and hydropower. Everyone can help too, for example by cycling, using public transport, eating less meat and producing less rubbish.

begriffe.erklaerung: Gas in the air that absorbs and holds back the Earth’s heat radiation.
Gas produced when coal, oil, gas and wood are burned, CO2 for short.
Greenhouse gas that is produced, for example, when cows digest their food.
Long-term change in the climate, today above all the warming caused by people.
Parts per million, used to say how much of a gas there is in the air.

gewusst: Over a period of a hundred years, methane is about 25 to 30 times stronger per kilogram than carbon dioxide.
Venus has an extreme greenhouse effect, which is why it is more than 400 degrees hot there.
Swiss glaciers have lost more than half of their ice since 1850.

teile.einleitung: The Milankovitch cycles are slow, regular changes in the Earth's orbit and axis. They change how much sunlight falls on the Earth, when and where. In this way they explain the rhythm of the ice ages.
wichtigste: They are named after **Milutin Milanković**, a professor in Belgrade.
The **tilt of the Earth's axis** varies between 22.1° and 24.5° over about 41,000 years.
**Precession** has a period of around 23,000 years.
The **eccentricity** of the Earth's orbit changes over around 100,000 and 405,000 years.
What matters most is the **summer sunshine** at high northern latitudes.
About a million years ago, the ice age rhythm changed from 41,000 to 100,000 years.

abschnitte.text: **Milutin Milanković** was a Serbian mathematician and engineer. He was a professor at the University of **Belgrade**. In years of work by hand, he calculated how much sunlight fell on different latitudes of the Earth over hundreds of thousands of years. From this he developed a theory of how the Earth's orbit controls the **ice ages**.

abschnitte.titel: The tilt of the Earth's axis
abschnitte.text: The Earth's axis is tilted, which is why there are seasons. This tilt is called the **obliquity of the ecliptic**. It swings back and forth between around **22.1° and 24.5°** over about **41,000 years**. Today it is around 23.4° and slowly decreasing. A greater tilt increases the difference between summer and winter. The **Moon** stabilises the axis and prevents bigger swings.

The Earth's axis wobbles slowly like a spinning top. This **precession** shifts the season in which the Earth is closest to the Sun. Its rhythm for the climate is around **23,000 years**, or more precisely about 19,000 to 23,000 years. Today the Earth reaches the point closest to the Sun, the **perihelion**, at the beginning of **January**. The shape of the Earth's orbit, its **eccentricity**, becomes sometimes rounder and sometimes more elliptical because of the pull of the other planets. This happens with periods of around **100,000** and **405,000 years**.

According to Milanković, the **summer sunshine** at high northern latitudes is what matters. Often the value at **65° North** is looked at. If summers in the north are cool, the winter snow does not melt completely. Year after year more is left lying, and **ice sheets** can grow. Because the ice reflects sunlight, the cooling becomes stronger.

Until about a million years ago, the ice ages followed a rhythm of roughly **41,000 years**. After that the cycles became longer, at around **100,000 years**. This change is called the **Mid-Pleistocene Transition**. Its cause is not yet fully understood. During the cold periods, large parts of Switzerland were also covered by glaciers.

gewusst: Milanković did his calculations without a computer, using only paper, pencil and tables.
In January the Earth is closest to the Sun, and yet it is winter here then.

teile.einleitung: The tropical rainforest is a dense forest in the warm regions around the equator. It rains a great deal there, and it is warm all year round. No other habitat on land is home to so many different animals and plants.
wichtigste: In the tropical rainforest it is warm and damp all year round.
The Amazon rainforest lies mainly in South America.
Most animal species live high up in the treetops.
Lianas climb up the trees towards the light.
The sloth hangs upside down from branches and moves very slowly.
Many rainforests are being cut down to make room for fields and pastures.

abschnitte.text: Tropical rainforests grow near the **equator**. There it is **warm and damp** all year round, and there is no winter. It can rain heavily almost every day. There are large rainforests in South America, Central Africa and South-East Asia. The largest is the **Amazon rainforest**, which lies mainly in **South America**.

The rainforest is built like a house with **storeys**. Right at the top, single giant trees stick out. Below them, the treetops form a dense roof, the **canopy**. On the ground it is dark, because little light gets through. **Lianas** are climbing plants that grow up the trees to reach the light. Some plants even grow directly on the branches of other trees.

Most animal species live **high up in the treetops**, where there is plenty of light, leaves and fruit. Monkeys climb there, and colourful birds such as parrots fly around. The **sloth** hangs upside down from branches and moves very slowly. It eats leaves and so saves a lot of energy. Other animals live on the ground and in the rivers, for example frogs, snakes and fish.

Every year, large areas of rainforest are **cut down**. This is often done to make room for **fields and pastures**. Soya or oil palms are grown there, for example, or cattle graze. Valuable timber is also felled. Many animals and plants lose their habitat as a result.

Rainforests store a great deal of **carbon** in their trees and so affect the climate. Many things we buy in Switzerland come from tropical regions, for example **cocoa** for chocolate, coffee or bananas. There are labels that show that products were made without cutting down rainforest. In this way everyone can help when shopping.

gewusst: Tiny algae grow in the fur of sloths and turn it greenish.
A small patch of rainforest can have more kinds of tree than the whole of Europe put together.

teile.einleitung: The North Pole is the northernmost point on Earth. There is no land there, but a sea covered with ice. Around the North Pole lies the Arctic, with polar bears, reindeer and the Inuit.
wichtigste: At the North Pole there is sea with floating ice on it.
It lies in the middle of the Arctic Ocean.
At the North Pole, day and night each last about half a year.
In summer the midnight sun shines in the Arctic.
The polar bear is the large predator of the Arctic.
The compass needle points roughly north.

abschnitte.titel: Right at the top of the Earth
abschnitte.text: The Earth spins around an axis. The point where this axis comes out of the Earth in the north is the **geographic North Pole**. From there, every direction points south. The needle of a **compass** is a small magnet. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field and points roughly north. But the **magnetic North Pole** is not exactly at the geographic pole, and it slowly moves.

There is no solid land under the North Pole. It lies in the middle of the **Arctic Ocean**, which is more than 4,000 metres deep there. A layer of **sea ice**, usually only a few metres thick, floats on the water. The ice drifts slowly with the wind and currents. That is why no permanent station can be built at the North Pole, unlike at the South Pole, which lies on a continent.

At the North Pole, the sun rises only once a year and sets only once. That is why **day and night** there each last about **half a year**. In winter it stays dark for months. In summer the sun does not set in the Arctic for days. You can even see it at midnight, which is why it is called the **midnight sun**.

The **polar bear** is one of the largest predators on land. Its thick fur and a thick layer of fat keep it warm. It hunts mainly seals on the sea ice. In the **tundra**, the treeless land around the Arctic Ocean, **reindeer** roam in large herds. In North America they are called caribou. Arctic foxes, walruses and many seabirds also live in the Arctic.

Nobody lives at the North Pole itself. But people have lived in the coastal areas of the Arctic for a long time. The **Inuit**, for example, live in **Greenland**, Canada and Alaska. In the past they mainly hunted seals and whales and travelled by dog sled and kayak. Today many live in settlements with schools and shops, but they keep up their language and traditions.

gewusst: At the North Pole, every direction points south.
The word kayak comes from the language of the Inuit.
The South Pole lies on a continent, whereas the North Pole lies on a sea.

teile.einleitung: Strahler search the Alps for rock crystals and other minerals. Crystal hunting has a long tradition in Switzerland and is still carried out today with great patience and knowledge.
wichtigste: The name comes from “Strahl”, an old word for rock crystal.
Crystals grow in cavities in the rock called fissures.
White bands of quartz in the rock can point to a fissure.
In 2005, two Strahler found a huge crystal treasure at the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri.
The find is on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
In many cantons you need a permit to hunt for crystals.

abschnitte.text: In the past, rock crystals were called **“Strahlen”** in German. That is why someone who searches for them is a **Strahler**, and the activity is called “strahlen”. Strahler climb into the mountains and search the rock for cavities containing crystals. As well as rock crystal, they also find other minerals. **Pink fluorite** is especially sought after; it is rare and occurs, for example, in the Göschenen area.

Crystals grow in cavities in the rock that Strahler call a **fissure** (in German “Kluft”). Long ago in the Alps, hot water rich in minerals flowed through such cracks. As it cooled, it slowly left crystals behind. Clues to a fissure are often **white bands of quartz** in the rock. They show that water has flowed there. Then the Strahler carefully knock and dig further.

In **2005**, the Strahler **Franz von Arx** and **Paul von Känel** opened a large fissure at the **Planggenstock** above Lake Göscheneralp in the canton of Uri. It contained almost two tonnes of rock crystal. The largest single crystal is around **1 metre** long. The largest group weighs about 300 kilograms. Since 2011, the **Natural History Museum in Bern** has been showing the find.

In Switzerland, crystal hunting is regulated by the **cantons**. Often you need a licence or a **permit**. You have to follow rules that protect nature, for example in protected areas. In **Naters** in Valais there is a crystal hunters' museum in an old fortress. It shows how Strahler work and how crystals form.

gewusst: Rock crystal is a clear form of the mineral quartz.
Giant crystals like those at the Planggenstock only grow in large, undisturbed fissures.

teile.einleitung: In a geomagnetic reversal, the Earth's magnetic north and south poles swap places. This has happened very often in Earth's history. Traces of it are stored in rocks.
wichtigste: The Earth's magnetic field is created by currents of liquid iron in the outer core.
The last complete reversal took place around 780,000 years ago.
The Laschamp event around 41,000 years ago was a short excursion of the magnetic field.
According to current estimates, a reversal takes a few thousand years.
Reversals happen irregularly, on average every few hundred thousand years.
In the 1960s, magnetic stripes on the sea floor supported seafloor spreading.
In 1906, Bernard Brunhes was the first to find rocks with reversed magnetism.

abschnitte.text: The Earth has a **magnetic field** that a compass needle lines up with. It is created deep inside: in the **outer core**, liquid iron flows and produces electric currents. This process is called the **geodynamo**. The magnetic field partly protects the Earth from charged particles from space. But it does not stay the same forever; it is constantly changing.

In a **geomagnetic reversal**, the direction of the magnetic field turns around. Afterwards a compass would point south. The last complete reversal took place around **780,000 years** ago. According to current estimates, a reversal takes **a few thousand years**. Sometimes the field only wavers briefly and then returns; this is called an **excursion**. One example is the **Laschamp event** around 41,000 years ago.

Volcanic rocks contain **magnetic minerals**. When lava cools, they line up with the magnetic field of the time and stay fixed like that. In 1906, the French geophysicist **Bernard Brunhes** was the first to find rocks magnetised in the opposite direction to today's field. Later the idea was confirmed that the whole magnetic field had reversed.

In the 1960s, a pattern of **magnetic stripes** was discovered on the sea floor. They lie symmetrically on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges. There new rock constantly rises and stores the magnetic field of its time. The stripes show that the sea floor is slowly growing apart. This was important evidence for **seafloor spreading** and plate tectonics.

Reversals happen **irregularly**, on average about every few hundred thousand years. Sometimes they come quickly one after another, sometimes there are very long pauses. A period of more than ten million years without a reversal is called a **superchron**. A well-known example comes from the Cretaceous. Nobody can predict exactly when the next reversal will come.

gewusst: The present period of the magnetic field is called the “Brunhes chron” after Bernard Brunhes.
Animals such as migrating birds also use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way.

teile.einleitung: Lake Thun is a large lake on the edge of the Alps in the Bernese Oberland. It lies between the town of Thun and Interlaken, and the River Aare flows through it.
wichtigste: The Aare flows from Lake Brienz through Lake Thun and leaves it at Thun.
Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.
The lake is up to 217 m deep.
It is about 17.5 km long and up to 3.5 km wide.
Its area is just under 48 km².
On the shore stands Spiez Castle, and high above lie the St Beatus Caves.

abschnitte.titel: A lake in the Bernese Oberland
abschnitte.text: **Lake Thun** lies in the canton of Bern on the edge of the Alps. It is about **17.5 km** long and up to **3.5 km** wide. Its area is just under **48 km²**. That makes it about twelve times smaller than Lake Geneva. At its deepest point it measures around **217 m**. The lake fills a valley floor that glaciers carved out during the Ice Ages.

The **Aare** comes out of **Lake Brienz** and flows through Lake Thun. In the town of **Thun** it leaves the lake again and flows on towards Bern. Between the two lakes lies **Interlaken**. The name means **“between the lakes”**. The town lies on a plain that rivers built up with gravel.

On a peninsula on the south shore stands **Spiez Castle**. Together with its **Romanesque church** it towers over the Bay of Spiez. The view of castle, church and lake is one of the best-known views of Lake Thun. Thun itself also has a famous castle high above the old town. Other castles lie on the shore, such as Oberhofen.

High above the **north shore** lie the **St Beatus Caves**. They are named after **Saint Beatus**, who according to legend is said to have lived there. The caves stretch far into the mountain. You can visit them on secured paths. You can see stalactites and stalagmites, underground streams and waterfalls.

**Passenger boats** sail on Lake Thun, including a historic paddle steamer. Many people go sailing, swimming or on trips to the lakeside villages. Behind the lake rise mountains such as the **Niesen**, the Eiger, the Mönch and the Jungfrau. That is why the area is popular with tourists from all over the world.

gewusst: The Niesen on Lake Thun has an almost perfect pyramid shape and is therefore also called the Swiss pyramid.
After the last Ice Age, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz were once a single large lake.

teile.einleitung: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho for short, is the boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle. It was discovered by the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić in 1909. It lies much less deep under the oceans than under the continents.
wichtigste: The **Moho** separates the Earth's crust from the mantle.
**Andrija Mohorovičić** discovered it after an earthquake near Zagreb in 1909.
Under oceans it lies about **5 to 10 km** deep, under continents about **30 to 50 km**.
Under the Swiss Alps, the crust reaches down to about **55 km**.
At the Moho, the speed of P-waves jumps from about 7 to about 8 km/s.
The **Mohole** project wanted to drill down to the Moho but never reached it.

abschnitte.text: On 8 October 1909 an earthquake struck near **Pokupsko**, south of **Zagreb**. The scientist **Andrija Mohorovičić** analysed the recordings. He noticed two groups of **P-waves**, which are fast pressure waves. The faster group had travelled through a deeper layer in which waves spread faster. This is how he found the boundary between crust and mantle.

Oceanic crust is thin and is made mainly of basalt and gabbro. That is why under the oceans the Moho lies at a depth of only about **5 to 10 km**. Continental crust is thicker and lighter. On average it reaches about 35 km deep, usually **30 to 50 km**. Under mountain ranges the crust is thickened and forms a **root**. Under the **Swiss Alps**, the Moho lies at a depth of around 50 to 60 km.

At the Moho it is mainly the **type of rock** that changes. Above it lies crustal rock such as granite or basalt. Below it comes olivine-rich **peridotite**, which is denser. That is why seismic waves travel faster in the mantle. In the lower crust, P-waves travel at about 6.5 to **7 km/s**, and in the uppermost mantle at about **8 km/s**. This jump defines the Moho.

In the 1960s, researchers in the USA wanted to drill through the thin sea floor down to the Moho. The plan was called **Project Mohole**. In 1961 they made the first test drillings in the deep ocean off Mexico. But in 1966 the project was stopped because of **its cost**. The Moho was never reached.

Even so, rock from the mantle can be studied without drilling. In **ophiolites** it lies at the surface. These are pieces of oceanic lithosphere that were pushed onto continents when mountains formed. Well-known examples are in **Oman**, but also in the Alps near **Zermatt**. Within the continental crust, another boundary is often assumed, the **Conrad discontinuity**. It was described by Victor Conrad in 1925, but it is not clear everywhere.

gewusst: Because the name Mohorovičić is hard for many people to pronounce, people usually just say “Moho”.
Even the deepest borehole in the world got nowhere near the Moho.

teile.einleitung: The ozone hole is an area over Antarctica in which a large part of the protective ozone disappears every year. It was caused mainly by substances from aerosol cans and fridges. Thanks to a worldwide agreement, the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.
wichtigste: The ozone layer protects us from harmful UV radiation.
It lies mainly in the stratosphere.
The biggest ozone hole forms every year over Antarctica.
It is largest in the spring of the Southern Hemisphere.
The main cause is chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 banned CFCs step by step.

abschnitte.text: **Ozone** is a special form of oxygen in which three oxygen atoms are joined together. Most ozone molecules are found at a height of about 15 to 35 kilometres in the **stratosphere**. This layer lies above the weather layer. The **ozone layer** absorbs a large part of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation. Too much **UV radiation** can cause sunburn and skin cancer and can also harm plants.

**Chlorofluorocarbons**, or **CFCs** for short, used to be used in aerosol cans, fridges and foam materials. At ground level they are harmless and very long-lasting. That is why they slowly rise up into the stratosphere. There sunlight splits them, and **chlorine** is released. A single chlorine atom can destroy a great many ozone molecules.

Over the South Pole it is extremely cold in winter. Then special clouds form in the stratosphere. On them, chemical reactions take place that make the chlorine ready to act. When the sun returns after the **polar night**, its light sets the destruction of ozone going. That is why the ozone hole is largest in the **spring** of the Southern Hemisphere, in September and October. Researchers from the **British Antarctic Survey** reported this discovery in 1985.

The discovery quickly led to international action. In the **Montreal Protocol** of 1987, countries agreed to phase out ozone-damaging substances step by step. Switzerland is part of it too. The agreement is seen as one of the most successful environmental agreements in the world. According to a UN report from 2023, the ozone layer over Antarctica should return to its 1980 state by around **2066**.

In the Grisons village of **Arosa**, regular measurements of total ozone began in 1926. This became the longest series of measurements of its kind anywhere in the world. Today **MeteoSwiss** continues it, with instruments from Arosa that now stand in Davos. Such long series are very valuable, because they show how the ozone layer has changed over many decades.

gewusst: The ozone measurement series from Arosa is the longest in the world.
In 1995, three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on ozone depletion.
Ozone high up protects us, whereas ozone near the ground in summer smog irritates the airways.

teile.einleitung: Since the 20th century, the average sea level around the world has been rising, and faster and faster. The main reasons are the warming of the ocean and the melting of ice on land. For low-lying coasts and island states this is a great danger.
wichtigste: Warmer water **expands** and needs more space.
Melting ice on land makes sea level rise.
Melting **sea ice** hardly makes it rise, because it is already floating in the water.
According to the IPCC, the rise from 2006 to 2018 was around 3.7 millimetres a year.
It is measured with **tide gauges** and, since 1993, with satellites too.
Island states such as **Tuvalu** are especially threatened.

abschnitte.text: Water expands when it gets warmer. This **thermal expansion** acts in the whole huge ocean. That is why sea level rises with warming even when no ice melts. Along with the melting of glaciers and ice sheets, thermal expansion is one of the **main causes** of the rise.

abschnitte.titel: Ice on land and ice in the sea
abschnitte.text: Not all melting ice has the same effect. **Ice on land**, such as glaciers or the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, brings extra water into the sea when it melts. **Sea ice**, on the other hand, is already floating in the water. It already pushes aside as much water as it weighs. When it melts, the water level therefore hardly changes. You can try this out with an ice cube in a glass.

For a long time, the water level on coasts has been measured with a **tide gauge**. It shows the height of the water at a fixed place all the time. Since **1993**, **satellites** have also measured sea level around the whole world. According to the **IPCC**, it rose by around **3.7 millimetres a year** from 2006 to 2018. That is more than twice as fast as the average for the 20th century.

The island state of **Tuvalu** in the Pacific is made up of flat **atolls**. They mostly lie only a few metres above the sea. Even a small rise leads to flooding there. Salt water gets into the groundwater and makes it unusable. Other low-lying islands and coastal cities all over the world have similar worries.

About a quarter of the **Netherlands** lies below sea level. Large parts of it were won from the sea. **Dykes**, dunes and **storm surge barriers** protect the land. Other countries are also building protective structures or planning to move settlements. The most effective thing would be to slow down the warming. Switzerland also contributes to this with its climate targets.

gewusst: If all of Greenland's ice melted, sea level would rise by about seven metres.
Swiss glaciers also add a tiny bit to the rise with their meltwater.

teile.einleitung: A supercell is an especially strong and long-lasting thundercloud. Its updraught rotates, and it can bring large hail, strong gusts and sometimes tornadoes.
wichtigste: A supercell has a rotating updraught, the mesocyclone.
As well as unstable air, strong vertical wind shear is needed.
Supercells can last for several hours.
They often bring large hail, because the strong updraught keeps the hailstones in the cloud for a long time.
A hook echo often shows up on radar.
A rotating wall cloud sometimes hangs below the cell.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary thunderstorm cell often lives for less than an hour. A **supercell**, on the other hand, has a **rotating updraught**. This spinning updraught is called a **mesocyclone**. Because the updraught and the downdraught are separate in the cloud, the falling rain or hail does not choke off the updraught. That is how a supercell can stay active for **several hours**.

Supercells first need **unstable air**, which means warm, moist air at the ground and colder air above it. Strong **vertical wind shear** is also especially important. This means that the wind gets much stronger with height and changes direction. This creates horizontal rolls of air. The powerful updraught tips them upright, and the cell begins to rotate.

On weather radar a **hook echo** often shows up, usually on the south-western edge of the cell. It forms because rain and hail are carried around the mesocyclone. Below the updraught, a low, rotating lowering of the cloud base sometimes hangs down: the **wall cloud**. **Tornadoes** can come out of it. When the updraught is very strong, a dome sticks up above the anvil: the **overshooting top**.

Supercells often bring **large hail**. The strong updraught keeps the hailstones in the supercooled cloud for a long time. There they circle around and grow layer by layer. Only when they are too heavy do they fall to the ground. In Switzerland too, supercells sometimes cause great hail damage in summer.

Supercells can split into a right-moving and a left-moving cell. In the **Northern Hemisphere**, the **right-movers** are the most common. They move to the right of the average flow and usually rotate anticlockwise, which is called **cyclonic**. This is because of the typical wind profile in our latitudes.

gewusst: The overshooting top shoots up past the tropopause, the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
Most of the world's strong tornadoes form from supercells.

teile.einleitung: The source of the Rhine lies in the Alps of the Grisons. Traditionally, the small Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass is seen as the origin of the Rhine. But before the river becomes really big, many streams and a second source river join it.
wichtigste: Lake Toma is traditionally seen as the source of the Rhine.
It lies in the Grisons municipality of Tujetsch at around 2,350 m above sea level.
The lake is near the Oberalp Pass.
The Posterior Rhine rises in the Rheinwald below the Rheinwaldhorn.
The Anterior and Posterior Rhine join at Reichenau (Tamins).
The Ruinaulta is the deep gorge of the Anterior Rhine between Ilanz and Reichenau.
The Flims landslide around 10,000 years ago created the conditions for the gorge.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Toma** is a small mountain lake in the **Grisons**. In Romansh it is called **Lai da Tuma**. It lies at around **2,350 metres above sea level** in the municipality of **Tujetsch**, not far from the **Oberalp Pass**. Traditionally it is seen as the **source of the Rhine**. From here the water flows down into the valley as the young **Anterior Rhine**.

abschnitte.titel: A popular place to hike to
abschnitte.text: A hiking path leads up to the lake from the Oberalp Pass. Many people walk there to see the beginning of the great river. The lake is small and clear and surrounded by mountains. It is hard to imagine that this water later becomes a mighty river on which large ships sail. In winter the lake lies under snow and ice.

The Rhine has two large source rivers. The **Anterior Rhine** comes from Lake Toma and flows through the **Surselva**. The **Posterior Rhine** rises in the **Rheinwald** from glaciers below the **Rheinwaldhorn**. At **Reichenau** in the municipality of Tamins, the two join. From there the river is called the **Alpine Rhine**.

Around **10,000 years** ago, a huge mass of rock crashed into the valley near Flims. This **Flims landslide** is the largest known landslide in the Alps. The masses of rock blocked the valley of the Anterior Rhine. Since then the river has dug a new path through the debris. This created a special landscape.

Between **Ilanz** and Reichenau, the Anterior Rhine flows through a deep gorge, the **Ruinaulta**. It is also called the Swiss Grand Canyon. High, pale walls of landslide material tower above the river. The Rhaetian Railway runs through the gorge, and many people travel on the Rhine in boats or rubber rafts. The landscape is protected.

gewusst: In the Ruinaulta there is no road along the river, only the railway and hiking paths.

teile.einleitung: The Precambrian is the oldest and longest part of Earth's history. It stretches from the formation of the Earth around 4.6 billion years ago to the start of the Cambrian about 540 million years ago. During this time the first continents and the first life appeared.
wichtigste: The Precambrian makes up around 88 per cent of the whole of Earth's history.
It is divided into three eons: the Hadean, the Archean and the Proterozoic.
The Hadean is named after Hades, the Greek god of the underworld.
The oldest known minerals are zircons around 4.4 billion years old from the Jack Hills in Western Australia.
In the Archean, the first continental cores and the oldest definite traces of life formed.
In the Proterozoic, the first definitely proven cells with a nucleus appear.
The youngest period of the Precambrian is called the Ediacaran.

abschnitte.text: If you imagine the whole of Earth's history as one day, the **Precambrian** lasts until about 9 p.m. It makes up around **88 per cent** of Earth's history. The name means “before the Cambrian”. Experts divide this huge time into three **eons**: the **Hadean**, the **Archean** and the **Proterozoic**. An eon is the largest unit of time in Earth's history.

The oldest eon is named after **Hades**, the god of the underworld in Greek mythology. The young Earth was hot, and there were many impacts from space. Hardly any rocks from this time have survived. The oldest known minerals are tiny **zircon grains** from the **Jack Hills** in Western Australia. They are around 4.4 billion years old.

abschnitte.titel: Archean: the first continents and first life
abschnitte.text: In the **Archean**, the first solid **continental cores** formed. One of the oldest reliably dated rocks is the **Acasta Gneiss** in north-western Canada, at around 4 billion years old. The oldest definite **traces of life** also come from this eon. They were simple single-celled organisms without a nucleus. Some built up layers of lime called **stromatolites**.

The name **Proterozoic** means “age of earlier life”. In this eon, **oxygen** built up in the air, because tiny living things gave it off during photosynthesis. The first definitely proven **eukaryotes** appear, which means cells with a nucleus. Plants, animals and people are also made of such cells. There were also times with very strong glaciations.

The youngest period of the Precambrian is called the **Ediacaran**. It is named after the **Ediacara Hills** in South Australia, where special fossils were found. These living things were soft, flat and often leaf-shaped. After that came the **Cambrian**, in which many groups of animals with hard shells developed rapidly. This is where the Precambrian ends.

gewusst: The zircons from the Jack Hills are smaller than a grain of sand and yet almost as old as the Earth itself.
Stromatolites still grow in a few places today, for example in a bay in Western Australia.

teile.einleitung: A pyroclastic flow is a hot avalanche of gas, ash and lumps of rock that races down a mountain in some volcanic eruptions. It is one of the most dangerous things volcanoes do. In French it is called “nuée ardente”, which means glowing cloud.
wichtigste: A pyroclastic flow often forms when an ash column or a lava dome collapses.
It can travel at over 100 km/h, sometimes at several hundred km/h.
It is typically several hundred degrees Celsius hot.
The French technical term is “nuée ardente”, glowing cloud.
In the year 79, pyroclastic flows from Vesuvius struck the Roman town of Herculaneum.
In 1902, a pyroclastic flow from Mount Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre on Martinique.

abschnitte.text: In a violent eruption, a huge **ash column** shoots into the sky. If it gets too heavy, it can collapse. A **lava dome**, a plug of thick, sticky lava at the summit, can also break off. Then a mixture of hot gas, ash and lumps of rock crashes down the slope. This is a **pyroclastic flow**. The word “pyroclastic” means roughly “broken by fire”.

Pyroclastic flows often travel at over **100 km/h**, sometimes even several hundred km/h. They are typically **several hundred degrees Celsius** hot. Because they are heavier than air, they follow valleys and can still cause great damage far from the volcano. You can hardly outrun them. That is why evacuating in time is so important.

In the year 79, **Vesuvius** on the Bay of Naples erupted. As well as Pompeii, it also struck the Roman town of **Herculaneum**. Pyroclastic flows buried it under a thick layer. During excavations, hundreds of human skeletons were later found on what was then the beach. The people had probably looked for shelter there.

In 1902, **Mount Pelée** erupted on the Caribbean island of Martinique. A pyroclastic flow almost completely destroyed the town of **Saint-Pierre**, and a great many people died. In 1991, the well-known volcanologists **Katia and Maurice Krafft** died on the Japanese volcano **Unzen**. They had made many films about volcanoes to warn people of the dangers.

Today, dangerous volcanoes are closely monitored. Experts measure earthquakes, gases and the deformation of the ground. If warning signs appear, the authorities can close off areas and bring people to safety. There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland. But Swiss researchers take part in volcano research.

gewusst: The name “glowing cloud” comes from the fact that some flows seem to glow red at night.
In Saint-Pierre, one of the few people to survive did so because he was in a thick-walled prison cell.

teile.einleitung: The sea covers most of our Earth. It is salty, huge and full of life. Switzerland has no coast, and yet its water ends up in three different seas.
wichtigste: Around 71 per cent of the Earth, about **two thirds**, is covered by sea.
Seawater is too **salty** to drink.
The Rhine flows into the **North Sea**.
The Rhône flows into the **Mediterranean Sea**.
The Inn carries water via the Danube to the **Black Sea**.
The **blue whale** is the largest animal in the sea.

abschnitte.text: Around **71 per cent** of the Earth's surface is covered by sea. That is about two thirds. That is why the Earth looks blue from space. It is called the **blue planet**. The largest seas are called **oceans**: the Pacific, the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean are the three biggest.

Seawater contains a lot of **salt**. The salt comes from rock that rivers have washed out over a very long time and carried into the sea. You cannot drink seawater. If you drink it, you get even thirstier, because your body has to get rid of all that salt again. For this it needs extra water.

Switzerland is far from the sea, but its rivers flow there. The **Rhine** flows through Germany and the Netherlands into the **North Sea**. The **Rhône** flows through Lake Geneva and through France into the **Mediterranean Sea**. The **Inn** from the Engadine flows into the Danube, which empties into the **Black Sea**. That is why Switzerland is also called the water tower of Europe.

Countless animals live in the sea, from tiny plankton to huge whales. The largest animal is the **blue whale**. It can grow to over 30 metres long. It is even the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth, bigger than any dinosaur. Even so, it mainly eats tiny shrimps called **krill**.

The sea is important for the whole Earth. Water evaporates from it and falls as rain over Switzerland too. Tiny sea plants produce a lot of oxygen. The sea stores heat and so affects the weather. Many people make their living from fishing or from trade by ship.

gewusst: A drop of water from the Inn travels through several countries before it reaches the Black Sea.
A blue whale can weigh over 100 tonnes, as much as many elephants put together.

teile.einleitung: Sand lies on the beach, in the desert and in the playground. It is made of tiny grains of stone and is very useful for people: houses are built with it, and glass is made from it.
wichtigste: Sand is made of tiny grains of stone.
You can build better sandcastles with wet sand than with dry sand.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.
In the desert, the wind piles sand up into hills called dunes.
Glass is made from sand.
If you mix sand, gravel, cement and water, you get concrete.

abschnitte.text: Sand is made of **tiny grains of stone**. They form when wind, water and frost break up large rocks over a very long time. A grain of sand is bigger than a speck of dust but smaller than a pebble. Many grains of sand are made of the hard mineral **quartz**. Water poured onto sand **soaks away** quickly, because there is a lot of space between the grains.

The **Sahara** in Africa is the largest hot desert on Earth. In some parts there are huge areas of sand. The wind blows the sand along and piles it up into hills called **dunes**. Dunes can become very high and slowly move on, because the wind keeps carrying sand from one side to the other.

If you build a sandcastle, it is best to use **wet sand**. The water between the grains holds them together like a weak glue. Dry sand, on the other hand, trickles apart. But if the sand is too wet, it turns into mush and the castle falls down.

Sand is an important raw material. If you melt it at a very high temperature, you get **glass**. If you mix sand, gravel, cement and water, you get **concrete**, from which houses, bridges and roads are built. In an **hourglass**, sand trickles through a narrow gap and so measures **time**. Sand is also needed for playgrounds and sports pitches.

gewusst: Desert sand is not good for concrete, because its grains have been ground too round by the wind.
Window panes, drinking glasses and bottles are made largely of melted sand.

teile.einleitung: A thermocline is a layer of water in which the temperature drops sharply with depth. It is found in lakes and seas, where it separates warm surface water from cold deep water.
wichtigste: The thermocline is also called the metalimnion or, in German, “Sprungschicht” (jump layer).
Above it in a lake lies the warm epilimnion, and below it the cold hypolimnion.
In the ocean, the permanent thermocline lies roughly between 200 and 1,000 m deep.
In polar seas there is usually no marked thermocline.
The thermocline slows down the exchange of nutrients and oxygen.
Internal seiches can swing back and forth at the thermocline.

abschnitte.text: The **thermocline**, called the **“Sprungschicht”** (jump layer) in German, is a layer of water in which the temperature changes sharply over a short distance. At the top the water is warm, below it cold. Because cold water is heavier than warm water, a stable layering forms. If the **density** changes sharply with depth, this is called a **pycnocline**. Density depends on temperature and salt content.

In summer, a stratified lake is divided into three storeys. At the top lies the **epilimnion**, which the sun warms and the wind mixes. Below it comes the layer with the thermocline. Right at the bottom lies the cool **hypolimnion**, which the wind hardly reaches. Swiss lakes such as Lake Zurich or Lake Geneva are layered like this in summer too.

In tropical and temperate oceans there is a **permanent thermocline**. It lies roughly between **200 and 1,000 m** deep. Below it the deep water is cold and changes only a little. In **polar seas** there is usually no marked thermocline. There the surface water is almost as cold as the deep water. The layering is decided more by the **salt content**.

A marked thermocline acts like a **barrier**. Nutrients from the depths hardly get up to the top, and oxygen hardly gets down. That is why oxygen can run short in the deep water of a lake in late summer. Wind can push the warm water to one end of a lake, so that the thermocline tilts. When the wind drops, it swings back and forth. These swings are called **internal seiches**.

gewusst: Internal seiches can be several metres high, although you can hardly see anything at the surface.
Divers often clearly feel the thermocline, because the water suddenly gets much colder.

teile.einleitung: A **stalagmite** is a dripstone that grows upwards from the floor of a cave. It forms very slowly from lime dissolved in falling drops of water.
wichtigste: A stalagmite grows upwards from the floor.
It often stands exactly under a stalactite, because that is where the drops fall.
It needs dripping water containing lime to grow.
Its tip is usually round and blunt.
Stalagmites are usually thicker than stalactites.
Together, stalactites and stalagmites are called dripstones.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater seeps through limestone and dissolves a little **lime** as it does so. When this **water containing lime** drips from the cave ceiling, it falls onto the floor. There it gives off a gas, and a tiny bit of lime is left behind. Drop by drop, a mound grows **upwards from the floor** in this way. This is a **stalagmite**.

Often a **stalactite** hangs from the ceiling exactly above it. The drops fall from it, which is why the stalagmite stands **exactly underneath**. Together, stalactites and stalagmites are called **dripstones**. If both grow long enough, they can meet and become a **column**.

The tip of a stalagmite is usually **round and blunt**, because the drops splash when they land. Stalagmites are usually **thicker** than stalactites. They grow only very slowly. But over **a very long time** they can become **several metres high**. In Switzerland you can admire dripstones in show caves, for example.

A stalagmite grows layer by layer, a bit like the annual rings of a tree. Traces of the water that dripped down at the time are stored in these layers. From them researchers can tell **what the climate used to be like**, whether it was rather warm or cold, damp or dry. In this way a stalagmite tells the story of thousands of years.

gewusst: You should not touch dripstones: the grease from your skin can stop more lime from growing there.
The word stalagmite comes from the Greek word for “drop”.

teile.einleitung: The Molasse Basin is a huge hollow on the northern edge of the Alps. For millions of years, debris from the mountains collected here. Today a large part of the Swiss Plateau lies on it.
wichtigste: The Molasse Basin is a foreland basin north of the Alps.
It formed because the European Plate bent downwards under the weight of the Alps.
The Molasse was deposited mainly in the Oligocene and Miocene.
From oldest to youngest come the UMM, USM, OMM and OSM.
At the edge of the Alps lies the sliced-up Subalpine Molasse.
The Rigi and the Napf are made of Nagelfluh, Bern of Molasse sandstone.

abschnitte.titel: A hollow in front of the mountains
abschnitte.text: When the Alps formed, massive slabs of rock were pushed northwards. Their weight pressed the **European Plate** down in front of the mountains, just as a heavy stone bends a plank. This created a long **foreland basin**. Rivers filled it with the eroded debris of the Alps. Later the basin was lifted up again, and part of the deposits was worn away.

Deposition began around 34 million years ago in the **Oligocene** and lasted until the late **Miocene**. Experts divide the Molasse into four groups. At the bottom lies the **Lower Marine Molasse** (UMM), on top of it the **Lower Freshwater Molasse** (USM), then the **Upper Marine Molasse** (OMM) and at the top the **Upper Freshwater Molasse** (OSM). The abbreviations come from the German names. So sea and land took turns twice.

abschnitte.titel: Debris fans and the edge of the Alps
abschnitte.text: Where large ancient rivers flowed out of the Alps into the basin, massive **debris fans** of gravel formed. They turned into **Nagelfluh**, of which the Rigi and the Napf, for example, are made. On the southern edge of the basin, the layers were cut into slices, tilted steeply and partly overridden by nappes. This strip is called the **Subalpine Molasse**. Further north, on the Swiss Plateau, the layers lie almost flat.

At **Öhningen** on the Untersee, a large skeleton was found in limestone from the Miocene. In 1726, the Zurich naturalist **Johann Jakob Scheuchzer** thought it was a person who had drowned in the Great Flood. He called it “Homo diluvii testis” (man who witnessed the Flood). Later the Frenchman **Georges Cuvier** realised that it was a **giant salamander**. Today the fossil is a well-known example of how science can get things wrong and correct them.

The greyish-green **Bernese sandstone** comes from the Upper Marine Molasse. It was quarried around Bern and shapes the old town and **Bern Minster**. It is easy to work but weathers quickly. In the **Napf hills** between the Emmental and the Entlebuch, the gravels contain fine gold dust. People still pan for **river gold** in the streams today.

gewusst: Scheuchzer's “Flood man” was really a giant salamander.
In the Napf area you can still pan for gold in the streams today.
The basin formed because the weight of the Alps bent the tectonic plate downwards.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona is an area in the Alps of eastern Switzerland where you can see especially clearly how mountains form. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
wichtigste: The Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona lies in the cantons of Glarus, St Gallen and Grisons.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2008.
At the Glarus thrust, older rock lies on top of younger rock.
The old reddish rock is called Verrucano, the young rock flysch.
The upper mass of rock was pushed around 40 km northwards.
Twice a year the sun shines through the Martinsloch onto the church of Elm.

abschnitte.titel: A World Heritage Site of geology
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona** lies in the cantons of **Glarus**, **St Gallen** and **Grisons**. **UNESCO** made it a World Heritage Site in July **2008**. The reason: **mountain building by thrusting** can be seen there exceptionally well. A thrust happens when one mass of rock is pushed over another.

Normally younger layers of rock lie on top. At the **Glarus thrust** it is the other way round. There, rock from the **Permian**, around 260 to 300 million years old, lies on top of **flysch** that is only about 35 to 50 million years old. The old, reddish rock is called **Verrucano**. Its name comes from Monte Verruca near Pisa. The upper mass was pushed around **40 km** northwards.

Right at the thrust surface lies a thin, strongly deformed layer of limestone. It is called **Lochseiten limestone**. It is a **calc-mylonite**, which means a rock that was finely ground up by the movement and recrystallised. The upper mass of rock slid on it as if on a **layer of grease**. The line of the thrust can be seen as a sharp boundary on many mountainsides.

The Zurich geologist **Albert Heim** first explained the upside-down order of layers with two folds lying against each other, the **“Glarus double fold”**. In **1884**, the French geologist **Marcel Bertrand** suggested a large thrust, without ever having been there himself. He compared the Glarus Alps with the Ardennes. Only around **1902** did Heim accept this explanation.

In the **Tschingelhörner** there is a hole in the rock, the **Martinsloch**. It lies close to the thrust line. **Twice a year**, in March and in autumn, the sun is positioned so that its rays shine through the hole. Then they briefly hit the **church of Elm**. Many people come to see this spectacle.

gewusst: The thrust line can be seen on mountains such as the Tschingelhörner as a clear line in the rock.
Along with Jungfrau-Aletsch and Monte San Giorgio, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona is one of Switzerland's natural World Heritage Sites.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake, **seismic waves** spread out from the focus in all directions. Some travel through the inside of the Earth, others along the surface. With them, researchers can not only locate quakes but also look inside the Earth.
wichtigste: Seismic waves are divided into body waves and surface waves.
In a Rayleigh wave, the ground particles move in ellipses in a vertical plane.
A Love wave moves the ground only horizontally and at right angles to the direction of travel.
In the mantle the waves travel along curved paths, because their speed increases with depth.
With three measuring stations, an epicentre can be located.
After very strong earthquakes, the whole Earth vibrates for days.

abschnitte.text: Seismic waves are divided into two main groups: **body waves** and **surface waves**. Body waves travel through the inside of the Earth. They include the fast **P-waves**, which squeeze and stretch the rock, and the slower **S-waves**, which shake it sideways. Because their speed in the mantle increases with depth, they travel along **curved paths**.

**Surface waves** travel along the Earth's surface. They are slower but often cause great damage. In a **Rayleigh wave**, the ground particles move in **ellipses** in a vertical plane, similar to waves in the sea. A **Love wave** moves the ground only **horizontally** and at right angles to the direction of travel. Both are named after English scientists.

If you plot when the waves arrive at stations at different distances, you get a **travel-time curve**. From this, the distance to the focus can be worked out for each station. If you draw a circle around each station with this distance, the circles meet at the epicentre. You need at least **three stations** for this.

From a great many travel times, researchers calculate three-dimensional pictures of the inside of the Earth. This method is called **seismic tomography**, similar to a CT scan in hospital. It shows areas where the rock is warmer or colder. The boundaries between crust, mantle and core were also discovered with seismic waves.

The further they get from the focus, the **weaker** seismic waves become. Their energy spreads over a larger and larger area and is **damped** in the rock. But after very strong earthquakes the whole Earth vibrates like a bell that has been struck. These **free oscillations of the Earth** can be measured for days.

gewusst: After the strong earthquake in Chile in 1960, the free oscillations of the Earth could be measured clearly for the first time.
The seismic waves of a strong quake are still recorded by instruments on the other side of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The **Snowball Earth** hypothesis says that our planet was almost completely covered by ice about 700 million years ago, even at the equator. Many traces in the rock support this, but there are also other suggestions.
wichtigste: The great glaciations took place in the Cryogenian, a period of the Neoproterozoic.
The two most important glaciations are called the Sturtian and the Marinoan glaciations.
Glacial deposits that lay close to the equator at that time suggest an Earth that was almost completely frozen.
The ice-albedo feedback may have pushed the ice all the way to the equator.
Volcanic carbon dioxide probably ended the glaciation.
The geologist Joseph Kirschvink coined the term “Snowball Earth” in 1992.

abschnitte.text: In the **Neoproterozoic**, about 720 to 635 million years ago, there were extraordinarily strong ice ages. The period is named after them: the **Cryogenian**, from the Greek word for icy cold. The two great glaciations are the **Sturtian** and the **Marinoan glaciations**. According to the hypothesis, the Earth was almost completely covered by ice at that time. In 1992 the American geologist **Joseph Kirschvink** coined the term **“Snowball Earth”** for this.

**Glacial deposits** from this time have been found that lay close to the **equator** at that time. This can be read from the magnetism of the rocks. If there were glaciers even there, almost the whole Earth was probably frozen. Directly on top of these deposits there are often layers of limestone, the **cap carbonates**. They show that the climate then became very warm very quickly.

Ice and snow reflect a lot of sunlight. The more ice there is, the less heat the Earth takes in, and the more ice can form. This **ice-albedo feedback** may have pushed the glaciation all the way to the equator. Once an Earth is as white as that, it stays cold for a long time.

Even under the ice, **volcanoes** were active and gave off **carbon dioxide**. Because hardly any rain fell and there was no open water, this gas was hardly removed. Over millions of years it built up in the air. In the end the greenhouse effect was so strong that the ice melted. After that the Earth quickly became warm.

Not all researchers believe in a completely frozen Earth. The milder alternative hypothesis is called **“Slushball Earth”**. According to it, a strip of **open water** remained at the equator. Simple living things could have survived there more easily. Which idea is right is still being researched.

gewusst: After the Snowball glaciations, the first larger multicellular living things in Earth's history appeared.
The word Cryogenian comes from the Greek “kryos”, which means cold or frost.

teile.einleitung: Seismology is the science of earthquakes and of the waves that travel through the Earth. Seismologists measure where, when and how strongly the Earth shakes. Thanks to their measurements, we now even know how the Earth is built deep inside.
wichtigste: Seismology is the study of earthquakes and how seismic waves spread.
Earthquakes are measured with seismometers.
P-waves are compression waves and arrive first at a measuring station.
S-waves cannot travel through liquids, which is how we know that the outer core is liquid.
If the moment magnitude rises by 1, about 32 times more energy is released.
The Basel earthquake destroyed large parts of the city in 1356.
In Switzerland, the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich monitors earthquake activity.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek “seismos”, meaning shaking. **Seismology** studies how earthquakes happen and how their waves spread through the Earth. An earthquake usually happens when blocks of rock suddenly shift against each other along a fracture underground. The place underground where this happens is called the **focus** or hypocentre. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre.

Different waves travel out from the focus of an earthquake. **P-waves** are compression waves that squeeze and stretch the rock, as in a spiral spring. They are the fastest and arrive first. **S-waves** shake the rock sideways; they are slower and cannot travel through liquids. Surface waves also form at the surface, and these usually cause the greatest damage.

A **seismometer** measures the tiniest ground movements, and the recording is called a seismogram. From the time gap between the P-wave and the S-wave, you can work out how far away the focus is. If P-waves travel at 6 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s, and the S-wave arrives 25 seconds later, the focus is around 210 kilometres away. With measurements from several stations, the location of the quake can be determined precisely.

The strength of an earthquake is given as its **magnitude**. In the past, the Richter scale was mainly used; today it is usually the moment magnitude.
