If the magnitude rises by 1, about 32 times more energy is released, and with a rise of 2 even around 1,000 times more. The strongest earthquake ever measured happened in Chile in 1960, with a magnitude of 9.5. How strongly a quake is felt in a place and what damage it causes, on the other hand, is described by its **intensity**.

Seismic waves speed up, slow down or are bent depending on the rock. That is why they can be used to study the inside of the Earth, like an X-ray. Behind the core there is a **shadow zone** where no direct S-waves arrive. From this it was concluded that the outer core must be liquid. In 1936, the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann discovered the solid inner core in this way.

Switzerland has a medium earthquake hazard; Valais, Basel, the Grisons and central Switzerland are most at risk. The **Basel earthquake** of 1356 was the strongest known quake north of the Alps and destroyed large parts of the city. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors earthquake activity with a dense network of measuring stations. Every year it records about 1,000 to 1,500 earthquakes, most of which are too weak to be felt.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument that records the tiniest movements of the ground.
The fastest seismic wave, which squeezes and stretches the rock.
A slower seismic wave that shakes the rock sideways and does not travel through liquids.
A number that shows how much energy an earthquake releases.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.

gewusst: As early as the year 132, the Chinese scholar Zhang Heng built a device that indicated earthquakes.
Seismometers also measure explosions, surf and even the vibrations of football fans in a stadium.
A strong earthquake makes the whole Earth vibrate like a bell that has been struck.

teile.einleitung: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year round. When it thaws because of warming, this is called permafrost degradation. In the Swiss Alps it can trigger rockfalls, debris flows and damage to buildings.
wichtigste: Permafrost is permanently frozen ground.
In Switzerland it lies under around 3 to 5 per cent of the land area.
The top layer thaws every summer: this is the active layer.
Many rock glaciers are now creeping much faster.
Thawing ice in cracks can trigger rockfalls.
PERMOS measures the temperatures in boreholes.

abschnitte.text: **Permafrost** is ground or rock that stays frozen without a break for at least two years. In Switzerland it is found mainly above about **2,500 metres**, especially on north-facing slopes and scree slopes. According to an estimate by the **PERMOS** monitoring network, around 3 to 5 per cent of the country lies on top of it. That is more than the area covered by glaciers today. Because permafrost lies below the surface, you usually cannot see it.

The top layer of ground above the permafrost thaws every summer and freezes through again in winter. It is called the **active layer**. Its thickness is an important measurement, because it increases with warming. PERMOS measures the temperature with chains of **temperature sensors** in **boreholes** that reach dozens of metres deep. This shows how the warming is slowly pushing down into the ground.

**Rock glaciers** are masses of debris with ice inside that slowly creep down the valley. PERMOS has observed that many rock glaciers in the Swiss Alps are now creeping much **faster** than in the 1990s. Warmer ice is softer and deforms more easily, and there is also more meltwater. In steep rock faces, ice in the cracks acts like **glue**. When it warms up, it loses its holding power. In the hot summer of 2003, many rockfalls broke loose, including on the **Hörnli ridge** of the Matterhorn.

Many cable car stations and huts in the high mountains stand on frozen ground. When the ice thaws, the ground loses its ability to carry weight. **Foundations** can sink or shift and have to be adapted. Above **Pontresina**, a large **protective dam** was built in the early 2000s. It protects the village from avalanches and debris flows from the **Schafberg**, where the permafrost in the debris is partly thawing.

Permafrost is thawing in the Arctic too. When ice-rich ground thaws, its volume shrinks, and the ground sinks. This creates hollows and lakes called **thermokarst**. In Siberia and Canada there are many thermokarst lakes. The best-known example is the **Batagaika crater** in Yakutia. It formed after forest clearing and warming and has been growing for decades, because the exposed ground ice keeps thawing.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is more permafrost than glacier area.
On the Matterhorn in 2003, bare ice could be seen in the rock where pieces had broken away.
The Batagaika crater in Siberia gets bigger every year.

teile.einleitung: The avalanche bulletin is a warning about avalanches in the mountains. In Switzerland it is published by the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research **SLF** in Davos. Anyone going off-piste in winter should always read it.
wichtigste: The European avalanche danger scale has **five levels**.
The levels are called low, moderate, considerable, high and very high.
Level 1 is shown in green, and the higher levels in yellow, orange and red.
In winter the bulletin comes out every day at 5 p.m., with an update at 8 a.m.
Most fatal avalanche accidents happen at the levels moderate and considerable.
A slope of about 30 degrees or more counts as a steep slope.

abschnitte.text: The avalanche bulletin describes how great the avalanche danger is in the different regions of the Alps. To do this, **SLF** experts evaluate measurements, weather data and observations. In winter the bulletin comes out every day at **5 p.m.** and is valid for the next day. An update follows at 8 a.m. In this way skiers, mountaineers and municipalities can adapt their plans.

The European scale has five levels: 1 **low**, 2 **moderate**, 3 **considerable**, 4 **high** and 5 **very high**. On maps they are shown in colours, from green through yellow and orange to red. At level 3, a single person can already trigger an avalanche on many steep slopes. At level 4, large spontaneous avalanches are likely. At level 5, many large avalanches are to be expected even on moderately steep ground.

You might think that most accidents happen at the highest level. That is not true. Most fatal avalanche accidents involving snow sports enthusiasts happen at **moderate** and **considerable**. At these levels many people are out in the terrain and often underestimate the danger. When the danger is very high, on the other hand, most people stay at home.

As well as the danger level, the bulletin gives the **altitude** and the **direction a slope faces**, also called its aspect, where it is especially dangerous. The steepness is important too: a slope of about 30 degrees or more counts as a **steep slope**. From this steepness, slab avalanches can break loose. Anyone who knows this information can avoid dangerous slopes.

The bulletin also describes typical **avalanche problems**. One example is **wet snow**: warmth or rain soaks the snowpack. The water weakens the bonds between the snow grains. That is why the danger of wet snow avalanches often rises during the day and in spring. Other problems are caused, for example, by new snow or by snow blown by the wind.

gewusst: The SLF is based in Davos in the canton of Grisons.
The avalanche danger scale is the same throughout Europe, so experts understand each other across borders.

teile.einleitung: Natural hazards are processes in nature that can threaten people, houses and roads. In Switzerland these are mainly floods, avalanches, debris flows, landslides, rockfall, storms and earthquakes. Because the country is so mountainous, people here have always lived with these dangers.
wichtigste: Natural hazards are natural processes that can cause harm to people and property.
Risk is usually defined as the probability of occurrence times the extent of damage.
Switzerland's integrated risk management includes prevention, response and recovery.
On hazard maps, red marks areas with considerable danger, where building is generally not allowed.
The WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos publishes the avalanche bulletin.
Protection forest makes up around half of the Swiss forest.
In May 2025, a glacier collapse at the Birch Glacier buried large parts of the Valais village of Blatten.

abschnitte.text: In **gravitational natural hazards** such as avalanches, rockfall, debris flows and landslides, gravity moves snow, rock or earth down the valley. Then there are **weather hazards** such as floods, storms, hail, heat and drought. Earthquakes, on the other hand, are caused by movements deep inside the Earth. A natural event only becomes dangerous when people or buildings are affected. A rockfall in an uninhabited valley is a natural event, but not a disaster.

Experts usually define **risk** as the probability of occurrence times the extent of damage. So a rare event with huge damage can be just as great a risk as a frequent small one. People often speak of a **100-year flood**, which happens on average once in 100 years. But that does not mean it only comes every 100 years. The probability that it happens at least once in 30 years is around 26 per cent.

The cantons draw up **hazard maps** that show the level of danger in colours. Red means considerable danger, and building is generally not allowed there. Blue stands for medium danger; building is only allowed there with conditions, for example with reinforced walls. Yellow means low danger. Municipalities must take these maps into account when planning building zones.

Switzerland relies on **integrated risk management** with three pillars. Prevention includes protective structures such as avalanche barriers and dams, but also hazard maps and warnings. Response covers the work of the fire brigade, civil protection and the army during an event. In recovery, damage is repaired and lessons are learnt from the event for the future. Together the three pillars form a cycle.

Around half of the Swiss forest is **protection forest**. Its trees hold snow in place, slow down falling stones and strengthen the soil with their roots; in this way they protect against avalanches, rockfall and landslides. The **SLF** in Davos publishes the avalanche bulletin every day in winter. MeteoSwiss warns of severe weather. There are five danger levels in the warnings, from low to very high.

In May 2025, a huge mass of ice, rock and debris broke off the **Birch Glacier** in the Lötschental. It buried large parts of the Valais village of Blatten. Because experts had been watching the unstable mountain closely, the village had been evacuated a few days before. The event shows how important monitoring and early warnings are. With climate change, glaciers and **permafrost** are thawing, which could make such events more frequent in the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fast stream of water, mud, stones and wood that shoots down a mountain stream.
A map that uses colours to show how strongly an area is threatened by natural hazards.
A forest that protects houses and roads from avalanches, rockfall and landslides.
Ground or rock that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: A 100-year flood can also happen in two years in a row.
Because cut-down mountain forests made flooding worse, Switzerland passed a law to protect mountain forests as early as 1876.
A large debris flow can sweep along boulders as big as a car.

teile.einleitung: Magnitude tells you how strong an earthquake is at its source. It is a measure of the energy released and is calculated from measurements by seismometers. It is different from intensity, which describes what is felt at a particular place.
wichtigste: **Magnitude** measures the strength of a quake at its source.
**Intensity** describes the effects at a particular place.
The European intensity scale **EMS-98** has 12 levels.
For strong quakes, the **moment magnitude** is used today.
With each step in magnitude, the energy rises about 32-fold.
For very weak quakes, the magnitude can even be negative.

abschnitte.text: In an earthquake, energy is suddenly released underground. The shaking travels through the Earth as waves. **Seismometers** record them. From these measurements, experts calculate the **magnitude**. A quake has only one magnitude, no matter where it is measured. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes.

**Intensity** describes how strongly a quake affects a particular place. It depends on what people feel and what is damaged. Close to the source it is high, far away it is low. In Europe the **EMS-98** is used. It has **12 levels**, written in Roman numerals, from I (not felt) to XII (completely devastating).

The magnitude scale is **logarithmic**. With each step, the energy released rises about **32-fold**. So a quake of magnitude 6 releases about 32 times 32, around **1,000 times** more energy than one of magnitude 4. The scale has no lower limit: sensitive instruments also measure tiny quakes with **negative** values.

The first well-known scale came from **Charles Richter**. But it is inaccurate for very strong quakes. That is why experts today mainly use the **moment magnitude**. It was introduced in 1979 by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori. It takes into account the size of the **rupture surface** and how far the rock has moved. This makes it suitable even for the strongest quakes.

On **6 February 2023**, a severe earthquake struck south-eastern Turkey. The main quake had a magnitude of **7.8**. A few hours later, a second strong quake followed. Large areas in Turkey and Syria were affected. Many buildings collapsed, and a great many people lost their homes.

gewusst: In Switzerland, instruments record hundreds of earthquakes every year, but nobody feels most of them.
The strongest earthquake ever measured happened in Chile in 1960.

teile.einleitung: A radiosonde is a small measuring device that rises into the sky on a weather balloon. On the way up it measures temperature, humidity and air pressure and radios the values back to Earth. These data are very important for weather forecasts.
wichtigste: As it rises, a radiosonde measures temperature, humidity and pressure.
The wind high up is worked out from GPS tracking of its drift.
In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss radiosondes are launched from Payerne.
Around the world, radiosondes go up at the same time, mainly at 00 and 12 UTC.
The balloon is filled with hydrogen or helium and rises at about 5 m/s.
At a height of about 30 kilometres the balloon bursts because it expands.
The measurements are sent by radio to a ground station.

abschnitte.titel: A balloon with a measuring device
abschnitte.text: The **radiosonde** is a light box with sensors, a battery and a transmitter. It hangs on a string under a **weather balloon**. The balloon is filled with **hydrogen** or **helium**; both gases are lighter than air. It typically rises at about **5 metres per second**. On the way up the sonde measures **temperature**, **humidity** and **pressure**.

The radiosonde sends its measurements **by radio** to a ground station all the time. Modern sondes have a **GPS receiver**. The wind carries the sonde along with it, and from its **drift** the direction and strength of the wind high up are calculated. This gives an accurate picture of the air from the ground up into the stratosphere.

The higher the balloon rises, the thinner the air becomes. The pressure outside falls, and the balloon **expands**. At a height of about **30 kilometres** it becomes so big that it bursts. The sonde then falls back down, often on a small parachute. An ascent usually takes about one and a half to two hours.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** launches radiosondes at **Payerne** in the canton of Vaud. There are hundreds of such stations around the world. They mainly launch at the same time, at **00 and 12 UTC**, which is Coordinated Universal Time. In this way weather services everywhere on Earth get a picture of the atmosphere at the same time. These data are fed into the computer models for weather forecasting.

The measurements from an ascent are plotted on a **thermodynamic diagram**, for example an **emagram**. In it, temperature is plotted against pressure. From it, experts can see whether the air is stable or whether thunderstorms can form. Fog layers and inversions, which means warm air above cold air, also become visible.

gewusst: A weather balloon can swell to many times its starting size before it bursts.
Radiosondes are usually used only once and often land far from where they were launched.

teile.einleitung: Greenhouse gases are gases in the air that hold back heat radiation. Without them the Earth would be much colder, but the extra greenhouse gases released by people are warming the climate.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases hold back heat radiation in the atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide contributes most to the man-made greenhouse effect.
A CO2 molecule is made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Joseph Fourier described the effect around 1824, and Svante Arrhenius calculated it in 1896.
Global warming potential compares the effect of a gas with CO2.
Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms the Earth’s surface. The surface gives off heat as **infrared radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** absorb this **heat radiation** and radiate part of it back towards the Earth. This keeps the surface warmer. The main components of air, **nitrogen** and **oxygen**, make up around 99 per cent of dry air. Their molecules, made of two identical atoms, hardly absorb heat radiation at all.

The most important greenhouse gas released by people is **carbon dioxide** (CO2). A molecule consists of one **carbon atom** and two **oxygen atoms**. It is straight, but it can vibrate and absorb heat radiation as it does so. CO2 is mainly produced by burning **coal, oil and natural gas**. It is responsible for most of the extra warming.

Other gases warm the climate too. **Nitrous oxide** (N2O) is commonly called **laughing gas**, because it used to be used as an anaesthetic. It comes mainly from **nitrogen fertiliser** in farming. The artificial gas **sulphur hexafluoride** (SF6) insulates well against electrical voltage and is used in switchgear. Per kilogram it is more than 20,000 times stronger than CO2 and stays in the air for thousands of years.

To compare gases there is the **global warming potential**. It shows how strongly a gas warms over a period, usually **100 years**, compared with the same amount of CO2. CO2 has the value **1**. Gases with a high value matter even in small amounts. Switzerland also calculates its climate targets with such values.

Around **1824** the French mathematician **Joseph Fourier** noticed that, given its distance from the Sun, the Earth should actually be colder. He suspected that the layer of air holds back heat, similar to a **glass bell jar**. In **1896** the Swedish researcher **Svante Arrhenius** was the first to calculate how much the Earth would warm with more CO2. He is regarded as a pioneer of climate research.

gewusst: Without natural greenhouse gases the average temperature of the Earth would be far below freezing.
Water vapour is also an important natural greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: A lake is a large area of water surrounded by land on all sides. Switzerland has around 1,500 lakes, which is why the country is also famous for its lake landscapes. Lakes are habitats for fish and birds, stores of drinking water and popular places for outings.
wichtigste: A lake is a body of still water surrounded by land on all sides.
Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.
Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland.
Lake Constance lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
A small, often shallow body of still water is called a pond.
The water in Swiss lakes is fresh, not salty.
Many Swiss lakes formed in glacial valleys after the last Ice Age.

abschnitte.text: A lake is a body of **still water**, which means water that does not flow in one direction like a river. Usually streams or rivers flow into a lake, and a river flows out again. Small, often shallow bodies of water are called **ponds**. Most lakes contain fresh water. But there are also salt lakes such as the Dead Sea, which is so salty that you almost float in it by yourself.

Most Swiss lakes were shaped by the **glaciers** of the Ice Age. The masses of ice scraped out deep basins, which filled with water after the ice melted. Other lakes formed because a landslide blocked a valley, as with Lake Cauma in the Grisons. Lakes that people create with a dam wall are called **reservoirs**. There are many of them in the Alps, for example Lac des Dix behind the Grande Dixence dam in Valais.

**Lake Geneva** is the largest lake in Switzerland, at around 580 square kilometres, although part of it belongs to France. Lake Constance lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria. **Lake Neuchâtel** is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland. Other well-known lakes are Lake Lucerne, Lake Zurich, Lake Thun and Lake Maggiore in Ticino. Many cities, such as Geneva, Zurich, Lucerne and Lugano, lie right on a lake.

Fish such as whitefish, perch and lake trout live in lakes. Reeds and water lilies grow along the shore, and birds such as great crested grebes and coots nest there. Tiny algae and creatures, the **plankton**, are the basic food for many animals. In summer the surface water is warm, while deep down it stays cold all year round. Many lakes used to be badly polluted, but thanks to sewage treatment plants their water is very clean again today.

More than 5,000 years ago, people were already building their villages on stilts by Swiss lakes. These **pile dwellings** have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. Today lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Zurich supply drinking water for many people. In summer you can swim, go boating or do stand-up paddleboarding in most Swiss lakes. Scheduled boats run on many large lakes, including historic paddle steamers.

The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth, and its water is slightly salty. Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world, at more than 1,600 metres. A large share of the fresh water on the Earth's surface is stored in the Great Lakes of North America. Compared with these giants, even the largest Swiss lake, Lake Geneva, seems small.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body of water whose water does not flow in one direction, for example a lake or pond.
A small, often shallow body of still water.
A lake made artificially by a dam wall or embankment.
Houses from the Stone Age and Bronze Age that stood on wooden stilts by the lakeshore.

gewusst: At its deepest point, Lake Geneva is around 310 metres deep.
In very cold winters even large lakes freeze over; the whole of Lake Constance last froze in 1963, which in Swiss German is called a “Seegfrörni”.
Lake Geneva has a kind of small-scale tide in which the water sloshes back and forth; this is called a seiche.

teile.einleitung: Stromboli is a small volcanic island in the Mediterranean north of Sicily. Its volcano is active almost all the time and spits glowing lava into the air several times an hour.
wichtigste: Stromboli is a volcanic island in Italy.
The volcano very often has small eruptions, usually several times an hour.
It is called the lighthouse of the Mediterranean.
Its summit is about 920 metres above the sea.
Lava rolls into the sea over the Sciara del Fuoco.
Small, regular eruptions are named “Strombolian” after it.

abschnitte.titel: An island made of a volcano
abschnitte.text: **Stromboli** is one of the Aeolian Islands off the coast of Sicily in Italy. The whole island is an **active volcano**. Its summit is about **920 metres** above the sea. But most of the volcano is under water. Measured from the sea floor, it is much higher.

Stromboli has been active almost all the time for a very long time. There are usually small eruptions **several times an hour**. Glowing scraps of lava fly into the air. You can see this best **at night**, when the lava glows brightly. During the day you mainly see smoke. Sailors saw the glow from far away, which is why the volcano is called the **lighthouse of the Mediterranean**.

On one side of the island there is a steep slope with no houses. It is called the **Sciara del Fuoco**, which means roughly “fire slide” in Italian. Glowing lumps and sometimes lava flows roll down this slope into the sea. You can watch this well from a boat.

There are small **villages** by the sea on Stromboli. A few hundred people live there, many of them from tourism. Visitors come to see the eruptions. The climb to the summit is often restricted, because larger eruptions can be dangerous.

Experts divide volcanic eruptions into different types. Small, regular eruptions in which scraps of lava fly up are called **Strombolian**. They are named after Stromboli. At other volcanoes around the world, too, people speak of Strombolian activity.

gewusst: Stromboli is one of the volcanoes on Earth that has been continuously active for the longest time.
Scraps of lava that fly through the air and solidify are called lava bombs.

teile.einleitung: **Sedimentation** means that particles such as sand, gravel or mud settle and are deposited. This happens mainly where water flows more slowly. Over a long time, sedimentation changes whole landscapes, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Sedimentation is the deposition of particles.
A river deposits a lot of material when its current slows down.
Coarse and heavy particles settle first.
A delta can form at river mouths.
In 1714 the Kander was diverted into Lake Thun, where it is building a delta.
In undisturbed layers, the bottom one is normally the oldest.

abschnitte.text: Rivers carry a lot of material with them: stones, gravel, sand and fine mud. As long as the water flows fast, the material stays on the move. When the **current slows down**, it sinks to the bottom. This process is called **sedimentation**, and the deposited material is called **sediment**. The **coarse and heavy** particles settle first, and fine mud only in very calm water.

When a river flows into a lake or the sea, it suddenly slows down. There it deposits a lot of material. This creates a **delta**, a flat landform at the mouth. A well-known example in Switzerland is the **Kander**: in **1714** it was diverted into **Lake Thun** to prevent flooding. Since then it has been building up a delta there.

The **Rhône** brings a lot of fine material down from the mountains of Valais. Where it flows into **Lake Geneva**, it is cloudy and grey. In the lake, this **suspended material** slowly settles. That is why the Rhône is much clearer where it flows out in **Geneva**. So lakes act like huge settling tanks.

Sediments are deposited layer by layer. In undisturbed deposits, the **bottom layer is normally the oldest**, and the top one the youngest. As in a book, you can read the history of a landscape in this way. Over a very long time, sediments can turn into solid **sedimentary rocks**.

If rivers keep bringing material into a lake, it becomes shallower and smaller over time. On the shore, reeds and other plants grow further and further into the lake. In the long run the lake **silts up** and becomes a bog or solid land. With large lakes, however, this takes a very long time.

gewusst: Lake Brienz and Lake Thun probably used to form a single lake. The rivers Lütschine and Lombach built up the Bödeli between them, on which Interlaken stands today.
When the Kander was diverted, a new deep gorge formed, through which the river has flowed into Lake Thun ever since.

teile.einleitung: A **sandy beach** is more than a place to swim. The sand tells you where it came from, and many animals live there. There are also rules on the beach that protect swimmers.
wichtigste: A line of seaweed and shells shows how high the water came at high tide.
Black sand, as in Iceland, comes from volcanic rock.
White sand in the Caribbean is made of ground-up coral and shells.
Sea turtles lay their eggs in the sand.
Crabs often walk sideways across the beach.
On many beaches a red flag means: no swimming.

abschnitte.text: Not all sand looks the same. In **Iceland** there are black beaches, because the sand comes from dark **volcanic rock**. In the **Caribbean** the sand is often white. It is made of ground-up **coral** and **seashells**. Many beaches in Europe have pale sand made of the mineral quartz. If a beach is made of lots of small stones, it is called a **shingle beach**.

By the sea, the water rises and falls regularly. At **high tide** it brings seaweed, shells and pieces of wood with it. When the water goes back again, they are left behind. This creates a line, the **strandline**. It shows how high the water came at the last high tide.

**Sea turtles** crawl onto land and lay their eggs in the warm sand. When the young hatch, they scramble straight to the sea. **Crabs** often walk sideways across the sand and quickly hide in holes. Gulls and other birds also look for food on the beach.

A sandcastle holds better if it is made of **damp sand** than of dry sand. The water between the grains holds it together. Dry sand simply trickles apart. But if you add too much water, the sand turns into mush.

On many beaches, **flags** show whether it is safe to swim. A **red flag** means: no swimming, for example because of high waves or dangerous currents. You should always follow these signs and listen to the lifeguards.

gewusst: Some of the white sand on tropical beaches comes from parrotfish, which nibble coral and pass it out again finely ground.
Young sea turtles find their way to the sea by heading for the brighter horizon above the water.

teile.einleitung: A U-shaped valley, or glacial trough, is a valley with a U-shaped cross-section that a glacier has carved out. There are many U-shaped valleys in the Swiss Alps; the best known is the Lauterbrunnen Valley.
wichtigste: A U-shaped valley has a U-shaped cross-section, a river valley a V-shaped one.
The Lauterbrunnen Valley is a well-known U-shaped valley in the Bernese Oberland.
Side valleys that end high above the valley floor are called hanging valleys.
The flat ledge above the steep walls is called the trough shoulder.
A U-shaped valley flooded by the sea is called a fjord.
A rock barrier across the valley is called a rock bar.

abschnitte.text: A river cuts downwards and forms steep slopes that meet at the bottom. This creates a **V-shaped valley** with a **V-shaped** cross-section. A **glacier**, on the other hand, fills the whole valley. It grinds away the slopes and the floor and forms a wide **U**. Such a valley is called a **U-shaped valley**. During the Ice Ages the Alpine valleys were filled with huge glaciers.

A well-known example is the **Lauterbrunnen Valley** in the Bernese Oberland. It has a flat valley floor and almost vertical rock walls. Above the walls lies a flatter ledge, the **trough shoulder**. There you find Alpine pastures and villages such as **Mürren** and **Wengen**. The flat valley floor formed because streams and lakes deposited a lot of **gravel and sand** after the glacier retreated.

The large main glacier carved its valley much deeper than the small side glaciers. That is why the side valleys end high up in the rock wall. They are called **hanging valleys**. Their streams plunge as **waterfalls** over the steep trough wall into the main valley. A well-known example is the **Staubbach Falls** near Lauterbrunnen.

Not all rock is equally hard. A glacier grinds hard rock away less strongly. So **rock barriers** are left standing across the valley. They are called **rock bars**. Rivers have often cut through such bars in narrow gorges. After the Ice Age there was sometimes a lake behind a rock bar.

After the Ice Age the **sea level** rose because a lot of ice melted. On some coasts the sea pushed into deep glacial valleys. A U-shaped valley flooded by the sea is called a **fjord**. The fjords in **Norway** are especially famous. They are often very deep and surrounded by steep rock walls.

gewusst: In the Lauterbrunnen Valley there are a great many waterfalls that plunge down from hanging valleys.
The Reuss Valley in Uri and the Hasli Valley are also U-shaped valleys formed by glaciers.

teile.einleitung: A volcano is a mountain or an opening in the Earth’s surface from which hot, liquid rock, ash and gases come out. Volcanoes show us how hot it is deep inside the Earth. Some have been sleeping for thousands of years, others erupt almost every day.
wichtigste: A volcano forms where molten rock from inside the Earth reaches the surface.
The hot, liquid rock that flows out of a volcano is called lava.
The opening at the top of a volcano is called a crater.
When a volcano throws out lava and ash, this is called an eruption.
Etna on the Italian island of Sicily is a famous, very active volcano.
Today there are no active volcanoes in Switzerland.
Worldwide there are around 1350 volcanoes on land that are considered possibly active.

abschnitte.text: A volcano is a place where **magma** from inside the Earth pushes up to the surface. Beneath the volcano there is often a **magma chamber** in which the molten rock collects. It rises through a vent and comes out at the top in the **crater**. As soon as it is at the surface, the molten rock is called lava. Over time lava and ash pile up into a mountain.

Depending on its type, **lava** is about 700 to 1200 degrees Celsius hot. Runny lava flows down the slope like a glowing river. Thick, sticky lava, on the other hand, builds up and can lead to violent explosions. The volcano then hurls ash, lumps of rock and gases high into the air. Cooled lava becomes solid rock such as basalt.

Runny lava forms flat, wide **shield volcanoes**, like the volcanoes on Hawaii. Many layers of lava and ash build up steep, cone-shaped **stratovolcanoes**, such as Vesuvius near Naples or Fuji in Japan. Small hills of cinders are called cinder cones. If a volcano collapses in on itself after a huge eruption, a large basin forms, a caldera.

**Etna** on Sicily is the highest active volcano in Europe at more than 3300 metres and erupts often. On the island of Stromboli, the volcano of the same name spits small fountains of lava into the air almost all the time. In the year 79 AD Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii. In Iceland and on Hawaii you can sometimes even watch lava flows from a safe distance. The largest volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa on Hawaii.

Today there are no active volcanoes in Switzerland. But very close by, in the **Hegau** in southern Germany north of Schaffhausen, stand the remains of volcanoes that were active about 15 to 7 million years ago. There are also extinct volcanoes in the Eifel in Germany and in the Auvergne in France. The nearest active volcanoes from Switzerland are in Italy.

Experts who study volcanoes are called **volcanologists**. They measure small earthquakes, gases and the swelling of the ground to predict eruptions. Despite the danger, millions of people live near volcanoes. This is because volcanic soils are very fertile, and in Iceland volcanic geothermal heat is used for heating and to produce electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molten rock below the Earth’s surface.
Molten rock that flows out of a volcano onto the surface.
Opening at the top of a volcano from which lava and ash come out.
Researcher who studies volcanoes.

gewusst: The largest known volcano in the solar system is Olympus Mons on Mars; it is about three times as high as Mount Everest.
Most of the Earth’s volcanoes lie unseen under the sea.
On Hawaii the land keeps growing a little bigger because of new lava.

teile.einleitung: Quartz is one of the most common minerals in the Earth's crust. It comes in colourless, purple, yellow or smoky brown forms. Quartz is found in sand, in many rocks and even in watches.
wichtigste: Quartz is made of silicon dioxide (SiO₂).
The purple variety is called amethyst, the yellow one citrine.
Smoky quartz is brown to almost black and is often found in the Swiss Alps.
Pale sand is usually made mostly of quartz.
Quartz has no cleavage and breaks with a shell-like fracture.
Watches contain a quartz crystal because it vibrates very evenly.

abschnitte.text: Quartz is made of **silicon dioxide**, a compound of silicon and oxygen (SiO₂). It is very hard: on the Mohs scale it has a hardness of 7, so it scratches glass. Well-grown crystals are six-sided columns with a point. Quartz has no **cleavage**. When it breaks, a curved surface forms that looks like a shell. This is called **conchoidal fracture**.

Pure, see-through quartz is called **rock crystal**. Small amounts of other substances or natural radiation give quartz its colour. The purple variety is called **amethyst**, the yellow one **citrine**. There is also pink **rose quartz**. Brown to almost black **smoky quartz** gets its colour from natural radiation from the rock.

In the Swiss Alps there are often beautiful crystals in cracks in the rock, called **fissures**. People who search for them are called **Strahler** in Switzerland. They find rock crystal and **smoky quartz** especially often. At the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri, huge groups of smoky quartz were discovered. In many cantons crystal hunting comes with rules, and a permit is often needed.

Quartz is very resistant to weather and water. When rocks such as granite weather, the quartz grains are left behind. Rivers carry them away and round them off. That is why pale **sand** on beaches and in rivers is usually made mostly of quartz. **Glass** is also made from quartz sand.

If you press on a quartz crystal, a small electric voltage is produced. The other way round, a voltage makes the crystal vibrate. A small quartz in a **quartz watch** vibrates very **evenly**, many thousands of times a second. The electronics count these vibrations and work out the seconds from them. That is why quartz watches are very accurate.

gewusst: The quartz in many watches vibrates exactly 32,768 times a second.
In ancient times, people thought rock crystal was extremely deeply frozen ice.

teile.einleitung: The South Pole is the southernmost point on Earth. It lies in the middle of the continent of Antarctica, which is almost completely covered by a thick shield of ice.
wichtigste: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, on 14 December 1911.
Robert Scott arrived about a month later.
At its thickest, the ice on Antarctica is more than 4 kilometres thick.
In 1983, −89.2 °C was measured at Vostok Station, a world record.
Penguins live in Antarctica, but no polar bears.
There are no permanent inhabitants, only researchers who stay for a while.

abschnitte.text: At the **South Pole**, all the lines of longitude meet. From there, every direction points north. The pole lies on the continent of **Antarctica**, high up on a huge sheet of ice. At its thickest the ice is **more than 4 kilometres** thick. That is higher than most Alpine peaks.

At the beginning of the 20th century, several explorers wanted to be the first to reach the South Pole. The Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** made it on **14 December 1911** with dog sleds. The Briton **Robert Scott** arrived about a month later and found Amundsen's tent. Scott and his companions died on the way back in the cold and storms.

Antarctica is the coldest continent on Earth. In **1983**, **−89.2 °C** was measured at the Russian **Vostok** Station. That is the lowest air temperature ever measured. It is also very dry there and often stormy. In winter it stays dark for months, and in summer the sun does not set.

**Penguins** live on the coasts of Antarctica. They cannot fly, but they are excellent swimmers, because their wings have become flippers. Seals and whales also live in the sea around it. There are no **polar bears** there. They live only in the far north, around the North Pole.

There are **no permanent inhabitants** in Antarctica. Researchers live there for a few months in **stations**. Right at the South Pole there is an American research station. The scientists study, for example, the ice, the weather and the sky. An international treaty says that Antarctica must be used peacefully and for research.

gewusst: Most of the Earth's fresh water is stored in the ice of Antarctica.
Swiss researchers also drill ice cores in Antarctica to study the climate of past times.

teile.einleitung: Avalanche barriers are structures that protect villages, roads and railway lines from avalanches. In Switzerland you can see them on many steep mountain slopes. Some stop an avalanche from breaking loose at all; others steer it or slow it down.
wichtigste: **Supporting structures** such as snow bridges stand in the starting zone, where avalanches break loose.
**Snow fences** hold back snow blown by the wind.
An **avalanche gallery** is a roof over a road that the avalanche slides over.
**Deflecting dams** steer avalanches past villages, and **catching dams** stop them.
Young trees are planted so that a protection forest can take over the job later.
Safety services also trigger avalanches on purpose with explosives.

abschnitte.titel: Snow bridges on the steep slope
abschnitte.text: Avalanches usually break loose in the upper part of a steep slope, in what is called the **starting zone**. **Supporting structures** are put up there. The best known are **snow bridges**: lattice-like steel frames that stand in long rows on the slope. They support the snowpack so that it does not start to slide. This means no avalanche forms at all.

The wind can move large amounts of snow. Behind ridges it settles and forms dangerous **cornices** and thick cushions of snow. **Snow fences** on the ridges slow down the wind. This makes the snow drop in a place where it is not dangerous. In this way it stops too much snow from collecting on the steep slope.

Further down in the valley, roads and railways are protected with **avalanche galleries**. These are structures open at the side with a strong roof. The avalanche slides over them, and the cars underneath stay protected. A **deflecting dam** is a wall built at an angle that guides the masses of snow past a village. A **catching dam** stands across the path of the avalanche and holds it back before it reaches the houses.

A healthy **mountain forest** also holds the snowpack in place. In Switzerland, a large part of the forest is protection forest. That is why young trees are often planted above barriers. The barriers protect the small trees until the forest is big enough. Later the forest can take over part of the job, and that is cheaper than new structures.

Sometimes it is safer to set off an avalanche deliberately. When the avalanche danger is high, safety services blow up dangerous slopes with explosives. Pistes and roads are closed while this happens. In this way the avalanche comes down under control before it can unexpectedly endanger people. This method is often used in ski areas and along mountain pass roads.

gewusst: Many Swiss mountain villages are protected today by rows of snow bridges kilometres long.
In Switzerland, protection forest is seen as one of the most important and cheapest ways of protecting against natural hazards.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's mantle is solid almost everywhere, and yet it is moving. Hot rock rises very slowly, and cooler rock sinks. This mantle convection carries heat from inside the Earth and is closely linked to the movement of the tectonic plates.
wichtigste: Over millions of years, the solid mantle rock **creeps** like a very thick liquid.
Hot rock expands, becomes less dense and rises.
Around 1930, **Arthur Holmes** suggested mantle convection as the driving force of continental drift.
The **Rayleigh number** decides whether convection starts.
**Mantle plumes** are thought to lie under Hawaii and Iceland.
At the bottom of the mantle lies the **D'' layer**.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's mantle is made mostly of solid rock. But at the high temperatures inside the Earth, the crystals can deform very slowly. This happens through tiny faults in the crystal lattice that move around. Over geological timescales, the mantle therefore behaves like an extremely thick liquid. It moves only a few centimetres a year.

You know convection from a pot of soup on the stove. Heat makes the rock expand, and its **density** falls. **Buoyancy** makes it rise, while cooler, denser rock sinks. Whether convection starts in a heated layer is described by the **Rayleigh number**. It compares buoyancy with the slowing effect of thickness and with heat conduction. For the Earth's mantle it is far above the critical value.

Alfred Wegener had described continental drift but could not explain what moves the continents. Around 1930, the British geologist **Arthur Holmes** suggested that heat from radioactive decay drives currents in the mantle. Today it is known that the plates themselves also play a part. The raised mid-ocean ridges push the plates away sideways; this is called **ridge push**.

**Mantle plumes** are probably chimney-like upwellings of hot rock from great depth. Under the plate they partly melt. This creates volcanic areas away from plate boundaries, for example under **Hawaii** and **Iceland**. At the bottom of the mantle there are two huge zones where seismic waves travel more slowly, under **Africa** and under the **Pacific**. Many plumes seem to rise from their edges.

With **seismic tomography**, researchers use seismic waves to make pictures of the Earth's interior. They show that some diving plates sink below 660 km deep into the **lower mantle**. Under America and South-East Asia, cold remains of plates reach almost to the core. There lies the **D'' layer**, a few hundred kilometres thick. Sunken plates could collect here and plumes could start.

gewusst: The plates move about as fast as fingernails grow.
The huge zones at the bottom of the mantle are thousands of kilometres across.

teile.einleitung: A **sandbank** is a hill of sand in shallow water. Sometimes it lies just below the surface, sometimes it appears at low tide. It can be dangerous for ships, but for seals it is a good resting place.
wichtigste: A sandbank is a hill of sand in shallow water.
Ships can run aground on sandbanks and get stuck.
On the North Sea, many sandbanks appear at low tide.
Seals like to rest on sandbanks.
Buoys and navigation marks show where sandbanks lie.
Currents keep moving sandbanks around.

abschnitte.text: A **sandbank** forms where water deposits sand. This can happen in the sea, at river mouths or in rivers. The water brings sand with it and leaves it where it flows more slowly. In this way a hill grows under the water over time. Because **currents** and waves constantly carry sand away and deposit it elsewhere, a sandbank does not always stay in the same place.

On the **North Sea**, the water rises and falls twice a day. At **low tide** the water is low, and many sandbanks appear. At **high tide** they disappear under the water again. That is why in the Wadden Sea you can walk across the sea floor at certain times, but only with an experienced guide.

**Seals** like to lie on sandbanks. There they rest, warm themselves in the sun and have their young. Because the sandbank is surrounded by water, they are fairly safe there. But you should not go too close to them, so that they are not disturbed.

If a sandbank lies just below the water, you often cannot see it. A ship can **run aground** on it and get stuck. That is why **buoys** and other **navigation marks** show where the water is deep enough. Sandbanks are marked on sea charts. Because they move, they have to be surveyed again and again.

In the middle of the North Sea lies the **Dogger Bank**, a huge sandbank. There the sea is only a few dozen metres deep. The Dogger Bank is an important fishing ground. During the last Ice Age, sea level was lower, and the area was dry land at that time.

gewusst: During the Ice Age, the Dogger Bank was dry land on which people and animals lived.
Some sandbanks grow so high over time that they become islands.

teile.einleitung: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell of the Earth. It is made up of the Earth's crust and the uppermost part of the mantle. It is broken into large plates that move slowly.
wichtigste: The lithosphere includes the **crust** and the uppermost **mantle**.
Below it lies the softer **asthenosphere**; the boundary is usually drawn at about 1,300 °C.
Oceanic lithosphere gets thicker with age, up to about 100 km at most.
Under old continental cores, the **cratons**, it can be up to about 250 km thick.
The largest plate is the **Pacific Plate**.
When the Alps formed, the **Adriatic Plate** pushed against Europe.

abschnitte.text: The word lithosphere comes from Greek and means “sphere of rock”. It is made up of the **Earth's crust** and the uppermost, cool part of the **mantle**. Below it comes the **asthenosphere**. The boundary is usually drawn at a temperature of about **1,300 °C**. Below that, the mantle rock is so hot that it can slowly creep over a long time. Above it, it behaves rigidly.

New oceanic lithosphere forms at the **mid-ocean ridges**. There it is very thin. As it moves away from the ridge, it **cools down**. Upper mantle rock becomes rigid and is added to it. At the same time, the rock contracts, becomes denser and sinks deeper. In this way it becomes up to about **100 km** thick. The oldest ocean crust in the open ocean is around **180 million years** old and lies in the western Pacific.

Under the continents, the lithosphere is usually thicker. It reaches especially deep under very old continental cores, the **cratons**, for example in Canada or South Africa. There the boundary lies at 200 to **250 km**. Continental lithosphere is lighter than oceanic lithosphere and so hardly ever dives down into the depths.

The lithosphere is broken into large and small **plates**. The largest is the **Pacific Plate**, with around 100 million square kilometres. It is made almost entirely of oceanic lithosphere. Important for Switzerland is the smaller **Adriatic Plate**, also called the Apulian Plate. When the **Alps** formed, it pushed against Europe from the south. Its rock now forms parts of the Southern Alps.

Although the lithosphere is rigid, it can **bend elastically** under a heavy load, like a plank with a weight on it. Under large volcanic islands such as **Hawaii**, the plate bends downwards. All around it a trench forms, and further out a slight bulge. Thick ice sheets also press the lithosphere down.

gewusst: Oceanic lithosphere is much younger than many rocks on the continents, because it keeps diving down in subduction zones.
Under cratons, rigid rock reaches about twice as deep as under old oceans.

teile.einleitung: **Salinity** tells you how much salt is dissolved in water. In the sea it is on average about 35 grams per kilogram of water, but the value can vary a lot depending on the place.
wichtigste: The average salinity of seawater is about 35 grams per kilogram.
Chloride makes up the largest share of the dissolved salts.
The Red Sea is especially salty, with values around 40 grams per kilogram.
The Baltic Sea is a brackish sea with little salt.
Today salinity is usually measured by electrical conductivity.
Practical salinity is dimensionless, which means it has no unit.

abschnitte.text: Many substances are dissolved in seawater, especially **chloride** and **sodium**. Together they form ordinary table salt. Chloride makes up the largest share by mass. There are also sulphate, magnesium, calcium and potassium, among others. According to the **principle of constant proportions**, the ratios of these main ions are almost the same everywhere in the sea; only the total amount changes.

Where a lot of water evaporates and little fresh water is added, salinity rises. This is the case in the **Red Sea**, with values around 40 grams per kilogram. In the **subtropics**, the surface is also especially salty, because more water evaporates there than falls as rain. The **Baltic Sea**, on the other hand, is a **brackish sea**: many rivers bring fresh water, and there is little exchange with the North Sea.

Salt water conducts electric current better than fresh water. That is why salinity is usually measured today by **electrical conductivity**. Since 1978 there has been the **practical salinity scale** for this. The values are **dimensionless**, so no unit is written after them. Even so, you often see figures given as “per mille” or “PSU”.

When **sea ice** forms, most of the salt is pushed out as the water freezes. The water around it becomes saltier and therefore heavier. Salty, cold water sinks into the depths. In this way salinity helps to drive large **ocean currents** that spread heat over the whole Earth.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea, the salt content is almost ten times as high as in the open ocean.
Sea ice contains much less salt than the seawater it formed from.

teile.einleitung: Ocean waves are movements of the water's surface. Most of them are made by the wind. Some are gentle and good for surfing; others are huge and dangerous.
wichtigste: Most waves are made by the **wind**.
The highest point of a wave is called the **crest**, and the lowest the **trough**.
The stronger the wind blows, the **higher** the waves get.
In a wave, it is mainly the movement that travels; the water stays almost in place.
A **tsunami** is caused by an undersea earthquake.
**Rogue waves** are single, especially high waves.

abschnitte.text: When the **wind** blows over the water, it pushes it up into waves. First small ripples form. If the wind blows harder and for longer, it gives the water more energy, and the waves get **higher**. The distance over which the wind blows also plays a part. That is why the waves on the open sea are much bigger than on a Swiss lake.

Every wave has a highest point, the **crest**. That is where the water is highest. Between two crests lies a hollow, the **trough**. The distance from one crest to the next is called the **wavelength**. The difference between crest and trough is the **wave height**.

If a ball is floating in the sea and a wave passes under it, it does not travel along with it. It **rises and falls** in almost the same place. In a wave, it is mainly the **movement** that travels on. The water itself only moves up and down in a circle. Only close to the beach, where it gets shallow, does the wave break and the water roll onto the land.

You can **surf** on good waves. In surfing, you glide down the wave on a board. Surfers wait for waves of the right size and shape. Famous surfing areas are, for example, on the coasts of Hawaii, Portugal or Australia. In Switzerland there are also facilities with artificial waves.

Not all waves come from the wind. An **undersea earthquake** on the sea floor can lift the water strongly. This creates a **tsunami**. On the open sea it can hardly be seen, but at the coast it can become very high and cause great damage. **Rogue waves** are single waves that are much higher than the waves around them. They are rare, but dangerous for ships.

gewusst: The word tsunami comes from Japanese and means “harbour wave”.
For a long time, rogue waves were thought to be sailors' tall tales, until one was measured at an oil platform in the North Sea in 1995.

teile.einleitung: A **seismometer** measures how the ground moves. It is the heart of every earthquake station. Seismometers stand not only on the Earth; they have also been taken to the Moon and to Mars.
wichtigste: A classic seismometer uses an inert mass that stays still while the ground moves.
Modern seismometers measure in three directions: vertical, north-south and east-west.
They turn the ground movement into electrical signals.
They are often placed in tunnels, caves or boreholes, where there is less disturbance.
Apollo astronauts set up seismometers that detected moonquakes.
In 2018, NASA's InSight probe took a seismometer to Mars; ETH Zurich helped build it.

abschnitte.titel: The principle of the inert mass
abschnitte.text: A classic seismometer has a **heavy mass** hanging on a spring or a pendulum. When the ground moves, the mass stays almost still because of its **inertia**. The casing, on the other hand, moves with the ground. From the difference between the mass and the casing, the ground movement can be measured.

Modern seismometers measure the movement in **three directions**: **vertical**, **north-south** and **east-west**. They turn the movement into **electrical signals**, which a computer stores. Around 1900, the German geophysicist **Emil Wiechert** built large pendulum seismographs in Göttingen, which were used all over the world for a long time.

Seismometers are very sensitive. Traffic, wind and even footsteps can disturb the measurements. That is why they are often placed in **tunnels**, **caves** or **boreholes**. It is quieter there. To work out the **epicentre** of a quake from the distances, you need data from at least **three stations**.

During the **Apollo missions**, astronauts set up seismometers on the Moon. The instruments detected **moonquakes**. Some were caused by meteorite impacts, others deep inside the Moon. In this way researchers learnt that the Moon is not completely still either.

In **2018**, NASA's **InSight** probe landed on Mars. It took a seismometer with it, which **ETH Zurich** helped to build. The instrument recorded many **marsquakes**. From these measurements, researchers were able to work out how big the core of Mars is and how thick its crust is.

gewusst: Moonquakes can ring on much longer than earthquakes, because the dry moon rock hardly damps the waves.
A good seismometer notices ground movements much smaller than the thickness of a hair.

teile.einleitung: The Rhine is one of the largest rivers in Europe. It rises in the Alps of the Grisons and flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands. For Switzerland it is very important as a waterway to the sea.
wichtigste: The Anterior Rhine and the Posterior Rhine join at Reichenau to form the Alpine Rhine.
The Alpine Rhine flows past Chur to Lake Constance.
Along the Alpine Rhine, Liechtenstein and Austria border the canton of St Gallen.
Between Lake Constance and Basel, the river is called the High Rhine.
In Basel, the Rhine makes the “Rhine knee” and turns north.
The Aare is the Rhine's tributary that carries the most water.
The Rhine ports in Basel connect Switzerland with the sea by ship.

abschnitte.text: The Rhine begins in the mountains of the **Grisons**. Its source is said to be the small **Lake Toma** near the Oberalp Pass. From there the **Anterior Rhine** flows eastwards. At **Reichenau** it joins the **Posterior Rhine**. From here the river is called the **Alpine Rhine**. It flows north past the cantonal capital, **Chur**.

abschnitte.titel: A border river to Lake Constance
abschnitte.text: The **Alpine Rhine** stretches from Reichenau to **Lake Constance**. For a long stretch it forms a border. On the west side lies the canton of **St Gallen**, and on the east side lie **Liechtenstein** and **Austria**. Then the Rhine flows into Lake Constance. This large lake lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria.

After Lake Constance, the river is called the **High Rhine**. This section goes as far as **Basel**. Near Schaffhausen, the water plunges over the **Rhine Falls**, one of the largest waterfalls in Europe. Further down, the Rhine takes in the **Aare**. It is the Rhine's **tributary that carries the most water** and, where they meet, it even brings more water than the Rhine itself.

abschnitte.titel: Basel and the way to the sea
abschnitte.text: In **Basel**, the Rhine makes a large bend, the **Rhine knee**, and turns **north**. From here, large ships can sail. The **Rhine ports** in Basel connect Switzerland with the sea by ship. Oil, grain and containers, for example, come into the country this way. For a country with no sea coast this is very important.

abschnitte.titel: Through Germany to the North Sea
abschnitte.text: After Basel, the Rhine flows as the **Upper Rhine** between Germany and France. Later come the **Middle Rhine**, with many castles, and the **Lower Rhine**. In the **Netherlands** it splits into several branches and flows into the **North Sea**. Altogether the Rhine is more than 1,200 kilometres long. It is one of the busiest rivers in the world.

gewusst: Where it flows into the Rhine, the Aare brings more water than the Rhine itself, and yet the river is still called the Rhine afterwards.
The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen are around 23 metres high and around 150 metres wide.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's surface is not all in one piece, but put together from plates like a giant jigsaw. These plates move a few centimetres every year. Plate tectonics explains how mountains, oceans, earthquakes and volcanoes form.
wichtigste: The lithosphere is the rigid outer rock shell of the Earth and is broken into plates.
The plates glide on the partly plastic asthenosphere in the upper mantle.
Plates move about as fast as fingernails grow, a few centimetres a year.
At divergent plate boundaries such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates drift apart.
In subduction, an oceanic plate dives under another plate.
The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform fault.
The Alps formed mainly through the collision of the African and Eurasian Plates.

abschnitte.text: The outer shell of the Earth is called the **lithosphere**; it is made of the Earth's crust and the uppermost mantle. It is broken into seven large and many smaller **lithospheric plates**. The large ones include the Pacific, Eurasian, African and North American Plates. The plates glide on the **asthenosphere**, a hot, partly plastic layer. You can imagine it like chewy bubble gum that deforms very slowly.

As early as 1912, the German scientist **Alfred Wegener** put forward the idea of continental drift. He noticed that South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces and that the same fossils are found on both continents. Many experts rejected his idea at the time, because he could not explain what drove it. Only in the 1960s did studies of the sea floor show that the plates really do move. Around 300 million years ago, all the continents were joined in the supercontinent **Pangaea**.

At a **divergent plate boundary**, two plates drift apart, and magma rises from the depths, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At a convergent plate boundary, plates collide. If a heavy oceanic plate dives under another, this is called **subduction**. At transform faults, plates slide past each other, as at the San Andreas Fault in California between the Pacific and North American Plates. Strong earthquakes happen there again and again.

In the mantle, hot rock rises extremely slowly, cools and sinks again. This **mantle convection** is thought to be an important driver of plate movement. Then there is **slab pull**, because a diving plate is heavy and pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. The movements are usually only 2 to 10 centimetres a year. But over millions of years this adds up to thousands of kilometres.

The Alps formed mainly through the **collision** of the African and Eurasian Plates. Between them there was once an ocean, the Tethys, which disappeared in the process. Layers of rock were pushed together, folded and stacked on top of each other like carpets, forming what are called **nappes**. That is why fossils of sea creatures are found high up in the mountains today. The Alps are still rising slightly, but erosion is wearing them away at the same time.

Most **earthquakes** and volcanoes lie at plate boundaries. Around the Pacific there are so many of them that people speak of the Pacific Ring of Fire. In Iceland you can even see a plate boundary: in Thingvellir National Park, cracks gape between the North American and Eurasian Plates. In Switzerland too, there are small earthquakes again and again because of plate movements.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rigid outer rock shell of the Earth, made of the crust and the uppermost mantle.
A partly plastic layer in the upper mantle on which the plates glide.
The diving of an oceanic plate under another plate.
A plate boundary where two plates slide past each other sideways.
A supercontinent in which all the continents were joined around 300 million years ago.

gewusst: The Atlantic gets about 2 to 3 centimetres wider every year.
The Himalayas formed because the Indian Plate collided with Eurasia, and they are still growing today.
Alfred Wegener died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, long before his idea was generally accepted.

teile.einleitung: At the Permian-Triassic boundary, around 252 million years ago, the largest mass extinction in Earth's history took place. A large share of all animal and plant species disappeared. It was triggered by huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia.
wichtigste: The boundary lies around 252 million years ago.
It separates the Palaeozoic from the Mesozoic.
Around 90 per cent of marine species died out.
The main cause was the Siberian Traps.
In the sea there was acidification, warming and a lack of oxygen.
The trilobites disappeared for good, and Lystrosaurus survived.

abschnitte.text: Earth's history is divided into ages. The **Permian** is the last period of the **Palaeozoic**, the era of ancient life. The **Triassic** is the first period of the **Mesozoic**, the middle era of Earth's history. The boundary between them lies around 252 million years ago. The international reference section is at **Meishan** in China. There the boundary is defined by the first appearance of the conodont **Hindeodus parvus**, a tiny fossil.

At this boundary, according to common estimates, around **90 per cent** of marine species died out, perhaps even more. On land too, a large share of the vertebrates disappeared. The event is called “**The Great Dying**”. It is the largest known mass extinction. The **trilobites**, arthropods that had lived in the seas for around 270 million years since the Cambrian, now disappeared for good.

The main cause is thought to be the **Siberian Traps**. In Siberia, huge amounts of **basalt lava** poured out over a long time. This released gases such as **carbon dioxide**. They led to strong warming. In terms of Earth's history the event lasted only a short time, but long enough to change living conditions all over the Earth.

A lot of dissolved carbon dioxide made the seawater more **acidic**. This made it harder for many animals to build chalky shells. Warmer water also contains less **oxygen**. So zones with little oxygen spread. **Acidification**, **warming** and **lack of oxygen** together played a major part in the dying in the sea. Reefs disappeared almost completely for a long time.

Some species survived the crisis. **Lystrosaurus**, a plant-eater with two tusks, was widespread on several continents in the early Triassic. It belonged to the dicynodonts, relatives of the ancestors of mammals. Life recovered only slowly. Around ten million years later, many fish and marine reptiles were living again in the sea near today's **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino. Their fossils are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: After the extinction, Lystrosaurus was so common that it is almost the only animal found in some rock layers.
The trilobites lived for around 270 million years before they disappeared.
It was only after the great dying that the rise of the dinosaurs began.

teile.einleitung: The Staubbach Falls are one of the best-known waterfalls in Switzerland. Near the village of Lauterbrunnen in the Bernese Oberland, they plunge almost 300 metres over a vertical rock face into the valley.
wichtigste: The Staubbach Falls are near the village of Lauterbrunnen in the canton of Bern.
The water falls around 297 metres.
They are among the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.
The water falls almost freely over the rock face and turns to spray.
Goethe wrote the poem “Song of the Spirits over the Waters” here in 1779.
The stream carries the most water during the snowmelt in early summer.

abschnitte.text: The Staubbach Falls are right by the village of **Lauterbrunnen** in the Bernese Oberland. The Lauterbrunnen Valley is a deep valley with almost vertical rock walls. A glacier carved it out during the Ice Age. The Staubbach stream comes from a side valley higher up and plunges over the edge of the wall into the main valley. Such side valleys are called **hanging valleys**.

The water falls around **297 metres**, almost freely through the air. On the long way down it breaks up into many tiny droplets. The wind scatters them in all directions, and it looks like fine **dust** or mist. That is how the Staubbach got its name (“Staub” means “dust” in German). Often only a fine spray reaches the bottom.

In **1779**, the poet **Johann Wolfgang von Goethe** travelled through Switzerland and visited the Staubbach Falls. The swirling water impressed him greatly. His poem **“Song of the Spirits over the Waters”** was written there. In it, he compares the human soul with water, which comes from the sky and rises up again. Many painters also came to Lauterbrunnen to paint the waterfall.

In summer, a path leads up to a **gallery in the rock** behind the waterfall. From there you can see the water from very close up. In winter and spring the path is closed, because of the danger of **falling ice** and **rockfall**. The stream carries the most water in **early summer**, when the snow is melting in the mountains. In winter much of it is frozen, and the falls are much weaker.

gewusst: The Lauterbrunnen Valley has a great many waterfalls, which is why it is also called the valley of waterfalls.
When the sun shines into the spray of the Staubbach Falls, you can often see a rainbow.

teile.einleitung: A debris flow is a fast flood of water, mud and stones that shoots down a steep gully. In the Swiss Alps, debris flows are among the most important natural hazards. Researchers measure them precisely to protect people better.
wichtigste: A debris flow is a mixture of water, mud, stones and wood.
Common triggers are violent thunderstorms or rapid snowmelt.
The biggest boulders collect at the front, in the head of the flow.
Debris flows are much denser and heavier than floods.
Where a torrent comes out into the valley, an alluvial fan forms.
Thawing permafrost can make debris flows more frequent.

abschnitte.text: In steep gullies there is often a lot of loose material: stones, gravel and soil. During **violent thunderstorms** or rapid **snowmelt**, this material gets soaked. Suddenly it starts to move and shoots down the valley as a thick mass. A large part of a debris flow is solid material, not just water. It can sweep tree trunks and boulders along with it.

A debris flow often comes in surges. At the front, the **head of the flow**, the biggest boulders collect. This front is especially destructive. Because a debris flow is much denser and heavier than water alone, it can destroy houses, bridges and roads and bury everything under rubble. That is why it is more dangerous than a normal flood.

Where the torrent comes out into the flatter valley, the mass loses speed and comes to a stop. Over a long time, this creates a fan-shaped **alluvial fan**. Villages often stand on such fans, because the ground there is dry and slightly raised. At the same time, they lie right in the path of possible debris flows. Protective structures such as **debris basins**, dams and nets are meant to hold back the material.

The **Illgraben** near Leuk in Valais is one of the most active debris flow torrents in the Alps. The research institute **WSL** has been measuring every debris flow there for years. Instruments record the height, speed and weight of the mass. A warning system can alert people nearby in time. The measurements help to plan protective structures all over Switzerland better.

In August 2017, around three million cubic metres of rock crashed down from **Piz Cengalo** in the Bregaglia valley. This set off several debris flows that reached the village of **Bondo** and caused great damage. At higher altitudes, **permafrost**, which is permanently frozen ground, is thawing because of climate change. This frees a lot of loose material, which can flow down as a debris flow in heavy rain.

gewusst: Several debris flows are measured in the Illgraben every year.
A debris flow can sweep along boulders as big as a car.
Many Alpine villages stand on the alluvial fans of old debris flows.

teile.einleitung: The Rhône Glacier is a large glacier in the canton of Valais, right at the top of the Rhône Valley. The Rhône forms from its meltwater. It is one of the glaciers studied for the longest time anywhere in the world.
wichtigste: The Rhône Glacier lies in the canton of Valais.
In the 2020s it is just under 8 kilometres long.
In 2018 it covered an area of around 15 square kilometres.
At its greatest extent in 1856, it reached down to Gletsch.
Gletsch lies between the Furka and Grimsel Passes.
The glacier has been measured almost without a break since 1874.
Every year an ice grotto is carved into the glacier anew.

abschnitte.titel: Right at the top of Valais
abschnitte.text: The **Rhône Glacier** lies in the canton of **Valais**, at the upper end of the Rhône Valley. The **Rhône** forms from its meltwater. In the 2020s it is **just under 8 kilometres** long. In 2018 it covered an area of around **15 square kilometres**. It lies close to the **Furka Pass**, over which a famous pass road runs.

During the **cold periods**, the whole Rhône Valley was filled with ice. In some places the ice was up to **2,000 metres** thick. Even in more recent times the glacier was much bigger than today. At its **greatest extent in 1856**, it reached all the way down to **Gletsch**. This small hamlet lies between the **Furka** and **Grimsel** Passes.

Since **1874**, the Rhône Glacier has been **measured** almost without a break. This makes it one of the glaciers observed for the longest time anywhere in the world. Experts measure how long it is and how much ice it loses. The measurements show that it has retreated a long way since the 19th century. Like most Alpine glaciers, it is melting because the climate is warming.

Every year an **ice grotto** is carved into the glacier anew. Visitors can then walk into the blue ice. Because the glacier moves and melts, the grotto has to be rebuilt again and again. In summer, part of the glacier near the grotto is covered with **white sheets**. They reflect sunlight and so slow down the melting.

Since about **2007**, a **glacial lake** has formed in front of the glacier's snout. It formed where the ice retreated and a hollow was uncovered. Meltwater collects in it. The lake clearly shows how much the glacier has shrunk in recent decades.

gewusst: In the 19th century there was a hotel in the hamlet of Gletsch from which you could see the glacier almost on the doorstep.
The ice of the Rhône Glacier slowly flows down the valley, even though the glacier as a whole is getting shorter and shorter.

teile.einleitung: Rime is a white coating of fine ice crystals on branches, grasses and fences. It makes a winter landscape magically white even when no snow has fallen. Rime forms in frost and damp air.
wichtigste: Rime is made of fine ice crystals on branches and grasses.
It forms in frost and damp air, often in fog.
Rime is white.
Here it can be seen in winter.
It grows most on the side the wind comes from.
When a great deal of rime hangs on trees, branches can break off.
When it gets warmer, it melts and drips off.

abschnitte.text: **Rime** is a coating of many fine **ice crystals**. It forms on branches, grasses, fences and power lines. It is **white** and looks a little like icing. Here it can be seen in **winter**. It is especially beautiful on sunny days after a cold, foggy night.

Rime forms when it is **freezing** and the air is very **damp**. There is often **fog** in the air then. The tiny fog droplets are colder than zero degrees and yet still liquid. When they hit a cold twig, they freeze at once. In this way a coating of ice grows layer by layer. In Switzerland this often happens under the blanket of fog over the Swiss Plateau.

The wind carries the fog droplets against the twigs. That is why rime grows most on the side **the wind comes from**. Sometimes long ice needles form that all point in the same direction. If you look closely, you can tell from them where the wind was blowing from. On mountain tops, such ice shapes can become very large.

If the weather lasts for several days, the layer of ice gets thicker and thicker. When a great deal of rime hangs on trees, it becomes heavy for them. Then **branches can break off**. Power lines can also be damaged under the load. When it gets warmer or the sun shines strongly, the rime **melts** and drips off.

Related to rime are **ice flowers**. These are patterns of ice that grow on cold **window panes**. They form when damp air in a room freezes on a very cold pane. The crystals form shapes like ferns or feathers. Because modern windows are well insulated, ice flowers are seen less often than in the past.

gewusst: No two coatings of rime are the same, because every ice needle grows a little differently.
On high mountain tops, rime can form thick armour of ice on summit crosses and weather stations.

teile.einleitung: The Austroalpine nappes are one of the large nappe units of the Alps. Their rocks come from the edge of the Adriatic Plate in the south. In Switzerland they are found mainly in the Grisons, and a remnant of them even sits on top of the Matterhorn.
wichtigste: The rocks of the Austroalpine nappes come from the edge of the Adriatic Plate.
They were pushed far northwards when the mountains formed.
There is a Lower Austroalpine and an Upper Austroalpine.
In the Engadine Window, the Penninic nappes appear underneath.
Piz Bernina is the only four-thousander in the Eastern Alps.
The summit of the Matterhorn belongs to the Dent Blanche nappe.

abschnitte.text: The Alps are built of large slabs of rock that were pushed on top of each other. These slabs are called **nappes**. The **Austroalpine** unit originally formed the northern edge of the **Adriatic Plate**. When the mountains formed, it was carried far northwards over other units. That is why today it usually lies at the top of the stack of nappes. In Austria, the Austroalpine nappes make up a large part of the Alps.

Experts divide the Austroalpine into two sub-units. The **Lower Austroalpine** is the deeper part, which was originally closer to the ocean. In the Upper Engadine, it includes the **Err nappe** and the **Bernina nappe**. Above it comes the **Upper Austroalpine**. It includes the **Silvretta nappe**, made of old gneiss and amphibolite. It builds the Silvretta group between the Prättigau and the Lower Engadine.

abschnitte.titel: Piz Bernina and the limestone Alps
abschnitte.text: **Piz Bernina** is around 4,049 metres high and the highest mountain in the Grisons. It is the only four-thousander in the Eastern Alps and is made of rocks of the Bernina nappe. Further north, in Austria and Bavaria, lie the **Northern Limestone Alps**. They are sheared-off sedimentary nappes of the Upper Austroalpine, made of Triassic limestones. They include, for example, the Wetterstein mountains and the Karwendel.
