In some places, erosion has cut through the Austroalpine nappes. Deeper units appear underneath. Such a hole is called a **tectonic window**. In the **Lower Engadine** near Scuol lies the **Engadine Window**. There, Penninic **Bündner schists** appear beneath the Austroalpine. The largest window in the Eastern Alps is the **Tauern Window** in Austria, with the Grossglockner and the Grossvenediger. It is around 175 kilometres long.

There are rocks of Adriatic origin in Valais too. The upper part of the **Matterhorn** is made of gneisses of the **Dent Blanche nappe**. It is counted as part of the Adriatic Plate, which is often described as part or an offshoot of Africa. That is why it is sometimes said that the summit of the Matterhorn is “African”. Below it lie rocks of the Penninic nappes, which belong to the ancient ocean and to Europe.

gewusst: The Matterhorn has rock of Adriatic origin on its summit.
Near Scuol you can see under the Austroalpine nappes through a tectonic window.
Piz Bernina is the only four-thousander in the Eastern Alps.

teile.einleitung: A storm is a very strong wind that can blow trees over and make high waves. In Switzerland, orange flashing lights at many lakes warn of storms.
wichtigste: The Beaufort scale divides wind into forces from 0 to 12.
Force 12 is called a hurricane and starts at about 118 km/h.
A gust is a short, strong blast of wind.
Storm Lothar blew over millions of trees in Switzerland on 26 December 1999.
During a storm warning, orange lights at the lake flash about 90 times a minute.
In a storm you should avoid the forest and return from the lake to the shore.

abschnitte.text: About 200 years ago, the Englishman **Francis Beaufort** invented a scale for sailors. The **Beaufort scale** divides wind into forces from **0 to 12**. 0 means calm. From force 9 it is called a storm (a strong gale). The highest level, 12, is called a **hurricane**. It starts at about **118 kilometres an hour**, which is as fast as a car on the motorway.

The wind never blows completely evenly. A **gust** is a short, strong blast of wind. For a few seconds the wind suddenly becomes much stronger, then it eases off again. Gusts are often more dangerous than the average wind, because they come as a surprise. That is why weather forecasts often give the strongest gusts.

On **26 December 1999**, St Stephen's Day, Storm **Lothar** swept across Switzerland. It blew over **millions of trees** and caused huge damage to forests and houses. Many roads and railway lines were blocked. Lothar is one of the strongest storms Switzerland has experienced.

At many Swiss lakes there are **orange flashing lights** on the shore. If they flash about **40 times** a minute, they are warning of strong wind. If they flash quickly, about **90 times** a minute, it is a **storm warning**. Anyone on the lake should then go back to the shore at once. A storm makes high waves and can capsize boats.

In a storm you should **not go into the forest**. Strong wind can tear off branches and blow whole trees over. Roof tiles and loose objects can also fly around. The safest place is inside a building. It is best to close windows and shutters beforehand.

gewusst: Storms in Europe are given names, similar to the hurricanes in America.
The Beaufort scale originally described how many sails a ship could set in a particular wind.

teile.einleitung: Ocean trenches are long, narrow channels in the seabed and the deepest places on Earth. They form where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.
wichtigste: Ocean trenches form at subduction zones.
The deepest point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench at just under 11,000 m.
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached it in 1960 in the submersible Trieste.
The Trieste is based on an invention by the Swiss Auguste Piccard.
Below about 6000 m the hadal zone begins.
At the bottom of the Mariana Trench the pressure is around 1100 bar.

abschnitte.text: The Earth’s surface is made of large **plates** that move slowly. Where an oceanic plate sinks beneath another, this is called a **subduction zone**. An **ocean trench** forms there. Nearby there are often **volcanic arcs** and strong **earthquakes**. Many ocean trenches lie around the Pacific.

The **Mariana Trench** in the western Pacific is the deepest. In its **Challenger Deep** just under **11,000 m** has been measured. The second deepest is the **Tonga Trench** north of New Zealand. Its Horizon Deep reaches just under 10,800 m. The deepest point of the Atlantic lies in the **Puerto Rico Trench** at around 8400 m. From about **6000 m** down, people speak of the **hadal zone**, named after the Greek Hades.

The Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard** developed the principle of the **bathyscaphe**, a submersible for the deep sea. The **Trieste** was built to his plans in Italy in **1953**. Later the US Navy took it over. On **23 January 1960** his son **Jacques Piccard** and **Don Walsh** dived in it to the Challenger Deep. It was the first crewed visit to the deepest point of the ocean.

On **26 March 2012** the film director **James Cameron** reached the Challenger Deep. In the submersible **Deepsea Challenger** he was the first person to dive there alone. Such dives are very rare, because the materials must withstand enormous forces.

In water the pressure increases by about **1 bar** for every **10 m** of depth. Just under 11,000 m divided by 10 m gives around **1100 bar**. That is more than a thousand times the air pressure at the sea surface. Even so, animals live down there too, for example amphipods and other small animals. It is always dark and cold.

gewusst: Mount Everest would fit into the Challenger Deep, and its summit would still be more than 2000 m below the water surface.
Before his submersibles, Auguste Piccard also rose into the stratosphere in a balloon.

teile.einleitung: A meander is a loop in a river. On flat land, a river often winds through the landscape in many bends. The name comes from a river in what is now Turkey.
wichtigste: Meanders are river loops on flat land.
The name comes from the River Maiandros in what is now Turkey.
On the outer bank the river wears away land, and on the inner bank it deposits material.
Loops that are cut off become oxbow lakes.
There are famous Swiss river loops at Rheinau and at the Clos du Doubs.
Many Swiss rivers were straightened.

abschnitte.text: In Asia Minor, in what is now **Turkey**, flowed the ancient River **Maiandros**. It was known for its many bends. Today it is called the Büyük Menderes. Its name became the technical term for all river loops. A decorative band of winding lines, known from old Greek vases, is also called a meander.

Meanders form mainly on **flat land** with little slope. There the water flows slowly and moves sideways. In a bend, the water presses against the outer bank and wears it away. This steep bank is called the **cut bank**. On the inside, the water flows slowly and deposits gravel and sand. This creates a gently sloping bank, the **slip-off slope**. Over time the loop gets bigger and bigger.

Sometimes a loop becomes so tight that the river breaks through it during a flood. The old bend then no longer has water flowing through it and is left behind as still water. This is called an **oxbow lake**. Oxbow lakes are valuable habitats for frogs, dragonflies, water birds and fish. Over time they can silt up and turn into marsh.

At **Rheinau** in the canton of Zurich, the Rhine winds in a famous double loop. The former **Rheinau Abbey** stands on an island there. In the canton of Jura, the **Doubs** forms a large loop near Saint-Ursanne. It flows from France into Switzerland, makes a wide bend and returns to France. This loop is called the **Clos du Doubs**.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, many Swiss rivers were **straightened** and confined by embankments. People wanted to gain land, drain marshes and carry floodwater away faster. That is why there are only a few natural meanders left today. It is now known that rivers with more space cope better with floods and offer habitats to more animals. That is why some stretches are now being **revitalised**, which means made more natural again.

gewusst: Over time, a meander can slowly shift across the valley.
Rheinau Abbey stands on an island in a loop of the Rhine.
At the Clos du Doubs, the Doubs flows from France into Switzerland and back again.

teile.einleitung: Numerical weather prediction uses computers to calculate the weather for the next few days. To do this, physical equations are solved for the whole atmosphere. Almost every weather forecast you see on your mobile phone is based on it.
wichtigste: Weather models solve physical equations on a grid.
Lewis Fry Richardson calculated a forecast by hand and published it in 1922.
In 1950 the first successful computer forecast ran on ENIAC.
Data assimilation creates the starting state from measurements.
Small processes are described using parameterisation.
Since 2024, MeteoSwiss has been using the ICON model.

abschnitte.text: The air follows the laws of **physics**. Equations describe how wind, pressure, temperature and humidity change. A **weather model** divides the atmosphere into a three-dimensional **grid** of many cells. For each cell, the computer calculates step by step how the weather develops. The finer the grid, the more computing power is needed.

During the First World War, the Briton **Lewis Fry Richardson** spent weeks calculating a forecast for six hours by hand. In 1922 he described it in a book. The result was wrong, but the method showed the way forward. In 1950, **Jule Charney**, **Ragnar Fjørtoft** and **John von Neumann** produced the first successful numerical forecast on the **ENIAC** computer. They calculated a simplified 24-hour forecast.

A forecast is only as good as its starting state. Weather stations, balloons, aeroplanes, ships and satellites constantly supply measurements. In **data assimilation**, these observations are combined with a short model forecast. This produces the best possible starting state. Because small errors grow over time, many slightly changed versions are often calculated. Such an **ensemble** shows how certain a forecast is.

Many processes are smaller than a grid cell, for example single clouds, raindrops or swirls in the air. The model cannot calculate them directly. Their effect is therefore estimated from the grid values using approximate formulas. This is called **parameterisation**. It is one of the biggest challenges in building a weather model.

In 2024, MeteoSwiss replaced its earlier model COSMO with **ICON**. ICON was developed by the German Weather Service and the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology. Its grid cells are **triangles** that cover the globe evenly. In 2025, the finest Swiss version, ICON-CH1-EPS, worked with a grid spacing of around 1 kilometre, and ICON-CH2-EPS with around 2.1 kilometres. For global forecasts, Switzerland, as a member state, also uses the **ECMWF**, which has its headquarters in Reading in England.

gewusst: Richardson imagined a hall with thousands of people calculating the weather together.
The fine resolution of ICON shows the narrow Alpine valleys much better.
ICON's grid is based on an icosahedron, a solid with 20 triangular faces.

teile.einleitung: Inside, the Earth is built like an onion with several layers. Right on the outside is the thin crust, beneath it the massive mantle and in the centre the hot core. Nobody has ever been down there, and yet researchers know surprisingly well what the inside of the Earth is like.
wichtigste: According to their chemical make-up, the Earth is divided into three main layers: crust, mantle and core.
The Earth's radius is around 6,370 kilometres.
The mantle makes up most of the Earth's volume.
The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid.
Researchers worked out the structure of the Earth mainly with seismic waves.
The lithosphere is made of the crust and the uppermost mantle.
The asthenosphere is a soft, plastic layer in the upper mantle on which the plates glide.

abschnitte.text: According to their chemical make-up, there are three main layers: the **crust**, the **mantle** and the **core**. From the edge to the centre it is around 6,370 kilometres. In proportion, the crust is as thin as the skin of an apple. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets and the higher the pressure. At the centre of the Earth it is estimated to be about 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius.

The crust is the outermost, solid layer, on which we live. Under the oceans it is only about 5 to 10 kilometres thick and is made mainly of basalt. Under the continents it is usually 30 to 40 kilometres thick, and under high mountains such as the Alps much more. The boundary between crust and mantle is called the **Moho**, after the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić, who discovered it in 1909.

The mantle reaches down to a depth of about 2,900 kilometres and makes up most of the Earth's volume. It is made of hot, solid rock that can, however, deform very slowly over a long time. In the upper mantle lies the soft, plastic **asthenosphere**. Above it, the uppermost mantle together with the crust forms the rigid **lithosphere**, which is broken into plates. Slow currents in the mantle help to move these plates.

The core is made mainly of **iron** and nickel. The outer core is liquid, and its movements create the Earth's magnetic field. This magnetic field makes compass needles point north and protects us from particles from space. The inner core is solid despite the enormous heat, because the pressure there is huge. The Danish scientist Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936.

Nobody can drill down to the core; the deepest borehole in the world, on the Russian Kola Peninsula, only reaches a little over 12 kilometres deep. That is why researchers use **seismic waves**, which travel through the whole Earth. Depending on the material, the waves speed up, slow down or are bent. Certain waves, the S-waves, cannot travel through liquids and do not arrive on the other side of the Earth. From this it was concluded that the outer core must be liquid.

The layered structure explains many processes at the Earth's surface. Heat from inside the Earth drives the plate movements, and these create mountains, earthquakes and volcanoes. The magnetic field from the outer core helps migrating birds find their way. **Geothermal heat**, which is used in Switzerland to heat many houses through borehole heat exchangers, also partly comes from inside the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost, thin and solid layer of the Earth, on which we live.
A thick layer of hot rock between the crust and the core.
The innermost part of the Earth, made of iron and nickel, liquid on the outside and solid on the inside.
The boundary between the crust and the mantle.
The rigid shell of rock made of the crust and the uppermost mantle.

gewusst: If you shrank the Earth to the size of an apple, the crust would be thinner than the apple's skin.
In the Earth's core it is about as hot as on the surface of the Sun.
The deepest borehole in the world has not even made it one per cent of the way to the centre of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A low-pressure area, or low for short, is an area with low air pressure. Lows often bring clouds, wind and rain and have a strong influence on the weather in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In the centre of a low the air rises.
Rising air cools down, and clouds form.
In the northern hemisphere the air flows anticlockwise around a low.
Lows usually move from the west, from the Atlantic, to Switzerland.
The Icelandic Low is a common low over the North Atlantic.
The Genoa low often brings a lot of precipitation to the southern side of the Alps.

abschnitte.text: In a **low-pressure area** the air flows together near the ground and then **rises**. As it rises it expands and **cools down**. The water vapour condenses into cloud droplets. That is why lows often bring lots of **clouds** and rain. With a high it is the other way round: there the air sinks, and the weather is usually fine.

The air does not flow straight into the low. The **Earth’s rotation** deflects it. In the **northern hemisphere** it therefore turns **anticlockwise** around the low. In the southern hemisphere it is the other way round. On weather maps you can recognise lows by the letter L (T in German) and by closely spaced lines of equal air pressure.

At our latitudes **westerly winds** mainly blow high up. They drive the lows from the **Atlantic** across Europe. That is why bad weather in Switzerland usually comes from the west. Around Iceland the air pressure is low on average; this is the **Icelandic Low**. Many lows that move to Europe form or grow stronger there.

When cold air flows over the Alps into the Mediterranean, a low can form in the Gulf of Genoa. It is called a **Genoa low**. It brings damp air towards the Alps. In **Ticino** it then often rains or snows heavily. Sometimes a Genoa low also moves further east and brings precipitation to the Eastern Alps.

A **cut-off low** is a detached low of very cold air at great height, about 5 to 10 kilometres above the ground. Because it is very cold up there, tall heaped clouds with showers and thunderstorms easily grow beneath it. In meteorology, a **hurricane** is a very strong **tropical low**. It forms over warm seas and has very low air pressure at its centre.

gewusst: Many lows over Europe are given names every year, similar to storms.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer, usually in hectopascals.

teile.einleitung: An ophiolite is a piece of old ocean floor that now lies on land. Such rocks show how the Earth's crust under the seas is built. In the Swiss Alps near Zermatt there are also remains of an ancient ocean.
wichtigste: An ophiolite is oceanic lithosphere on dry land.
The sequence goes from mantle rock through gabbro and dykes to pillow lava.
Pushing onto a continent is called obduction.
Famous examples are Semail in Oman and Troodos in Cyprus.
In Switzerland, ophiolites are found in the Zermatt-Saas Fee zone.
Water often turns mantle rock into serpentinite.

abschnitte.text: Ophiolites are sequences of rock from the **mantle** and the **oceanic crust**. They were pushed onto continents at plate boundaries. Normally, an oceanic plate dives down into the depths in **subduction**. In **obduction**, on the other hand, it is pushed over the edge of the continent. Only in this way are parts of the ocean floor preserved on land. The name comes from the Greek word for snake, because of the greenish, mottled rocks.

A complete ophiolite sequence is like a cross-section through the ocean floor. At the bottom lies **mantle rock**, above it **gabbro**, a coarse-grained intrusive rock. Then comes a swarm of closely packed, vertical basalt dykes, the **sheeted dyke complex**. It forms at the mid-ocean ridge, where magma keeps pushing into new cracks. At the top are **pillow lavas**, which form when basalt flows out under water. Above them come deep-sea sediments.

The mantle rock of an ophiolite is originally made mainly of the minerals **olivine** and **pyroxene**. When it comes into contact with seawater, serpentine minerals form from them. The rock is then called **serpentinite**. It is greenish, often shiny, and sometimes feels smooth. Serpentinite is widespread in the Alps and is also used as a decorative stone.

The **Semail ophiolite** in **Oman** is one of the largest and best exposed in the world. It covers around 100,000 square kilometres and formed in the Late Cretaceous. In **Cyprus**, the **Troodos Mountains** are made of an almost complete sequence. By studying them in the 1960s, researchers came to understand better how new ocean crust forms at spreading zones.

Before the Alps formed, the **Piedmont-Liguria Ocean** lay between Europe and the Adriatic Plate. Around **Zermatt** and **Saas Fee**, serpentinites, metagabbros and pillow lavas from this ocean can be seen today. When the Alps formed, they were buried deep, strongly changed and lifted up again. So anyone hiking there is walking over former sea floor. There are such rocks in the Grisons too.

gewusst: Near Zermatt you can stand on rock that was once the floor of an ocean.
Pillow lavas look like pillows stacked on top of each other.
Ophiolites give a view of rock that is otherwise hidden under the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: **Sedimentary rocks** form from particles that have been deposited and later hardened. They cover about three quarters of the Earth's land areas. Many mountains in Switzerland, for example in the Jura and the Prealps, are made of them.
wichtigste: Sedimentary rocks form from deposited particles that harden.
The process of hardening is called diagenesis.
In rock faces you can often see layers lying on top of each other.
Breccia is made of cemented, angular fragments of rock.
Rock salt forms when seawater evaporates.
Coal formed mainly from the remains of plants.
Sedimentary rocks cover about three quarters of the land areas.

abschnitte.text: Water, wind and ice wear rock away and deposit the particles somewhere else. Layer after layer is added. The weight of the upper layers presses the lower ones together. Dissolved substances cement the grains together. This process, in which loose deposits turn into solid rock, is called **diagenesis**.

**Layers lying on top of each other** are typical of sedimentary rocks. In many rock faces you can see them like the pages of a book. Each layer tells something about the time when it formed. **Fossils**, the fossilised remains of living things, are also often found in sedimentary rocks.

Some sedimentary rocks are made of fragments of other rocks. **Breccia** is made of cemented, **angular** fragments, and **conglomerate** of rounded pebbles. In Switzerland such a rock is often called **Nagelfluh**. **Sandstone** is made of grains of sand. The rock made of the very finest particles is **mudstone**.

**Rock salt** forms when seawater evaporates and the salt is left behind. **Limestone** often forms from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. **Coal** formed mainly from the **remains of plants** that grew in swamps millions of years ago. The rock **dolomite** and the mountain range of the **Dolomites** are named after the French scientist **Déodat de Dolomieu**.

Sedimentary rocks cover about **three quarters of the Earth's land areas**. But usually they form only a thin skin over older rock. In Switzerland, the **Jura**, large parts of the Prealps and the Swiss Plateau are made mainly of sedimentary rocks. The limestone of many Alpine peaks once lay as mud on a sea floor.

gewusst: On some Alpine peaks you can find fossilised shells that once lived on the floor of a sea.
The Nagelfluh of the Rigi formed from gravel that rivers carried down from the young Alps.

teile.einleitung: Sea level is the height of the surface of the sea. It is the zero point from which the height of mountains and places is measured. When it rises, low-lying coasts and islands are in danger.
wichtigste: Sea level is the **zero point** for heights; it is at **0 metres**.
“Metres above sea level” tells you how high a place is above sea level.
When a lot of ice on land melts, sea level **rises**.
Low-lying islands such as the **Maldives** are especially threatened.
The Netherlands protect themselves with **dykes**.
In **Venice**, squares are often under water during high tides.

abschnitte.text: Heights are measured from the surface of the sea. On maps, **sea level** has a height of **0 metres**. Anything higher has a positive height. The figure “**metres above sea level**”, written m a.s.l. (in German “m ü. M.”), tells you how high a mountain or a place is above sea level. In this way all the mountains in the world can be compared, even if they are far from the sea, like the Swiss Alps.

When a lot of ice on land melts, for example from **glaciers** or large ice sheets, the water flows into the sea. Then the sea has more water and sea level **rises**. Warmer water also takes up more space. That is why sea level is slowly rising because of global warming.

Low-lying islands are especially at risk. Most islands of the **Maldives** in the Indian Ocean lie only about one metre above the sea. If the water keeps rising, they could be flooded. On other coasts too, a higher sea level leads to **flooding** more often. In storms, the sea then gets into the land more easily.

Large parts of the **Netherlands** lie very low, some even below sea level. To protect themselves, people there have built long **dykes**. These are walls of earth and stone. They keep the sea away from the low-lying land. Without dykes, part of the country would be under water.

The city of **Venice** in Italy is built on many small islands in a **lagoon**. When the sea is high, squares and alleys are flooded. In Italian this high water is called “**acqua alta**”. Then people walk on wooden walkways. For some years now, movable barriers in the sea have protected the city during strong floods.

gewusst: The lowest point in Switzerland is Lake Maggiore, at around 193 m above sea level.
Sea level is not exactly the same height everywhere, because wind, currents and gravity change it slightly.

teile.einleitung: A mass extinction is an event in which a great many species disappear in a short time in terms of Earth's history. In the last 540 million years or so there have been five especially large ones, the “Big Five”. Many experts fear that a sixth one is happening today.
wichtigste: Usually **five great mass extinctions** are recognised.
They come at the end of the **Ordovician**, **Devonian**, **Permian**, **Triassic** and **Cretaceous**.
The oldest happened at the end of the Ordovician around 444 million years ago.
**David Raup** and **Jack Sepkoski** described the Big Five in 1982.
Between the events there is a normal **background extinction**.
A mass extinction is often followed by an **adaptive radiation**.

abschnitte.text: Species die out again and again, for example because of competition or climate change. This steady disappearance is called **background extinction**. A **mass extinction** only happens when the extinction rate rises far above this. In 1982, **David Raup** and **Jack Sepkoski** analysed a large database of fossil families of sea creatures. In it, five events with unusually high rates stood out: the **Big Five**.

The oldest of the great mass extinctions happened at the end of the **Ordovician** around 444 million years ago. The main cause is thought to be glaciation on the southern continent of **Gondwana**. Sea level fell, and many sea creatures disappeared. In the Late Devonian came, among others, the **Kellwasser event** around 372 million years ago. It is named after a stream in the Harz mountains. Reefs and tropical sea creatures suffered especially.

At the end of the **Permian**, around 252 million years ago, the largest known mass extinction happened. A very large share of sea species disappeared. At the end of the **Triassic**, around 201 million years ago, the supercontinent **Pangaea** began to tear apart. In the **Central Atlantic Magmatic Province**, huge amounts of lava poured out. The gases strongly changed the climate and the chemistry of the oceans.

The best-known mass extinction happened at the end of the **Cretaceous** around 66 million years ago. At that time the dinosaurs disappeared, except for the ancestors of the birds. The main cause is thought to be the impact of a large asteroid. Afterwards **mammals** spread widely. Such a rapid splitting into many new species is called **adaptive radiation**. The survivors move into habitats that have become free.

Today many animal and plant species are disappearing faster than the natural background rate. That is why many experts speak of the **sixth mass extinction**. The causes are mainly the destruction of habitats, overuse and **climate change**. In Switzerland too, many species are considered endangered. Protected areas and preserving habitats are meant to help.

gewusst: The mass extinction at the end of the Permian is often called the largest in Earth's history.
Without the extinction of the dinosaurs, mammals would probably never have developed in so many different ways.

teile.einleitung: A fossil shows the remains or traces of living things that lived a very long time ago. Fossils reveal what the Earth and its animals and plants looked like in the past.
wichtigste: Petrified remains are also called fossils.
They form over many thousands to millions of years.
For this, the living thing is covered by layers of sand or mud.
Ammonites were sea creatures with a spiral-shaped shell.
In the canton of Jura there are thousands of fossilised dinosaur footprints.
Palaeontologists are researchers who study fossils.
Fossilised shells are found on Swiss mountains because there used to be sea there.

abschnitte.text: When an animal dies in water, it often sinks to the bottom. There it is covered by **sand or mud**. The soft parts decay, while hard parts such as bones, teeth or shells last longer. Over time minerals from the water seep in and turn the remains to stone. Sometimes only an **imprint** is left in the rock. All this takes a very, very long time.

Very well-known fossils are **ammonites**. They were sea creatures with a spiral-shaped shell that looks like a snail shell. They died out a long time ago. On Swiss mountains you can find fossilised shells and ammonites. The reason: a very long time ago there was a **sea** there. Later the seabed was folded up into mountains when the Alps formed.

Not only body parts can become fossils, but also **tracks**. In the **canton of Jura**, thousands of fossilised dinosaur footprints were found when the A16 motorway was built. They show where the animals once walked along a shallow seashore. There are such tracks in the Alps too.

**Amber** is fossilised tree resin and shimmers yellow to orange. When the resin was still sticky, small animals sometimes got stuck in it. So today insects that lived millions of years ago are found in amber. They are often so well preserved that you can see fine hairs and wings.

Researchers who study fossils are called **palaeontologists**. They carefully dig out finds, clean them and compare them with others. In this way they learn which animals and plants lived in the past and how life on Earth has changed. A famous site is **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, where many fossils of sea creatures and reptiles were found.

gewusst: Because of its fossils, Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Fossilised animal droppings are also fossils; they are called coprolites.

teile.einleitung: Molasse is a rock that lies under your feet almost everywhere on the Swiss Plateau. It is made of the debris that rivers carried from the young Alps into the foreland. Over time this debris turned into sandstone, marl and Nagelfluh.
wichtigste: Molasse is the eroded debris of the Alps in the foreland.
It was deposited about 35 to 5 million years ago.
The Swiss Plateau lies on Molasse almost everywhere.
Typical rocks are sandstone, marl and Nagelfluh.
At times there was a shallow sea over the Swiss Plateau.
At the edge of the Alps lies the tilted Subalpine Molasse.
The Molasse Basin stretches from Lake Geneva to Austria.

abschnitte.text: As the **Alps** rose, rain, frost and rivers attacked the young mountains. Huge amounts of rock were worn away and washed northwards. There lay a large hollow, the **Molasse Basin**. In it the debris collected layer by layer and over time turned into solid rock. Together these rocks are called **Molasse**.

Where the rivers flowed fast, coarse, round stones were left behind. These became **Nagelfluh**. Where the water flowed more calmly, sand settled and turned into **sandstone**. Fine mud became **marl**, a soft rock made of clay and lime. In many rock faces you can see these layers on top of each other like the layers of a cake.

The Molasse formed over a long time, roughly from 35 to 5 million years ago. Sometimes the basin was a shallow **sea**, sometimes a landscape with rivers and lakes. At the time of the **Upper Marine Molasse**, around 20 million years ago, a sea lay over today's Swiss Plateau. That is why shells and even **sharks' teeth** are found in these layers.

abschnitte.titel: Swiss Plateau and edge of the Alps
abschnitte.text: The Molasse Basin runs as a long trough along the northern edge of the Alps, from **Lake Geneva** across southern Germany to **Austria**. In Switzerland, the Molasse forms the ground beneath the **Swiss Plateau** between the Alps and the Jura. Often it is hidden under gravel and loam from the Ice Age. At the edge of the Alps, the layers were pushed together and tilted when the mountains formed. This zone is called the **Subalpine Molasse**, and the Rigi, for example, belongs to it.

Molasse sandstone is easy to work. After the great fire of 1405, the **old town of Bern** was rebuilt with sandstone from the surrounding area. Many churches, fountains and houses in other places on the Swiss Plateau are also made of this stone. Because sandstone weathers over time, old façades have to be repaired again and again.

gewusst: Sharks' teeth are found in the Molasse of the Swiss Plateau because a sea once lay here.
The arcades and houses of Bern's old town are made of sandstone that formed from Alpine debris.
The Molasse Basin is around 1,000 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: In geology, metamorphism is the change of rock through pressure and temperature without it melting. New minerals and textures form in the solid state. From the kinds of minerals, you can tell under what conditions a rock formed.
wichtigste: Metamorphism happens in the **solid state**, without melting.
Limestone turns into **marble**.
Mudstone turns step by step into shale, phyllite, mica schist and **gneiss**.
Contact metamorphism of mudstone produces **hornfels**.
Under very high pressure, basalt becomes **eclogite**.
The **blueschist facies** stands for high pressure at low temperature.

abschnitte.text: In **metamorphism**, the minerals and texture of a rock change while it stays solid. **Limestone**, for example, becomes **marble**: the calcite recrystallises into a grainy texture, and fossils and layering are usually lost. At very high temperatures, the light parts of a gneiss can partly melt while the dark parts stay solid. This creates a **migmatite** with light and dark layers, a mixed rock on the border with igneous processes.

In **regional metamorphism** you can see clearly how the **metamorphic grade** rises. **Mudstone** turns step by step into shale, **phyllite**, **mica schist** and finally **gneiss**. The minerals get bigger and bigger. Plate-like minerals such as **mica** grow at right angles to the direction of the greatest pressure. This creates **schistosity**, along which the rock can be split.

In **contact metamorphism**, the surrounding rock is changed by the heat of magma pushing in. There is no directed pressure. That is why mudstone turns into a dense, fine-grained, splintery rock without schistosity: **hornfels**.

When cold oceanic crust is quickly pulled down into the depths, the pressure rises more than the temperature. Then the **blueschist facies**, with the blue mineral **glaucophane**, is typical. At even higher pressure, basalt becomes **eclogite**. It is made mainly of red **garnet** and green **omphacite** and is much denser than basalt. Eclogite is also found in the Alps, for example in the Zermatt area.

Some minerals reveal the conditions under which a rock was changed. **Andalusite**, **kyanite** (in German “Disthen”) and **sillimanite** all have the formula Al₂SiO₅ but different crystal structures. Andalusite is stable at low pressure, sillimanite at high temperature and **kyanite at high pressure**. Experts group such sets of minerals into **metamorphic facies**.

gewusst: Kyanite has a different hardness in different directions, which is why in German it is also called “Zweihärter” (double hardness).
Eclogite shows that rock from depths of many dozens of kilometres can come back to the surface.

teile.einleitung: Air always contains some invisible water vapour. How much it contains is described by the humidity. Humidity helps decide whether fog and clouds form and whether we feel comfortable in a room.
wichtigste: **Absolute humidity** tells you how many grams of water vapour there are in a cubic metre of air.
**Relative humidity** tells you, as a percentage, how much of the possible amount the air contains.
**Warm air** can hold more water vapour than cold air.
At 100 per cent the air is saturated, and water vapour turns into droplets.
In fog, the relative humidity is around 100 per cent.
In living rooms, about 40 to 60 per cent is considered comfortable.

abschnitte.text: When water evaporates, it turns into **water vapour**. This gas is invisible and mixes with the air. **Absolute humidity** tells you how much water vapour is really in the air. It is usually measured in **grams per cubic metre**. An instrument for measuring humidity is called a **hygrometer**.

Air cannot take up as much water vapour as it likes. How much is possible depends on the temperature. **Warm air** can contain much more water vapour than cold air. At 30 °C it is a good six times as much as at 0 °C. That is why a hot summer's day often feels muggy.

**Relative humidity** compares the actual amount of water vapour with the largest possible amount at that temperature. An example: air could hold 20 grams per cubic metre but only contains 10 grams. Then you calculate 10 divided by 20. That gives 0.5, which is **50 per cent**. This is the figure you hear in the weather forecast.

If air cools down without any water being added, the relative humidity **rises**. After all, cooler air can hold less. When it reaches **100 per cent**, the air is saturated. Any more water vapour **condenses** into tiny droplets. This is how **fog** and **clouds** form. That is why the relative humidity in fog is around 100 per cent.

Most people feel comfortable in living rooms at about **40 to 60 per cent**. If it is damper for a long time, **mould** can form. In winter, on the other hand, the air in heated rooms is often dry. Cold outside air contains only a little water vapour. When it is warmed up indoors, it could hold much more, and the relative humidity falls sharply. Airing rooms regularly helps to keep a good indoor climate.

gewusst: Dew in the morning forms because the air cools down during the night and water vapour condenses on grass and leaves.
Steamed-up glasses show that warm, damp air has met a cold surface.

teile.einleitung: Peat is a brown to black soil made of dead plants that forms in bogs and moors. It grows very slowly and stores a lot of carbon.
wichtigste: Peat forms in bogs because the plants there do not rot completely.
In a wet bog there is not enough oxygen for the decomposers.
A layer of peat grows by about one millimetre a year.
In the past people cut peat and burned it for heating.
Since a popular vote in 1987, bogs and moors are protected in Switzerland.
After millions of years peat can turn into coal.

abschnitte.text: In a **bog** the ground is wet all year round. Dead plants, above all **peat mosses**, sink into the water. Because there is no **oxygen** there, decomposers cannot break them down completely. The remains build up and become **peat**. It is brown to blackish brown, and you can often still see bits of moss and plants in it.

Peat grows very slowly, about **one millimetre a year**. So one metre of peat takes around **a thousand years**. Many bogs in Switzerland started to grow after the last Ice Age. That is why a bog that is destroyed can hardly be replaced.

Peat used to be an important **fuel**. People cut it out of the bog with spades in brick-shaped pieces. This is called **peat cutting**. Then they dried the pieces and burned them in the stove. Especially at times when there was little wood and coal, for example during the World Wars, a lot of peat was dug in Switzerland too.

Bogs are home to many **rare animals and plants** and store a lot of **carbon**. When peat is dug, this habitat is lost. In Switzerland bogs and moors have been protected since the **popular vote of 1987**. Peat may no longer be dug there. That is why you should also use **peat-free compost** in the garden, because imported peat comes from bogs in other countries.

When peat is covered by many layers of rock and pressed together, it changes. Water is squeezed out, and the share of carbon rises. After **millions of years** it can become **lignite** (brown coal) and later **hard coal**. So peat is an early stage of coal.

gewusst: The popular initiative of 1987 is also called the Rothenthurm Initiative, after a moor in the canton of Schwyz.
In bogs, wood and other remains often stay well preserved for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: The Penninic nappes are one of the large nappe units of the Alps. They are made of rocks from an ancient ocean and a narrow sliver of continent. The highest peak in Switzerland, the Dufourspitze, also belongs to them.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Pennine Alps in Valais.
The Penninic nappes include ocean basins and the microcontinent of Briançonnais.
The Valais Trough lay between Europe and the Briançonnais.
Bündner schists and ophiolites are typical rocks.
Eclogite shows that rock was buried deep.
In Ticino lies the Lepontine Dome, made of gneiss nappes.

abschnitte.text: The **Valais Alps** are also called the **Pennine Alps**. The name goes back to the Roman name of the Great St Bernard. The nappe unit is especially thick in this area, which is why it is called **Penninic**. In the stack of nappes of the Alps, it lies between the European units below and the **Austroalpine** above. In Switzerland it is found mainly in Valais, Ticino and the Grisons.

Before the Alps formed, an area of sea lay between Europe and the Adriatic Plate, part of the **Tethys**. In the north lay a narrow basin, the **Valais Trough**. South of it lay a sliver of continent, the **Briançonnais**. Its rocks are found today in the Bernhard nappe, for example. Further south still lay the **Piedmont-Liguria Ocean**. As the plates came closer, all these areas were pushed together.

The deep-water deposits of the ocean turned into limy, finely layered **Bündner schists**. They are widespread, for example, in the **Prättigau**. They weather easily and tend to slide. Near Zermatt lies the **Zermatt-Saas zone**. It contains serpentinite, metagabbro and metabasalt, which are changed ocean crust. Such sequences are called **ophiolites**. In the Grisons, at the base of the Austroalpine, lies the **Arosa zone**, a mixture of sheared remains of ocean.

During **subduction**, ocean crust was pulled to great depth. Under high pressure, basalt and gabbro turned into **eclogite**. This dense rock is made mainly of red **garnet** and green **omphacite**. In Penninic units, for example near Saas, eclogite proves how deep the rock once lay. Later these rocks were lifted back to the surface.

The **Dufourspitze** in the Monte Rosa massif is the highest peak in Switzerland, at 4,634 metres. It is made of gneisses of the Penninic **Monte Rosa nappe**. In **Ticino**, erosion has cut especially deep. In the Leventina and the Maggia Valley you can see the lowest Penninic gneiss nappes. This stack is called the **Lepontine Dome**. The rocks there were strongly heated and changed.

gewusst: The highest mountain in Switzerland is made of Penninic rock.
Garnet from eclogite shows that a rock once lay dozens of kilometres deep.
Bündner schists are one reason why there are many landslides in the Prättigau.

teile.einleitung: The dew point is the temperature at which water vapour in the air begins to condense. Weather experts use it to explain dew, fog, clouds and muggy weather.
wichtigste: At the dew point, the air is saturated with water vapour.
If air cools below the dew point, dew, fog or a cloud forms.
If the dew point is below 0 °C, frost forms.
The dew point can be at most as high as the air temperature.
The difference between the temperature and the dew point is called the spread.
In summer, a dew point above 18 °C usually means muggy air.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains some **water vapour**. When it cools down, it can hold less of it. The **dew point** is the temperature at which the air is **saturated**. If it cools down even further, the vapour condenses into droplets. The dew point can be at most as high as the **air temperature**. If both are the same, the air is saturated.

After clear, calm nights there is often **dew** on the grass. The ground gives off a lot of heat, and the air right next to the grass cools below the dew point. If the dew point is below **0 °C**, the vapour settles directly as ice crystals: **frost** forms. If the air temperature and dew point are almost the same, **fog** or clouds are likely. This difference is called the **spread**.

A glass with a cold drink gets wet on the outside. The water comes from the air, which cools below the dew point at the cold glass. **Glasses** also steam up in winter when you come into a warm room. The warm, damp room air cools below the dew point on the cold lenses. Tiny droplets form.

There is a **rule of thumb** for the base of heaped clouds: 125 times (temperature minus dew point) gives the height in metres. At 20 °C and a dew point of 12 °C, the difference is 8 degrees. 125 times 8 gives **1,000 metres**. So the bigger the spread, the higher the clouds.

A high dew point means a lot of water vapour in the air. If it is **above 18 °C** in summer, most people feel the air is **muggy**. Sweat then evaporates poorly, and the body cools down less well. It feels oppressive. Muggy air is often also the fuel for thunderstorms.

gewusst: The dew point tells you more about mugginess than the relative humidity does.
Pilots use the spread to estimate whether fog is likely.

teile.einleitung: Marble is a beautiful, often white stone with fine veins. For thousands of years people have used it to build palaces and carve statues. It forms deep inside the Earth from limestone.
wichtigste: Marble forms from **limestone** through great heat and high pressure.
Many kinds of marble have fine, coloured **veins**.
Polished marble is smooth and feels cool.
The famous **Carrara marble** comes from Italy.
Michelangelo's “David” is made of white marble.
The **Taj Mahal** in India is faced with white marble.

abschnitte.text: Marble starts out as **limestone**. When this limestone gets deep inside the Earth, for example when a mountain range forms, it is strongly heated and squeezed. It does not melt, but its small grains grow and change. In this way limestone turns into marble. Such changed stones are called **metamorphic rocks**.

Pure marble is white. But it often contains small amounts of other substances. These form fine, coloured lines called **veins**. You can often recognise marble by them. When polished, it has a very smooth surface. It feels **cool** even on warm days.

White marble can be worked finely and has a beautiful shine. That is why sculptors have made many famous **statues** from it. Michelangelo carved “**David**” from a large block of white marble. The statue stands in **Florence** in Italy. The ancient Greeks and Romans were already building temples and statues from marble.

**Carrara** is a town in Tuscany in Italy. White marble has been quarried there for more than 2,000 years. Carrara marble is famous all over the world. There is marble in Switzerland too, for example in Ticino. Today marble is also used for floors, stairs, kitchens and bathrooms.

One of the most famous buildings made of marble is the **Taj Mahal** in India. It is a tomb and is faced with white marble. Small things recall the stone too: in the past, playing balls were often made of marble. That is why they are still called **marbles** today (in German, “Murmeln”).

gewusst: Marble has the same make-up as limestone: both are made mainly of the mineral calcite.
Acid, for example vinegar, can attack polished marble and leave dull spots.

teile.einleitung: Lithium is a metal found in almost every rechargeable battery in mobile phones and electric cars. That is why more and more of it is being mined around the world. Mining brings economic opportunities, but it is also controversial because of its effects on the environment and people.
wichtigste: Lithium is the **lightest metal** and is very well suited to batteries.
It is obtained from **brine** in salt lakes or from **hard rock**.
Chile, Argentina and Bolivia form the **Lithium Triangle**.
In 2024, **Australia** was the largest producer of lithium.
The most important lithium ore in hard rock is **spodumene**.
There is criticism especially because of the high water use in dry areas.

abschnitte.titel: Why lithium is in such demand
abschnitte.text: Lithium is the **lightest metal**. It also has a very negative **electrode potential**, which makes a high voltage possible in a battery cell. Together, this gives a high **energy density**: a lot of energy in little weight. That is why **lithium-ion batteries** are used in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars. As the number of electric cars grows, so does the demand for lithium.

A large part of the known lithium deposits lies in the salt lakes of the Andes, the **salars**. That is why Chile, Argentina and Bolivia are called the **Lithium Triangle**. Well-known ones are the Salar de Atacama and the Salar de Uyuni. There, salty water containing lithium, the **brine**, is pumped from underground into large ponds. The sun makes the water evaporate for months, and then the lithium is separated chemically.

In 2024, **Australia** was the largest lithium producer in the world. There lithium is mainly obtained from hard rock in **open-cast mines**. The most important ore is **spodumene**, a mineral found in rocks called **pegmatites**. After mining, it is processed. Bolivia does have very large deposits, but so far it produces little.

When the brine evaporates, large amounts of water are lost. In the Atacama, one of the driest regions in the world, this is especially controversial. Critics fear falling **groundwater levels**, which affect lagoons, animals and indigenous communities. Supporters point to jobs and the importance of lithium for climate protection. In Serbia too, a planned project in the **Jadar Valley** is meeting strong protests. The mineral **jadarite** was discovered there in 2004.

In the **Upper Rhine Graben** between Germany and France, hot deep water contains dissolved lithium. This water is already used in **geothermal plants** to produce heat and electricity. Afterwards the lithium could be separated out and the water pumped back into the ground. In this way people hope to obtain lithium with less impact on the landscape.

gewusst: Lithium is so light that it would float on water, but it reacts violently with it.
Jadarite is a mineral known in large amounts only in the Jadar Valley anywhere in the world.

teile.einleitung: Pyrite is a mineral with a golden shine, which is why it is often mistaken for gold. It is made of iron and sulphur. Pyrite is one of the most common sulphide minerals on Earth.
wichtigste: Pyrite is made of iron and sulphur.
Because it shines like gold but is not gold, it is also called “fool's gold”.
The name comes from the Greek word for fire.
Pyrite crystals very often grow as cubes.
On a porcelain tile, pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak.
Pyrite is much harder than gold.
In the past, pyrite was mined mainly to make sulphuric acid.

abschnitte.text: Pyrite has a brassy yellow colour and a strong **metallic lustre**. That is why many people have taken it for gold. It is therefore also called **fool's gold**. Chemically it is made of **iron** and **sulphur**, and its formula is FeS₂. It has nothing to do with real gold.

The name **pyrite** comes from the Greek word for **fire**. If you strike pyrite against steel or a hard stone, sparks fly. In earlier times people used this to make fire. To this day the name recalls this property.

Pyrite crystals very often grow as almost perfect **cubes**. Some look as if someone had cut them. But there are other shapes too, for example crystals with twelve five-sided faces. Pyrite is also often found as small grains in rock. Sometimes pyrite even replaces fossils such as ammonites, which then shine like gold.

If you rub pyrite across an unglazed **porcelain tile**, it leaves a **greenish-black streak**. Gold, on the other hand, leaves a golden yellow streak. Its **hardness** gives it away too: gold can easily be scratched with a steel needle, pyrite hardly at all, because it is much harder. In addition, gold is soft and bendable, while pyrite is brittle and breaks.

In the past, pyrite was mined mainly to make **sulphuric acid**. Industry needs this for many products. But pyrite also has a weakness: in **damp air** it weathers. Pieces in collections can fall apart and turn into powder. That is why collectors keep pyrite as dry as possible.

gewusst: Pyrite is so hard that it can scratch glass.
When pyrite weathers, acid can form that even attacks labels and boxes in collections.

teile.einleitung: A kettle hole is a hollow in the ground that formed when buried glacier ice melted. Such holes are found where glaciers retreated after the Ice Age.
wichtigste: Dead ice is ice that has broken away from the glacier and no longer moves.
Sand and gravel cover the block of ice, so it melts only slowly.
When the ice melts, the ground sinks and a kettle hole forms.
If the hole fills with groundwater, a kettle lake forms.
In northern Germany small kettle ponds are called “Sölle”.
When a kettle lake silts up, it often turns into a bog.

abschnitte.text: When a glacier retreats, large **blocks of ice** are often left behind. They are no longer connected to the glacier and no longer move. This motionless ice is called **dead ice**. Meltwater deposits **sand and gravel** over the blocks. This layer acts like insulation, so the ice melts only very slowly.

At some point the buried block of ice does melt. Then the ice is missing under the layer of earth. The ground above it **sinks**, and a **hollow** forms. This is a **kettle hole**. Most kettle holes are **roundish** and smaller than one hectare. But they can be more than ten metres deep.

If the bottom of the hole lies below the **water table**, it fills with water. This creates a small **kettle lake**. In **northern Germany** such small round ponds are called a **“Soll”**, plural **“Sölle”**. They formed after the last cold period. There are also many kettle lakes in the **Swiss Plateau** and the Alpine foothills.

Over many centuries **plant remains** collect at the bottom of a kettle lake. Reeds and mosses grow into the lake from the shore. Gradually the lake becomes overgrown. People say it **silts up**. In the end a **bog** often forms. Such bogs are valuable habitats for rare plants and animals.

gewusst: Kettle holes are traces of the Ice Age that you can still see today in the middle of meadows and forests.
Some blocks of dead ice took hundreds to thousands of years to melt completely.

teile.einleitung: **Silicates** are the most important minerals on Earth. They make up more than 90 per cent of the Earth's crust. They are all built from the same basic building block, which can be linked together in very different ways.
wichtigste: The basic framework of all silicates is the SiO₄ tetrahedron.
Silicate minerals make up more than 90 per cent of the Earth's crust.
Olivine is an island silicate with single tetrahedra.
Amphiboles are made of double chains; beryl is one of the ring silicates.
Quartz and the feldspars are framework silicates.
Kaolinite is a sheet silicate and the main part of china clay.
“Mafic” means rich in magnesium and iron.

abschnitte.text: Every silicate is built from **SiO₄ tetrahedra**. A tetrahedron is a small pyramid with four corners. In the middle sits a **silicon** atom, and at each of the four corners an **oxygen** atom. Oxygen and silicon are the two most common elements in the Earth's crust. That is why silicate minerals are so widespread: they make up **more than 90 per cent** of the Earth's crust.

The tetrahedra can be linked together in different ways. Silicates are divided into classes accordingly. In **island silicates** such as green **olivine**, the tetrahedra stand alone. In **ring silicates** such as **beryl**, they form rings. **Chain silicates** such as the pyroxenes form single chains, and the **amphiboles** form **double chains**.

In **sheet silicates**, the tetrahedra are joined into flat sheets. These include the **micas**, which can be split into thin flakes, and **kaolinite**, the main part of **china clay**. In **framework silicates**, all the tetrahedra are linked in all directions. These include **quartz** and the **feldspars**, the most common minerals in the Earth's crust.

In some silicates, **aluminium** replaces part of the silicon in the tetrahedra. This is the case, for example, in the **feldspars** and the **micas**. To make up for this, other atoms such as potassium, sodium or calcium are built in. This creates a great variety of minerals.

Geologists distinguish between **mafic** and **felsic** silicates. **Mafic** means **rich in magnesium and iron**. Such minerals, like olivine or amphiboles, are usually dark. **Felsic** minerals such as quartz and feldspar are rich in silicon and usually light. Granite, which is often found in the Swiss Alps, is made mainly of quartz, feldspar and mica.

gewusst: The green gemstone emerald is a variety of the ring silicate beryl.
Glass, bricks and porcelain are also made from silicates.

teile.einleitung: Loam is a soil made of fine sand, silt and clay. It is soft and sticky when wet and hard when it dries. For thousands of years people have used it to build houses and make bricks and pots.
wichtigste: Wet loam is soft, sticky and can be shaped.
When loam dries, it becomes hard and often cracks.
Loam fired in a kiln turns into solid **bricks**.
Loam is often brown, yellowish or reddish because it contains iron.
Loam does not let water through well, so puddles stay.
**Swallows** build their nests from little lumps of mud.

abschnitte.text: Loam is made of very fine grains: **sand**, even finer **silt** and very fine **clay**. It often contains iron. That is why it is usually brown, yellowish or reddish. When loam is wet, it feels soft and sticky. It clings to shoes and hands.

When the water evaporates from loam, it becomes firm and hard. It shrinks a little as it does so, and **cracks** often appear. Because the fine grains lie close together, loam lets water through only poorly. That is why a **puddle** often stays on loamy ground for a long time after rain.

Loam is found almost everywhere, and it is cheap. That is why people in many countries have built houses from **mud bricks** for thousands of years. These are dried in the sun. Mud houses stay cool in summer and warm in winter. Today loam is popular again, because it is a natural building material.

If you shape loam or clay and fire it in a very hot kiln, it becomes firm and hard. This is how **bricks** for walls and roofs are made. **Pots**, bowls and jugs are also shaped from loam and clay. This craft is called **pottery**. Fired clay can never become soft again, not even in water.

Animals use mud too. The **swallow** collects damp lumps of mud in its beak. It uses them to stick its nest to house walls, under the eaves or in barns. It needs a great many small lumps for one nest. That is why swallows depend on puddles and damp soil.

gewusst: Some of the oldest cities in the world were built from mud bricks.
A swallow's nest is made of hundreds of tiny balls of mud.

teile.einleitung: Rain is water that falls in drops from the clouds to the Earth. It fills streams, lakes and puddles and makes plants grow. Without rain there would be no life on land.
wichtigste: A raindrop is made of water.
Rain forms in clouds when tiny water droplets grow together into bigger drops.
Plants need rain to grow.
After rain, puddles are often left on paths and roads.
Earthworms often come out of the ground after rain.
Rain is measured in millimetres; one millimetre means one litre of water per square metre.
With an umbrella your head stays dry in the rain.

abschnitte.text: The sun warms the water in seas, lakes and plants, and it **evaporates** into invisible water vapour. The vapour rises with warm air and cools down high up. Small droplets form on tiny specks of dust, and a **cloud** develops. When many droplets bump into each other, they get bigger and heavier. When they are too heavy, they fall as rain. Here, rain often leaves the cloud as snow first and only melts on the way down.

Raindrops are usually between half a millimetre and five millimetres across. Unlike in drawings, they are not pointed but rather round or a little flattened at the bottom. Very fine rain is called **drizzle**. A short, heavy rain from a tall, towering cloud is called a **shower**. In a thunderstorm it can rain very heavily, sometimes even with hail.

Plants need rain to grow, because they take water from the ground with their roots. Rainwater fills streams, rivers and lakes. Part of it soaks into the ground and becomes **groundwater**, from which around 80 per cent of Switzerland's drinking water comes. Farming families are glad of rain at the right time. But too much rain at once can lead to flooding.

After rain, **earthworms** often crawl out of the ground. Researchers think they use the wet surface to travel further without drying out. Snails and frogs are also especially lively in damp weather. Blackbirds then like to look for worms on the lawn. Many other animals, on the other hand, hide under leaves or in their burrows when it rains.

How much it rains is measured with a **rain gauge**. The amount is given in millimetres; one millimetre equals one litre of water on one square metre of ground. In Switzerland, the amount of rain varies a lot from place to place. Valais is rather dry, while a lot of rain falls on the northern edge of the Alps and in Ticino. MeteoSwiss weather stations measure rain all over the country.

With an umbrella, a raincoat and **wellies** you stay dry. Jumping in puddles is fun, best of all in waterproof shoes. In the rain the road is slippery, and cars need longer to brake. Drivers also see you less well. That is why you should take extra care on the way to school and wear light-coloured clothes or reflective strips.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heat turns water into invisible water vapour, which rises into the air.
Water that falls from the clouds to the Earth, for example as rain, snow or hail.
Water that soaks into the ground and collects underground.
An instrument for measuring how much rain has fallen.

gewusst: Raindrops do not look like drops at all; large drops are shaped more like a small bread roll.
The typical smell after a summer shower has its own name: it is called petrichor.
Large raindrops fall to the ground at up to about 30 kilometres an hour.

teile.einleitung: A natural hazard map shows where floods, avalanches, landslides or rockfall can threaten people and houses. Colours show how great the danger is. Municipalities use the maps to plan safely.
wichtigste: Hazard maps use colours to show the danger from natural hazards.
Red means considerable, blue medium and yellow low danger.
Yellow and white stripes show a residual danger.
The cantons draw up the hazard maps.
Federal laws have required such maps since 1991.
The danger level depends on intensity and probability.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a country with many mountains, rivers and lakes. That is why there are many **natural hazards**: floods, debris flows, avalanches, landslides and rockfall. A **hazard map** shows, for a settled area, where such events threaten and how strongly. Municipalities use them mainly in **spatial planning**. This is how it is decided where building is allowed and where not.

**Red** means considerable danger. There people are at risk even inside houses, and new buildings are usually forbidden. **Blue** means medium danger. Here building is only allowed with **conditions**, for example with reinforced walls. **Yellow** shows a low danger: people in buildings are hardly at risk, but damage to property is possible. **Yellow and white stripes** show a residual danger from very rare events that could have a big effect.

For the danger level, experts combine two things. The **intensity** says how strong an event is, for example how high the water rises. The **probability** says how often it happens. A frequent and strong event gives the highest level, which is red. A rare and weak event gives a low level. To make the assessment, experts study the terrain, past events and calculations.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** are responsible for the hazard maps. They often work with specialist firms. The **federal government** supports them with guidelines and money. Since **1991**, the federal Hydraulic Engineering Act and Forest Act have required such maps. Today they have been drawn up for most settled areas. Because the landscape and protective structures change, they are revised again and again.

There is also a rougher overview map, the **hazard indication map**. It shows over a large area where a natural hazard could happen at all, without grading it precisely. The more precise **hazard map** is then drawn up for inhabited areas. Many cantons make their maps available online on their geoportals. In this way anyone can check how much danger their home is in.

gewusst: Hazard maps help to avoid building new houses in dangerous areas.
Red means a prohibition zone, blue a zone with conditions and yellow an advisory zone.
Even an area outside the coloured zones is never completely without risk.

teile.einleitung: The P-wave is the fastest wave produced in an earthquake. It always reaches the measuring instrument first. Researchers have even used P-waves to explore the inside of the Earth.
wichtigste: P stands for primary, because the wave arrives first.
In a P-wave, the particles move back and forth in the direction the wave travels.
P-waves travel through solids, liquids and gases.
At the liquid outer core they are strongly refracted.
Their shadow zone lies between about 104° and 140°.
In 1936, Inge Lehmann used them to discover the solid inner core.

abschnitte.text: In an earthquake, different **seismic waves** spread out. In a **P-wave**, the rock is squeezed together and stretched in turn. The particles move back and forth **in the direction the wave travels**. Such waves are called **longitudinal waves**. They work in a similar way to sound waves in the air. In water, the P-wave is actually an ordinary sound wave travelling at around 1.5 kilometres per second.

The letter P stands for **primary**. The name goes back to the Latin “undae primae”, the first waves. The P-wave is the fastest seismic wave. In solid rock it is much faster than in water. That is why it is the first to reach the **seismometer**. After it come the slower **S-waves** and the surface waves, which often cause the greatest damage.

Every substance can be squeezed. That is why pressure waves can travel everywhere: through **solids**, **liquids** and **gases**. P-waves can therefore cross the Earth's **liquid outer core**. S-waves cannot do this, because liquids do not pass on a shearing movement. From this difference, researchers concluded that the outer core is liquid.

When P-waves enter the outer core, they slow down and bend towards the centre. That is why there is an area they do not reach directly: the **shadow zone**. It lies at a distance of between about 104° and 140° from the epicentre. In 1936, the Danish seismologist **Inge Lehmann** noticed weak P-waves in this zone. She explained them as reflections from a **solid inner core**.

P-waves rarely cause much damage, but they are an important warning signal. **Earthquake early warning systems** estimate the location and strength of a quake from the first seconds of the P-wave. Sometimes a few seconds remain before the stronger waves arrive. In this time, trains can brake, for example. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes.

gewusst: Inge Lehmann discovered the Earth's inner core without ever seeing it, using only waves.
The P-waves of a strong earthquake cross the whole Earth in around 20 minutes.
On the other side of the Earth, P-waves arrive that have travelled right through the core.

teile.einleitung: A **seismograph** is a measuring instrument for earthquakes. It records how strongly and for how long the ground shakes. With it, you can also measure quakes that no person feels.
wichtigste: A seismograph measures earthquakes.
It draws a zigzag line.
The recorded picture is called a seismogram.
A very big zigzag means a strong earthquake.
In Switzerland, the Swiss Seismological Service monitors earthquakes.
In Switzerland about 1,000 to 1,500 earthquakes are measured each year.

abschnitte.text: A **seismograph** senses the tiniest movements of the ground. In an earthquake it draws a **zigzag line**. The picture is called a **seismogram**. When the ground is still, the line is almost straight. When the Earth shakes, it swings back and forth. A **very big zigzag** means a **strong earthquake** or one nearby.

Seismographs are very sensitive. They also measure earthquakes that you **cannot feel yourself**. In Switzerland, the instruments record about **1,000 to 1,500 earthquakes** a year. Most are so weak that nobody notices anything. Only about 10 to 20 of them can be felt by people.

In Switzerland, the **Swiss Seismological Service** monitors earthquakes. It is part of ETH Zurich and has many measuring stations all over the country. After a quake it quickly works out where it was and how strong it was. This information also appears on the internet and in a weather app.

Almost 2,000 years ago, an earthquake indicator was built in **China**. The scholar **Zhang Heng** built a large bronze vessel with eight **dragons**. Each dragon held a ball in its mouth. In a quake, a ball dropped into the mouth of a toad below. In this way people could see that there had been a quake somewhere.

gewusst: Modern seismographs no longer draw on paper but store the measurements in a computer.
Seismographs also notice blasting in quarries and even the noise of the sea's waves.

teile.einleitung: The word tuff, or tuff stone, refers to two different rocks. Volcanic tuff is made of hardened volcanic ash. Calcareous tuff, on the other hand, forms when lime is deposited from spring water. Both are porous, light and easy to work.
wichtigste: Volcanic tuff is made of hardened volcanic ash and small fragments of rock.
Tuff is one of the pyroclastic rocks.
Calcareous tuff forms when lime is deposited from spring water, often around moss.
Tuff stone is light and easy to work.
In Cappadocia in Turkey there are rock towers and cave dwellings made of tuff.
Most of the moai statues on Easter Island are carved from tuff.
The early city wall of Rome was built from blocks of tuff.

abschnitte.text: In a volcanic eruption, ash and small fragments of rock are hurled into the air. They fall back down and settle in layers. When these layers harden, **volcanic tuff** forms. Such rocks are called **pyroclastic**, which means roughly “broken by fire”. They come from the volcano but are deposited like sand or mud.

**Calcareous tuff** has nothing to do with volcanoes. Lime-rich spring water gives off **carbon dioxide** in the air. As it does so, lime is deposited and coats mosses, stalks and leaves. When the plant parts later rot away, small holes and tubes are left behind. That is why calcareous tuff often looks like a sponge made of stone.

Tuff is **porous**, light and usually quite soft. You can saw and carve it with simple tools. It also keeps out heat and cold well. That is why people built with tuff stone early on. Rome lies in an area with old volcanoes, and the **Servian Wall** was built from large blocks of tuff. In Switzerland too you can find calcareous tuff in old churches and houses.

In **Cappadocia** in Turkey, wind and water have shaped the soft tuff into rock towers. People hollowed out homes, churches and even whole underground cities in them. On **Easter Island** in the Pacific, the inhabitants carved most of their large **moai statues** from tuff in the Rano Raraku quarry. The rock was easy to work with stone tools.

gewusst: Some rock towers in Cappadocia wear a hat of harder rock on top that protects the soft tuff below.
Calcareous tuff can still grow at springs today; sometimes you can see it at waterfalls with moss.

teile.einleitung: Plutonic rocks are rocks that form deep in the Earth's crust from hot molten rock. They are also called intrusive rocks. The best-known example is granite.
wichtigste: Plutonic rocks form when magma cools slowly deep underground.
Because cooling is slow, large crystals grow: plutonic rocks are coarse-grained.
Granite is made of feldspar, quartz and mica.
Syenite contains hardly any quartz; diorite is chemically like the volcanic rock andesite.
The Swiss Albert Streckeisen created the QAPF double triangle for classifying plutonic rocks.
A very large body of plutonic rock is called a batholith.
Peridotite is the most common rock of the upper mantle.

abschnitte.text: When **magma** rises in the Earth's crust, it often gets stuck before it reaches the surface. There the surrounding rock is hot and holds back the heat. That is why the melt cools very slowly, often over thousands or millions of years. The crystals have plenty of time to grow and become visible to the naked eye. This produces a **coarse-grained** rock. If the magma reaches the surface, on the other hand, it cools quickly and forms fine-grained **volcanic rocks**.

**Granite** is pale and rich in silica (SiO₂). It is made of feldspar, quartz and mica. A German memory rhyme goes: “Feldspat, Quarz und Glimmer, die vergess ich nimmer”, which means “feldspar, quartz and mica, I will never forget them”. **Syenite** looks similar but contains hardly any quartz and mainly alkali feldspar. Its name comes from the Egyptian city of Syene, today's Aswan. **Diorite** has a medium SiO₂ content and is the intrusive rock that matches andesite.

To tell the many plutonic rocks apart properly, a clear classification is needed. In the 1970s, the Swiss petrologist **Albert Streckeisen** proposed the **QAPF double triangle**. It sorts the rocks by their shares of quartz, alkali feldspar, plagioclase and feldspathoids. This classification is used all over the world today. A petrologist is an expert on rocks.

At the end of cooling, a watery **leftover melt** often remains. It is runny, and especially large crystals grow in it. This produces **pegmatite**, a vein rock with crystals from centimetres to metres in size. Very large bodies of plutonic rock covering more than 100 square kilometres are called **batholiths**. A well-known example is the Sierra Nevada Batholith in California.

Not all intrusive rocks come from the crust. **Peridotite** is a dark, ultramafic rock made of more than 40 per cent of the green mineral **olivine**. It builds the upper mantle. In the Swiss Alps there are many granites, for example in the Aar Massif around the Grimsel or in the Bregaglia. They were lifted to the surface when the mountains formed.

gewusst: Many plutonic rocks we see at the surface today once lay several kilometres deep and only came to light through erosion.
Crystals several metres long have been found in pegmatites.

teile.einleitung: The Richter scale is the best-known scale for giving the strength of earthquakes. It was developed in 1935 by Charles Francis Richter. Today experts mostly use a newer scale for large quakes, but the name Richter is famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Charles Francis Richter developed the scale in 1935.
He worked closely with the seismologist Beno Gutenberg.
The scale was originally developed for Southern California.
The local magnitude worked out by Richter's method has the abbreviation ML.
One step more means a ten times larger swing in the seismogram.
The scale has no upper limit.
It is not suitable for very strong quakes from about magnitude 7.

abschnitte.text: The American seismologist **Charles Francis Richter** developed the scale in **1935**. A seismologist studies earthquakes. Richter worked closely with **Beno Gutenberg**. Their aim was to be able to compare quakes in **Southern California** with each other. There are many earthquakes there because of the San Andreas Fault.

A **seismometer** records the movement of the ground; the picture is called a **seismogram**. Richter used a particular instrument, the **Wood-Anderson seismometer**. He measured how big the largest swing was and took the distance to the quake into account. From this he calculated the **magnitude**, in other words the strength. This local magnitude has the abbreviation **ML**.

The Richter scale is **logarithmic**. This means: one step more means a **ten times** larger swing in the seismogram. So a quake of magnitude 5 has a 1,000 times larger swing than one of magnitude 2. The energy released rises even more with each step, by about thirty times. The scale has **no upper limit**; there is no fixed highest value.

For very strong quakes, the original Richter scale reaches its limits. It **underestimates** quakes from about **magnitude 7**, because the swings stop getting bigger. Experts say the scale is then saturated. That is why the **moment magnitude** is mostly used for large quakes today. It is based on how large the rupture surface that moved is and how far the rock shifted.

The ground shakes in Switzerland too, usually so weakly that nobody notices. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors the whole country. It reports quakes and gives their magnitude. The strongest known earthquake in Switzerland was the **Basel earthquake** of 1356. Quakes are especially common in Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region.

gewusst: Richter took the word “magnitude” from astronomy, where it gives the brightness of stars.
Very weak quakes can even have negative values on the scale.

teile.einleitung: A **snowflake** forms high up in the clouds from tiny ice crystals. Every flake grows a little differently on its way down to Earth. That is why two snowflakes are practically never exactly the same.
wichtigste: Snowflakes form in the clouds.
An ice crystal grows around a tiny speck of dust.
There are practically never two exactly identical snowflakes.
Snow is white because the many ice crystals reflect light.
Fresh snow swallows sounds, which is why it is so quiet afterwards.
Especially large flakes fall when it is just around zero degrees.

abschnitte.text: In the **clouds** it is often much colder than on the ground. There are tiny **specks of dust** there. Water vapour freezes onto such a speck, and a small **ice crystal** begins to grow. It usually has six corners or six arms. When the crystal is heavy enough, it falls to the Earth as a snowflake. Often several crystals stick together on the way into a bigger flake.

On its way through the cloud, every flake passes through slightly different temperatures and humidity. That is why its arms grow a little differently. So two snowflakes that look exactly the same are **practically never** found. You can see the fine patterns best under a magnifying glass.
