A single ice crystal is actually see-through, like glass. But in a layer of snow, countless crystals lie jumbled together. They **reflect the light** in all directions. All the colours of sunlight together make **white**. That is why snow looks white.

After fresh snowfall it is often surprisingly **quiet** outside. There is a lot of air between the loose flakes. These gaps **swallow sounds** like a sponge. If the snow later becomes hard or icy, this effect is much smaller. At temperatures **just around zero degrees**, the flakes stick together easily. Then especially large, heavy flakes fall.

gewusst: An American farmer called Wilson Bentley photographed thousands of snowflakes through a microscope back in the 19th century.
Snowflakes fall much more slowly than raindrops, because they are light and have a lot of air resistance.

teile.einleitung: A spring is a place where water comes out of the ground by itself. Many streams and rivers begin at a spring. There are thousands of them in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A spring is a place where water comes out of the ground.
Spring water is often cool even in summer, because it comes from the cool ground.
Warm water comes out of a thermal spring.
A geyser shoots hot water high into the air again and again.
Mineral water contains many dissolved minerals.
The source of a river is at its beginning.
When it does not rain for a long time, a spring can dry up.

abschnitte.text: Rain and meltwater soak into the ground. The water slowly trickles down through soil and rock. If it meets a layer that does not let water through, it flows sideways. On a slope or in a valley it then comes out of the ground again. This is a **spring**. Because the water has been travelling for a long time, it is often clean and clear.

Spring water is often **cool** even in summer, because it comes from the cool ground. But if the water comes from great depth, it can be warm. Then it is called a **thermal spring**. In Switzerland there are thermal baths, for example in Baden, Leukerbad and Bad Ragaz. A **geyser** is a hot spring that shoots water high into the air again and again. There are famous geysers in Iceland.

On its way through the rock, spring water takes up **minerals**, for example calcium and magnesium. Water with many dissolved minerals can be bought in bottles as **mineral water**. In Switzerland, a large part of the drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. To keep it clean, the areas around many springs are protected.

The **source** of a river is at its beginning. Some rivers also begin at a glacier or a mountain lake. At the very beginning, the water of the Rhône comes from the **Rhône Glacier** in Valais. The Rhine begins at Lake Toma in the Grisons. In this way, many small springs and streams turn into large rivers.

A spring needs supplies from above. If it does not rain for a long time, the water in the ground sinks. Then a spring can give less water in summer or **dry up** completely. When enough rain comes again, it usually flows again. That is why experts regularly measure how much water comes from important springs.

gewusst: A raindrop can travel through the ground for years or even decades before it comes out of a spring.
The geyser Strokkur in Iceland shoots water into the air about every few minutes.

teile.einleitung: Snow is made of tiny ice crystals that fall from the clouds when it is cold. It turns landscapes into a white winter world and is very important in Switzerland for nature, water supply and winter sports. Every snowflake is a small work of art.
wichtigste: Snow forms when water vapour in cold clouds freezes directly into ice crystals.
A snowflake usually has six points.
When it gets warm, snow melts into water.
You can build a snowman out of snow.
When a large amount of snow slides down a mountain, it is called an avalanche.
Fresh snow is made mostly of air.
In spring, meltwater from the snow fills streams, rivers and lakes.

abschnitte.text: Snow forms in clouds when the temperature is below freezing. There, water vapour settles on tiny specks of dust and freezes directly into an **ice crystal**. The crystal keeps growing as more and more water vapour settles on it. Several crystals can stick together and form a large **snowflake**. When they are heavy enough, they fall to the Earth. If it is warmer lower down, they melt on the way and arrive as rain.

Snow crystals usually have six points or six corners, because water molecules arrange themselves in a **hexagon** when they freeze. Depending on temperature and humidity, they grow as fine stars, flat plates or small columns. Because every crystal meets slightly different conditions on its way through the cloud, hardly any flake is exactly like another. In 1885 the American Wilson Bentley was the first to photograph a snow crystal under a microscope.

Freshly fallen, loose snow is called **powder snow**; it is about 90 per cent air. That is why a fresh layer of snow muffles sounds and everything seems quiet. Wet, heavy snow is good for building snowmen and igloos. In spring, the snow thaws during the day and freezes again at night, creating grainy **corn snow**. If snow stays on the ground for several years, it turns into firn and finally into glacier ice.

When a large amount of snow slides down a steep slope, it is called an **avalanche**. Avalanches often happen after heavy snowfall, in wind or when the snow becomes wet and heavy in spring. In winter, the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos publishes the avalanche bulletin with five danger levels. Anyone going off-piste needs knowledge, equipment including an avalanche transceiver, and good planning.

In Switzerland, snow is a huge **water store**. In spring and summer it melts slowly and fills streams, rivers, lakes and reservoirs. The meltwater supplies drinking water and electricity from hydroelectric power stations. Snow is also very important for ski areas and tourism. Because of climate change, snow now lies for much less time on average at low altitudes than it did a few decades ago.

In the snow you can build a **snowman**, go sledging or have a snowball fight. Skiing, snowboarding and cross-country skiing are also very popular in Switzerland. Because snow reflects up to 90 per cent of sunlight, you should wear sunglasses in the mountains. Otherwise you can get painful snow blindness.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, regularly shaped piece of ice that snowflakes are made of.
A large mass of snow that slides or crashes down a mountainside.
Old, grainy snow that has survived at least one summer.
A painful irritation of the eyes caused by the bright light reflected by snow.

gewusst: Snow is actually as clear as ice and only looks white because the many crystals scatter light in all directions.
A fresh layer of snow swallows so much sound that it becomes noticeably quiet outside.
To keep an igloo warm, the air in the snow is used as insulation.

teile.einleitung: The sea floor is the ground beneath the oceans. It is not flat but has mountains, valleys and volcanoes. A large part of it lies in complete darkness and is still hardly explored.
wichtigste: The deepest point of all the seas lies in the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific.
It is almost **11,000 metres** deep.
In the deep sea it is **pitch dark**, because light only reaches a few hundred metres down.
In 1960, the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** dived to the bottom with Don Walsh.
The depth of the sea is measured with an **echo sounder**.
In warm seas, corals build large **reefs**.

abschnitte.text: The sea floor is very varied. There are huge **mountain ranges**, wide plains, deep **trenches** and many **volcanoes**. Some underwater mountains are higher than the Alps. In warm, shallow seas, **corals** build large reefs. Corals are small animals with a chalky skeleton that grow together over a long time.

The deepest point of all the seas lies in the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific. It is almost **11,000 metres** deep. Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, would fit inside it and would not even stick out of the water. In 1960, the Swiss **Jacques Piccard**, together with Don Walsh, dived to the bottom in the submersible **Trieste**. The vessel had been developed by his father, Auguste Piccard.

Sunlight only reaches a few hundred metres down into the water. Below that it is **pitch dark** and cold. Even so, animals live there. The **anglerfish** has a kind of fishing rod on its head with a glowing lure. Small animals swim towards the light and are eaten. Many deep-sea animals can make their own light.

The deeper you dive, the more water presses down from above. In the deep sea this **water pressure** is enormous. A submersible for the deep sea therefore needs very **thick walls**. Otherwise it would be crushed. That is why only a few people have ever been to the deepest point of the sea.

A ship measures how deep the sea is with an **echo sounder**. The device sends sound down to the floor and measures when the echo comes back. Because the speed of sound in water is known, the depth can be calculated. This is how maps of the sea floor are made. But large parts have still only been mapped roughly.

gewusst: There are fewer accurate maps of the sea floor than of the surface of the Moon.
The Piccard family is famous for records: grandfather Auguste flew a balloon into the stratosphere, and grandson Bertrand flew around the Earth in a balloon and in a solar-powered aeroplane.

teile.einleitung: Ocean currents are huge rivers in the middle of the sea. They move enormous amounts of water around the Earth and spread heat and nutrients as they do so. Without them, the climate in Europe would be much colder.
wichtigste: Ocean currents are driven by winds, the Earth's rotation and differences in temperature and salt content.
The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico towards the North Atlantic.
The thermohaline circulation is a worldwide overturning movement that connects all the oceans.
The Atlantic overturning circulation is known by the abbreviation AMOC.
The cold Humboldt Current flows northwards off the west coast of South America.
In upwelling, cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the surface along coasts.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current is the only current that flows all the way around the continent of Antarctica.
El Niño is a climate phenomenon with unusually warm surface water off Peru.

abschnitte.text: An ocean current is a lasting movement of seawater in a particular direction. There are **surface currents**, driven mainly by the wind, and **deep currents** hundreds to thousands of metres down. Some currents bring warm water, others cold. The Earth's rotation deflects the water, which is why huge circular current systems form in the large oceans.

The **Gulf Stream** starts in the Gulf of Mexico and flows north along the east coast of North America. After that it continues as the North Atlantic Current to western Europe and Norway. It works like central heating for Europe, which is why the harbours in northern Norway hardly freeze over in winter. The Gulf Stream is part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or **AMOC** for short. Researchers are watching closely to see whether the AMOC is weakening because of global warming.

The **thermohaline circulation** is driven by differences in temperature (thermo) and salt content (haline). Cold, salty water is heavier and sinks into the depths, for example in the North Atlantic near Greenland. From there it flows very slowly through the oceans of the world and rises again in other places. Because this system connects all the seas, it is also called the **global conveyor belt**. The water takes around 1,000 years for a whole round.

The cold **Humboldt Current** flows from south to north off the west coast of South America. There the wind drives the surface water away from the coast, and cold deep water rises to replace it. This rising is called **upwelling**. The deep water brings lots of nutrients with it, which is why especially large amounts of plankton grow there. That is why some of the richest fishing waters in the world lie off Peru and Chile.

The **Antarctic Circumpolar Current** is the only current that flows all the way around the continent of Antarctica. It is driven by strong westerly winds and is the ocean current that carries the most water on Earth. Because no continent stands in its way, it can flow around the globe without a break. It separates the icy water around Antarctica from warmer water further north.

Every few years, the trade winds over the Pacific become weaker. Then the cold upwelling off Peru stops, and the surface water becomes unusually warm: this is called **El Niño**. The Spanish name means “the Christ Child”, because the phenomenon often appears around Christmas. El Niño changes the weather across half the world, for example with droughts in Australia and heavy rain in South America. Its cool opposite is called **La Niña**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A worldwide ocean current driven by differences in the heat and salt content of the water.
Cold, nutrient-rich water from the depths rises to the surface along a coast.
Abbreviation for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which includes the Gulf Stream.
A recurring warming of the Pacific off South America that changes the weather worldwide.

gewusst: In 1992, almost 29,000 plastic bath toys fell from a cargo ship into the Pacific, and their journey helped researchers understand ocean currents better.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries more than a hundred times as much water as all the rivers on Earth together.
As early as the 18th century, Benjamin Franklin had a map of the Gulf Stream printed so that mail ships could cross the Atlantic faster.

teile.einleitung: Opalinus Clay is a very dense claystone from the Jurassic period. In northern Switzerland it is one day meant to seal in radioactive waste safely. That is why it is studied more closely than almost any other rock in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Opalinus Clay is named after the ammonite Leioceras opalinum.
It is around 174 million years old.
It lets almost no water through.
Cracks can seal themselves because the clay minerals swell.
It has been studied at the Mont Terri rock laboratory in the canton of Jura since 1996.
In the Nördlich Lägern area, the layer is around 100 metres thick.

abschnitte.text: Opalinus Clay was deposited as fine mud in a shallow sea in the **Lower Jurassic**, around 174 million years ago. This makes it much older than the folding of the Alps. It is named after the ammonite **Leioceras opalinum**, an extinct mollusc with a spiral shell. This **index fossil** marks the layer. Its shell often shimmers like mother-of-pearl, like an opal.

Opalinus Clay **lets very little water through**. Water hardly moves in it, and dissolved substances travel almost only by slow **diffusion**. In addition, the **clay minerals** have negatively charged surfaces. Many radioactive substances stick to them. This is called **sorption**. As a result they travel even more slowly than the water. These properties make the clay a good **host rock** for a deep repository.

A special property is **self-sealing**. If cracks form in the rock and water gets in, the clay minerals swell up. This closes the paths again. In this way Opalinus Clay hardly loses its tightness even after disturbances. This ability is important, because cracks can form around the tunnels when a repository is built.

Opalinus Clay has been studied since 1996 at the **Mont Terri rock laboratory** near St-Ursanne in the **canton of Jura**. It is run by **swisstopo**, the Federal Office of Topography. More than 20 partners from around ten countries do research there in tunnels about 1,200 metres long. In the **Nördlich Lägern** area, which Nagra has proposed as a site, the layer is around 100 metres thick and lies several hundred metres deep.

What is good for a repository can cause problems when building tunnels. In contact with water, and because of the release of pressure when rock is dug out, the clay can **swell** and deform. It then presses on the **tunnel lining**. This must be taken into account in building and maintenance. That is why experts measure in test tunnels exactly how much the rock moves.

gewusst: Ammonites such as Leioceras opalinum lived in the sea at the time of the dinosaurs.
At Mont Terri, experts from many countries do research together.
In some places in northern Switzerland, Opalinus Clay lies hundreds of metres deep.

teile.einleitung: An avalanche is a large mass of snow that suddenly breaks loose and slides or crashes down a mountain slope. Avalanches can destroy houses and are very dangerous for people in the mountains. In Switzerland, the SLF in Davos warns of the avalanche danger every day.
wichtigste: An avalanche is a large mass of snow that slides quickly down a slope.
Slab avalanches usually break loose on slopes of about 30 degrees or more.
In Switzerland, the SLF in Davos publishes the avalanche bulletin.
The European avalanche danger scale has five danger levels.
With an avalanche transceiver, buried people can be located.
Protection forest shields villages in the Alps from avalanches in a natural way.

abschnitte.text: An **avalanche** happens when the snowpack on a slope no longer holds. A lot of new snow, strong wind and weak layers in the snowpack are dangerous. Avalanches usually break loose on slopes of about **30 degrees** or steeper. Often it is the winter sports enthusiasts themselves who trigger an avalanche with their weight.

In a **slab avalanche**, a whole slab of snow breaks off at once; this is the most dangerous kind for skiers. Loose snow avalanches start at one point and widen into a pear shape. **Powder avalanches** of dry powder snow can travel at over 200 km/h. Wet snow avalanches happen mainly in spring, when the snow is melting.

In winter, the **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in Davos publishes the avalanche bulletin every day. It uses the European **avalanche danger scale**, with five levels from low to very high. Even at level 3, considerable, many fatal accidents happen. You can read the bulletin in the White Risk app or on the SLF website.

Anyone going off-piste needs an **avalanche transceiver**, a shovel and a probe. The transceiver sends out signals that companions can use to locate a buried person. Because buried people have less and less chance of survival after about 15 minutes, the search has to be fast. An avalanche airbag can help you stay on the surface.

The **protection forest** above many mountain villages holds the snow in place and slows avalanches down. Where no forest grows, **avalanche barriers** made of steel or wood are built to hold the snow back on the slope. Hazard maps show where building is not allowed. In the avalanche winter of 1999, a great many avalanches came down in Switzerland, including in Evolène in Valais.

begriffe.erklaerung: A connected slab of snow that breaks off as a whole.
A device for searching for people buried by avalanches, which locates them.
A daily report on the avalanche danger.
A forest that protects villages and roads from natural hazards such as avalanches.

gewusst: About half of the forest in Switzerland protects against natural hazards such as avalanches and rockfall.
The SLF in Davos is one of the best-known avalanche research institutes in the world.
Avalanche dogs can smell buried people even under metres of snow.

teile.einleitung: The polar vortex is a huge whirl of cold air over the polar regions. It forms mainly in winter, high up in the stratosphere. If it is disturbed, it can affect the weather far away.
wichtigste: The stratospheric polar vortex is strongest in the winter of each hemisphere.
In the Northern Hemisphere it turns anticlockwise, seen from above.
It is disturbed mainly by planetary waves travelling upwards.
A sudden stratospheric warming can weaken or split it within a few days.
The southern polar vortex is usually more stable than the northern one.
Polar stratospheric clouds form below about -78 °C and are important for the ozone hole.
A disturbed polar vortex can bring cold spells a few weeks later.

abschnitte.text: In the polar winter, the sun does not shine at the pole for a long time. The air in the **stratosphere**, the layer of air above a height of about 10 to 15 kilometres, cools down strongly. Around this cold a band of strong westerly winds forms. This is how the **polar vortex** develops. In the Northern Hemisphere it turns **anticlockwise**, seen from above. It is strongest in the winter of each hemisphere.

Mountains and the contrasts between land and sea create large waves in the atmosphere, the **planetary waves**. If they travel up into the stratosphere, they can disturb the vortex. Sometimes the stratosphere then warms up strongly within a few days. This is called a **sudden stratospheric warming**. The polar vortex can become weaker, shift or even split into two parts.

In the Southern Hemisphere there is a lot of sea and fewer mountains. That is why weaker planetary waves form there. The **southern polar vortex** is therefore usually more stable and colder than the northern one. The northern vortex is disturbed much more often, because large continents and mountain ranges such as the Rocky Mountains and the Himalayas lie there.

abschnitte.titel: Cold clouds and the ozone hole
abschnitte.text: In the very cold Antarctic polar vortex, **polar stratospheric clouds** form below about -78 °C. On them, chemical processes take place that release chlorine from certain substances. When the sun returns in spring, this chlorine destroys a lot of **ozone**. This is how the **ozone hole** over Antarctica forms. The vortex holds the air together as if in a container.

A disturbed polar vortex often only has an effect further down after a few weeks. Then cold polar air can push far to the south. In Europe, and so in Switzerland too, this can bring **cold spells**. But it does not happen every time. Weather services watch the polar vortex closely, because it is helpful for longer-range forecasts.

gewusst: In a sudden stratospheric warming, the temperature in the stratosphere can rise by several dozen degrees within a few days.
Polar stratospheric clouds sometimes shimmer in rainbow colours and are therefore also called mother-of-pearl clouds.

teile.einleitung: In August 2005 it rained very heavily in Switzerland for several days. Streams and rivers burst their banks, lakes rose and debris flows destroyed houses. The flooding caused the greatest total damage since systematic records began.
wichtigste: The main cause was heavy rain lasting several days on the northern side of the Alps.
Six people died in Switzerland.
According to the Federal Office for the Environment, the damage came to around 3 billion francs.
In Bern the Matte district on the Aare was under water.
In Brienz debris flows from the Glyssibach destroyed several houses.
For days Engelberg could only be reached by air.
Afterwards a relief tunnel for Lake Thun was built in Thun.

abschnitte.text: In August 2005 a **low-pressure area** sat over Central Europe in such a way that damp air flowed again and again towards the Alps. On the **northern side of the Alps** very large amounts of rain fell over several days. The ground could no longer soak up the water. Streams and rivers swelled and burst their banks. Many lakes also rose sharply.

In the city of **Bern** the Aare flooded the **Matte** district below the old town. Further upstream the Aare burst its banks in the Belpmoos and put **Bern-Belp** airport under water. In **Brienz** on Lake Brienz, huge **debris flows** from the Glyssibach broke into the village. A debris flow is a fast stream of water, mud and stones.

In the canton of Obwalden the **Engelberger Aa** destroyed the road and railway line into the valley. So for days the monastery and holiday village of **Engelberg** could only be reached by helicopter. Other valleys were cut off too. Many people had to leave their homes and were taken to safety. The fire brigade, civil protection and the army helped with rescue and clearing up.

According to the **Federal Office for the Environment**, six people died in Switzerland. The damage to houses, roads, railway lines and fields came to around **3 billion francs**. That was the greatest total damage since systematic records began in 1972. Insurance companies paid for much of the damage, but the Confederation, cantons and municipalities also had to spend a lot of money.

After 2005 Switzerland improved its **flood protection**. Dams were built, rivers were given more space and hazard maps were drawn up. In **Thun** a **flood relief tunnel** was built. During floods it carries extra water from Lake Thun into the Aare so that the lake level falls more quickly. Warnings of severe weather were also improved.

gewusst: A debris flow can carry away large boulders that are heavier than a lorry.
Today hazard maps show for many municipalities where floods or debris flows are a threat.

teile.einleitung: Minerals are the building blocks of rocks. Each mineral has a particular chemical make-up and usually a typical crystal shape. From glittering rock crystal to the salt on your plate, we come across them everywhere.
wichtigste: A mineral is a naturally formed solid substance with a particular chemical make-up.
Rocks are made of one or more minerals.
The Mohs scale compares the hardness of minerals from 1 to 10.
Diamond is the hardest and talc the softest mineral on the Mohs scale.
Rock crystal is a transparent form of quartz.
Table salt is made of the mineral halite.
Granite is made mainly of feldspar, quartz and mica.

abschnitte.text: A mineral is a solid substance that has formed in nature without help from people. Its atoms are usually arranged regularly and form a **crystal lattice**. That is why many minerals grow into beautiful **crystals** with smooth faces and sharp edges. Today about 6,000 different minerals are known (as of 2025). Only a few dozen of them are very common and make up most of the rocks.

To identify minerals, their **hardness** is tested, among other things. In 1812, the German scientist Friedrich Mohs arranged ten minerals by how easily they can be scratched: this is the **Mohs scale**. At the bottom is talc, with hardness 1, which you can even scratch with your fingernail. At the top is diamond, with hardness 10, which scratches all other minerals. In between are, for example, calcite at 3, quartz at 7 and corundum at 9.

As well as hardness, colour, lustre and cleavage help with identification. If you rub a mineral across a rough porcelain plate, it leaves a coloured line, the **streak**. It is often more reliable than the colour of the crystal itself. Some minerals have special properties: magnetite is magnetic, and halite tastes salty.

Rocks are mixtures of minerals. **Granite** is made mainly of feldspar, quartz and mica, which you can recognise as light, grey and glittering grains. **Quartz** is one of the most common minerals in the Earth's crust and very hard. Its transparent form is called rock crystal, and its purple form amethyst. Limestone, on the other hand, is made mostly of the mineral calcite.

We use many minerals every day, often without noticing. Table salt is the mineral **halite**, which in Switzerland is obtained, for example, at Schweizerhalle near Basel and at Bex in the canton of Vaud. Glass is made from quartz sand, and plasterboard from gypsum. Metals such as iron, copper or aluminium are obtained from **ores**. Every mobile phone also contains substances from dozens of different minerals.

The Swiss Alps are famous for their beautiful mineral finds. Someone who searches for crystals there is called a **Strahler**. Strahler search in fissures, which are cavities in the rock, for rock crystal, smoky quartz and other minerals. A famous find of giant rock crystals from the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri is on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid body with regularly arranged building blocks and smooth faces.
A hardness scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond) for comparing minerals.
The colour of the powder a mineral leaves on a rough porcelain plate.
In Switzerland, a person who searches for crystals in the mountains.

gewusst: Diamond and graphite, the material in pencil leads, are both made only of carbon.
Talc is so soft that it is ground into powder and used as baby powder.
Some rock crystals from the Swiss Alps weigh more than a hundred kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Polar ice is the ice in the cold regions around the North and South Poles. There are huge ice sheets on land and frozen seawater, called sea ice. Both are important for the climate of the whole Earth.
wichtigste: The largest ice sheet on Earth lies on the continent of Antarctica.
There is no land at the North Pole: the ice floats on the Arctic Ocean.
Arctic sea ice is smallest in September.
Ice has a high albedo and reflects a lot of sunlight.
Around 60 per cent of the Earth's fresh water is stored in the ice of Antarctica.
The Greenland Ice Sheet is around 3 kilometres thick at its thickest point.
Polar bears hunt seals on the sea ice.

abschnitte.text: An **ice sheet** is a huge mass of ice lying on land. Today there are two: the Antarctic and the Greenland Ice Sheets. **Sea ice**, on the other hand, forms when seawater freezes. At the North Pole there is no continent; the ice there floats on the **Arctic Ocean**. The South Pole, by contrast, lies in the middle of the continent of **Antarctica**.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet covers almost the whole continent. In some places it is more than 4 kilometres thick. Around **60 per cent of the Earth's fresh water** is stored in it. The Greenland Ice Sheet is smaller, but still around 3 kilometres thick at its thickest point. If these masses of ice melted, sea level would rise sharply.

Sea ice grows in winter and shrinks in summer. In the Arctic, its area is smallest in **September**, after the long summer. It is largest towards the end of winter, in March. Satellites have been measuring these areas for decades. They show that Arctic sea ice in summer has become much smaller.

White ice reflects a lot of sunlight back into space. This **reflectivity** is called **albedo**. Dark seawater, on the other hand, absorbs a lot of light and warms up. When ice melts, more heat is absorbed, and even more ice can melt. That is why the polar regions are so important for the climate of the whole Earth.

Tiny air bubbles are trapped in the ice. Researchers drill long **ice cores** and read from them the climate and air of earlier times. The University of Bern is also involved in this research. For animals, the ice is a habitat: the **polar bear** hunts seals on the Arctic sea ice and so depends on the ice. In Antarctica, on the other hand, penguins live.

gewusst: Polar bears live only in the Arctic, and penguins almost only in the Southern Hemisphere, so they never meet in the wild.
Ice cores from Antarctica contain air that is hundreds of thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: Metamorphic rocks are rocks that have been changed. They form when a rock gets deep into the Earth and is changed there by high pressure and high temperature. Many rocks in the Swiss Alps are metamorphic.
wichtigste: Metamorphic rocks form through **change** under high pressure and high temperature.
Metamorphosis means **transformation** in Greek.
The rock does not melt completely, otherwise it would become **magma**.
Sandstone turns into **quartzite**.
Next to hot magma, **contact metamorphism** happens.
All three groups of rock can be changed.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **metamorphosis** means **transformation** or change of shape. It is also used when a caterpillar turns into a butterfly. When a rock gets deep inside the Earth, pressure and heat change its **minerals** and its **texture**. But it stays solid. If it melts completely, it becomes **magma**, and later an igneous rock forms from it.

Metamorphic rocks form in large amounts deep inside mountain ranges. When **continental plates** collide, rocks are buried deep and strongly squeezed. This **regional metamorphism** affects huge areas. Many rocks of the **Alps** were shaped in this way, for example gneisses and mica schists.

When hot magma pushes into the Earth's crust, the neighbouring rock is strongly heated. Right where it touches the melt, it is changed. This is called **contact metamorphism**. It usually affects only a narrow zone around the magma. Here heat plays the main role, not pressure.

In many metamorphic rocks the minerals are **lined up in parallel**. When a rock is strongly squeezed from one direction, plate-like minerals line up across the pressure. This makes the rock look **striped** or **flaky**. **Sandstone**, which is made mainly of quartz grains, turns into very hard **quartzite**. Limestone turns into marble.

abschnitte.titel: Lavez from Ticino and the Grisons
abschnitte.text: A special metamorphic stone is **lavez**, also called **soapstone** or potstone. It is found in Ticino and the Grisons. Lavez is soft and stores heat very well. In the past, **cooking pots** were turned from it on a lathe. Even today, **stoves** that stay warm for a long time are built from it. Whether igneous, sedimentary or already metamorphic: every rock can be changed by metamorphism.

gewusst: Lavez stoves slowly give off their heat for hours after the fire has gone out.
Some rocks in the Alps were changed several times, one after another.

teile.einleitung: Weathering is the slow breakdown of rock where it is. Weather, water and living things loosen and break down the rock. Only after that can erosion carry the particles away.
wichtigste: During weathering the rock first stays in the same place.
Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, erosion carries it away.
There is physical, chemical and biological weathering.
When rainwater dissolves limestone, this is called chemical weathering.
Roots that push rocks apart are called root wedging.
Chemical weathering is strongest in the hot, humid tropics.
Karren are grooves that rainwater dissolves in limestone rock.

abschnitte.text: **Weathering** prepares the rock: it loosens it, makes cracks and breaks it into smaller pieces. These pieces stay where they are at first. Only during **erosion** do water, ice or wind carry the particles away. Both processes work together and shape mountains and valleys over a long time. Weathered rock also forms the **soil** in which plants grow.

In physical weathering, rock breaks without its substances changing. In **deserts** the rock gets very hot during the day and cools down sharply at night. The constant expanding and contracting causes cracks. This is called **thermal weathering**. In **salt weathering**, salty water seeps into pores and evaporates. The growing salt crystals push the rock apart. In the mountains, water freezing in cracks also splits the rocks.

Rainwater contains some **carbonic acid**, which can dissolve limestone. Because the substances change in the process, this is called **chemical weathering**. Such processes happen faster when it is warm and need water. That is why rock breaks down especially deeply in the **hot, humid tropics**. In cold or dry areas chemical weathering is weaker.

Living things also weather rock. Plant roots grow into fine cracks and get thicker. With great force they widen the gaps until the rock breaks. This is called **root wedging**. Lichens and mosses also give off substances that slowly attack the rock.

On bare limestone surfaces, rainwater dissolves grooves from very fine to a metre deep. These grooves are called **karren** or, in Swiss German, **Schratten**. When there are many side by side, this is called a **karren field** or limestone pavement. Well-known examples are on the **Schrattenfluh** in the canton of Lucerne, which is named after the Schratten, and in the **Silberen** area in the canton of Schwyz.

gewusst: The Schrattenfluh gets its name from the Schratten, the grooves in the limestone.
Water expands by about a tenth when it freezes, and that can split rocks.

teile.einleitung: A **stalactite** is a dripstone that hangs like an icicle from the ceiling of a cave. It is made of lime and grows very slowly, drop by drop.
wichtigste: A stalactite is made of lime.
It hangs from the ceiling like a pointed icicle.
Stalactites usually grow very slowly.
At the tip of a growing stalactite there is always a drop of water.
Very thin, hollow young stalactites are called soda straws.
When a stalactite and a stalagmite grow together, a column forms.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater seeps through the ground and through **limestone**. As it does so, it dissolves a little **lime**. When the water comes out of the ceiling in a cave, a **drop of water** forms. Before it falls, it gives off a gas, and a tiny ring of lime is left hanging on the ceiling. That is why there is always a drop at the tip of a growing stalactite.

Young stalactites are often **very thin and hollow**, like a little tube. They are called **soda straws** (in German “Makkaroni”, because they look like pasta). The water flows through the inside of the tube. If it gets blocked, the water runs down the outside. Then the stalactite gets thicker and takes on the shape of a **pointed icicle**.

Stalactites usually grow **very slowly**. Often it is only fractions of a millimetre a year. How fast it goes depends on how much water drips and how much lime is dissolved in it. That is why a large stalactite can be many thousands of years old. If it grows together with a **stalagmite** from the floor, a **column** forms.

Small stalactites sometimes form outside caves too. They can be found, for example, **under concrete bridges**, in tunnels or in cellars. There water dissolves substances from the concrete, which crystallise again as icicle shapes. These often grow much faster than real dripstones in caves.

The word **stalactite** comes from **Greek** and means **“dripping”**. A memory aid helps to tell stalactites and stalagmites apart: stalactites hang from the ceiling, stalagmites stand on the floor. A German memory aid goes: “Stalak**t**iten **t**ropfen herab” (stalactites drip down) and “Stalag**m**iten **m**achen sich am Boden breit” (stalagmites spread out on the floor).

gewusst: Under concrete bridges, small lime icicles can grow several centimetres long in a few years, much faster than in caves.
In some caves there are soda straws more than a metre long that are still only as thick as a drinking straw.

teile.einleitung: Rossby waves are huge waves in the air flow that wind around the Earth in snake-like lines. They decide whether high or low pressure dominates here. They are named after the meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby.
wichtigste: The planetary waves of the westerly wind belt are named after Carl-Gustaf Rossby.
They are based on the increase of the Coriolis force with latitude.
Relative to the main flow, Rossby waves travel westwards.
An area of low pressure high up that reaches southwards is called a trough.
When the amplitude is large, weather patterns stay in place longer.
Typically about three to seven large waves span the Northern Hemisphere.
Rossby waves also exist in the oceans.

abschnitte.text: In the middle latitudes, a strong **westerly wind** usually blows high up. But it does not flow straight; it winds around the Earth in large snake-like lines. These swings are called **Rossby waves** or planetary waves. They are named after the Swedish-American meteorologist **Carl-Gustaf Rossby**. He explained them in the 1930s.

The Earth rotates. Because of this, the **Coriolis force** acts on moving air and deflects it. This force is zero at the equator and increases towards the poles. If air is pushed north or south, this increase makes it swing back again. Experts describe this with **vorticity**, a measure of how the air is spinning. The absolute or potential vorticity stays the same as it does so.

A Rossby wave has parts that reach southwards and parts that reach northwards. The part that reaches southwards, with low pressure high up, is called a **trough**. It is often cool and changeable there. The part that reaches northwards, with high pressure, is called a **ridge**; there the weather is often calm. Typically about **three to seven** large waves span the Northern Hemisphere at the same time.

Rossby waves travel **westwards relative to the main flow**. Because the wind carries them eastwards at the same time, they often make only slow progress overall. When the waves become very large, the flow runs strongly north and south, which is called **meridional**. Then **weather patterns** can **stay** in the same place for a long time. This can bring weeks of heat, drought or a lot of rain, in Switzerland too.

Rossby waves exist **not only in the atmosphere**. Such waves also form in the **oceans**. There they are very slow and can take months or years to cross an ocean. At the surface of the sea they raise the water by only a few centimetres. Even so, satellites can measure them.

gewusst: Ocean Rossby waves can be hundreds of kilometres long but only a few centimetres high at the surface.
Long-lasting high-pressure situations in Europe are often linked to very large Rossby waves that hardly move.

teile.einleitung: Palaeoclimatology studies the climate of the past, long before there were thermometers. To do this, researchers read natural archives such as tree rings, ice, lake beds and dripstones. This helps to put today's climate into context.
wichtigste: Indirect climate indicators are called proxy data.
Dendrochronology uses the annual rings of trees.
The chalky shells of foraminifera reveal the amount of ice and the sea temperature.
Pollen analysis is used to reconstruct the plants of the past.
Dripstones are often dated with the uranium-thorium method.
Around 56 million years ago there was a rapid warm phase, the PETM.

abschnitte.text: Regular measurements with instruments have only existed for around 300 years. For the time before that, the climate has to be worked out from **natural archives**. Such indirect climate indicators are called **proxy data**. They include tree rings, ice cores, lake sediments, corals and dripstones. To make sure they are right, they are compared with real series of measurements and **calibrated**.

In good years, trees grow more and form wider **annual rings**. **Dendrochronology** uses the width and density of these rings. By lining up many pieces of wood, calendars accurate to the year can be made going back thousands of years. In **pollen analysis**, pollen in lake sediments is studied. Pollen survives for a long time and can be matched to plants. In Swiss lakes, for example, it shows how the forests returned after the Ice Age.

Tiny air bubbles are trapped in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. They show how much carbon dioxide used to be in the air. Researchers at the **University of Bern** have contributed a great deal to this. In deep-sea sediments, the chalky shells of **foraminifera**, tiny single-celled organisms, provide data on the amount of ice and the sea temperature. As they grow, **dripstones** take in a little uranium, which slowly decays into thorium. With **uranium-thorium dating**, ages of up to around 500,000 years can be determined in this way.

Around 56 million years ago, the Earth warmed rapidly by about 5 to 8 °C. This phase is called the **Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum**. At that time, large amounts of carbon got into the air and the ocean. The event is seen as a comparison for today's climate change. At the end of the last cold period, on the other hand, there was a sudden return to cold, the **Younger Dryas**, around 12,900 to 11,700 years ago. It is named after the mountain avens (Dryas), a plant of cold regions.

An astonishing hypothesis goes back much further still. Around 700 million years ago, the Earth may have been almost completely **frozen over**. This is called **Snowball Earth**. Glacial deposits from this time are found even in areas that were then close to the equator. Volcanic carbon dioxide may later have ended the glaciation. Experts are still discussing how complete the glaciation was.

gewusst: Ice cores from Antarctica go back around 800,000 years.
Tree rings can sometimes tell you the exact year in which a wooden beam was cut down.
The mountain avens, after which the Younger Dryas is named, grows in the Alps today.

teile.einleitung: Rodinia was a supercontinent in which almost all the Earth's land masses were joined around a billion years ago. Later it broke up again into separate pieces. Experts reconstruct what Rodinia looked like from ancient rocks.
wichtigste: Rodinia was a supercontinent around a billion years ago.
The name comes from Russian.
Important parts were welded together in the Grenville orogeny.
Before Rodinia there was the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna.
Rodinia was surrounded by the huge ancient ocean Mirovia.
According to most reconstructions, Laurentia lay at its centre.
The forming and breaking up of supercontinents is called the supercontinent cycle.

abschnitte.titel: One continent for almost all the land
abschnitte.text: A **supercontinent** is a huge land mass in which almost all the continents are joined. **Rodinia** existed around **a billion years** ago. The name comes from **Russian** and means roughly “homeland”. At that time there were no plants or animals on land yet. Life was in the sea and consisted mainly of simple living things.

The continents move very slowly because of **plate tectonics**. When they collide, mountains form; this is called **orogeny**. Important parts of Rodinia were welded together in the **Grenville orogeny**. Remains of this mountain range can be found today in North America, for example. According to most reconstructions, **Laurentia**, the ancient core of North America, lay at the centre of Rodinia.

Around Rodinia lay a huge ocean. It is called **Mirovia**, and this name also comes from Russian. Because Rodinia is so old, many traces have been changed by later mountain building. Experts compare rocks, mountain chains and the magnetism of ancient rocks on different continents. That is why there are different suggestions for how exactly the pieces fitted together.

About 750 million years ago, Rodinia began to **break up**. After that there were very strong glaciations, known as **Snowball Earth**. One explanation is that the break-up created more coastline and more rain fell on land. The stronger **weathering** of the rocks took a lot of **CO₂** out of the air. With less CO₂, it got colder.

Rodinia was not the only supercontinent. Even before it there was **Columbia**, also called **Nuna**. Later came **Pangaea**, the supercontinent from the time of the early dinosaurs. The repeated forming and breaking up of such land masses is called the **supercontinent cycle**. Experts think that the continents will join together again in the distant future.

gewusst: One cycle from the coming together to the break-up of a supercontinent takes hundreds of millions of years.
During Snowball Earth, according to some ideas, the ice reached almost as far as the equator.

teile.einleitung: Economic geology studies where and how valuable raw materials form inside the Earth. These include ores, salt, gemstones and metals such as gold or platinum. It helps to decide whether mining is worthwhile.
wichtigste: A reserve can be mined profitably with today's technology and at today's prices.
The cut-off grade is the minimum content from which rock is considered worth mining.
Most banded iron formations formed in the Precambrian more than 1.8 billion years ago.
Around 40 per cent of all the gold ever mined comes from the Witwatersrand Basin.
Primary diamonds are found mainly in kimberlite.
Most platinum comes from the Bushveld Complex in South Africa.
Swiss Saltworks obtains salt by solution mining.

abschnitte.text: A **deposit** is a place where a raw material is so concentrated that it can be mined. What matters is the **cut-off grade**. This is the **minimum content** from which rock is considered worth mining. Poorer rock is left where it is, because mining it would not pay. If prices rise, the cut-off grade can change.

Experts make a careful distinction. A **resource** is a known or suspected amount of a raw material in the Earth. A **reserve** is only the part of it that can be mined profitably with **today's technology** and at **today's prices**. That is why reserves can grow without any new finds being made. It is enough for technology to improve or prices to rise.

abschnitte.titel: Iron and gold from ancient times
abschnitte.text: The most important iron ores are **banded iron formations**. They are made of fine layers and formed mainly in the **Precambrian**, more than 1.8 billion years ago. At that time oxygen built up in the sea, and dissolved iron settled out. Gold is often very old too. Around **40 per cent** of all the gold ever mined on Earth comes from the **Witwatersrand Basin** in South Africa.

Diamonds form deep in the mantle. Melts that rise quickly bring them up, where they are found in the rock **kimberlite**. Most of the **platinum** mined worldwide comes from the **Bushveld Complex** in South Africa. **Rare earths** are needed for magnets, screens and electronics. In recent years, **China** has mined by far the most of them.

Switzerland has few mineral resources, but a lot of **rock salt** underground. **Swiss Saltworks** obtains it by **solution mining**. Water is pumped down deep, the salt dissolves, and the salty **brine** is pumped up. Then the water is evaporated, and the salt is left. There are saltworks, for example, at Schweizerhalle and Riburg on the Rhine and at Bex in the canton of Vaud.

gewusst: In the Bex salt mine you can visit tunnels where salt was mined centuries ago.
Diamonds in kimberlite are often much older than the rock in which they are found.

teile.einleitung: The Rhône is a large river that begins at the Rhône Glacier in Valais and flows into the Mediterranean Sea in France. On the way it flows through Lake Geneva. In Upper Valais it is called “Rotten” in German.
wichtigste: The Rhône is around 810 kilometres long.
It rises at the Rhône Glacier in Valais.
In Upper Valais it is called Rotten in German.
It flows past Sion, the capital of Valais.
At Martigny it turns north in a bend.
In Geneva it takes in the Arve, and in Lyon the Saône flows into it.
With the Rhône corrections, the river has been tamed since the 19th century.

abschnitte.titel: From the glacier into the valley
abschnitte.text: The Rhône begins at the **Rhône Glacier** in the canton of **Valais**. From there it flows west through the long Rhône Valley. In German-speaking **Upper Valais** it is called the **Rotten**, and in French-speaking Lower Valais the Rhône. On the way it takes in many streams from the side valleys. It also flows past the cantonal capital, **Sion**.

At **Martigny**, the Rhône turns **north** in a **bend**. After that it forms part of the border between the cantons of Valais and Vaud. Finally it flows into **Lake Geneva**. There it deposits a lot of the sand and mud it has brought down from the mountains. The water leaves the lake clear in **Geneva**.

In **Geneva**, the Rhône flows out of the lake. Shortly afterwards it takes in the **Arve**, a river from the French Alps. The Arve is often cloudy and grey, while the Rhône is clear blue. That is why you can see two colours side by side for a while where they meet. After that the Rhône leaves Switzerland and flows into France.

In the past, the Rhône often burst its banks in Valais. Its valley was marshy, and floods destroyed fields and villages. Since the **19th century**, the river has been tamed with large building projects, the **Rhône corrections**. Dams were built, and the riverbed was made straighter. Today another correction is under way, which is meant to bring more safety and give the river more space again.

In France, the Rhône flows to **Lyon**. There the **Saône**, a large tributary, flows into it. After that the Rhône flows south. Altogether it is around **810 kilometres** long. Shortly before the **Mediterranean Sea** it splits and forms a large river delta, the **Camargue**, which is famous for its flamingos and white horses.

gewusst: In Geneva, at the Jonction, you can see the clear water of the Rhône and the grey water of the Arve flowing side by side.
The Rhine and the Rhône rise not far from each other in the Swiss Alps, but flow into completely different seas.

teile.einleitung: In the **Bex salt mine** in the canton of Vaud, salt has been taken out of the mountain for more than 300 years. Today you can also visit the mine and ride deep inside on a little train.
wichtigste: The Bex salt mine is in the canton of Vaud.
Salt has been obtained there for more than 300 years.
The salt comes from an ancient sea.
All the tunnels and shafts together are about 50 kilometres long.
Visitors ride into the mountain on a little mine train.
Today the salt is dissolved out of the rock with water.

abschnitte.text: A very long time ago, there was a **sea** where the Alps are today. When parts of it dried out, the salt was left behind as a layer. Later it was covered by rock and pushed into the mountain when the Alps formed. That is why the salt is now in the rock near **Bex** in the Rhône Valley.

People here knew about salty springs early on. To get more salt, they began to dig **tunnels** into the mountain. This has been going on for more than 300 years. In the past it was hard work by hand with hammer and chisel. Over time a huge network grew: all the tunnels and shafts together are about **50 kilometres** long.

Today the salt is no longer chipped out as stone. It is **dissolved out of the rock with water**. This produces salty water, the **brine**. It is pumped up and heated until the water evaporates and the salt is left. It is used, for example, as table salt or as road salt.

Part of the mine is open to **visitors**. You ride deep into the mountain on a little **mine train**. On a guided tour you find out how the workers used to work. Deep inside the mountain there is even a **restaurant**. It is cool in the mine all year round, so it is best to take a jacket.

gewusst: In the Bex salt mine you can eat deep inside the mountain, in a restaurant in the middle of a tunnel.
The salt of Bex is many millions of years old, much older than the Alps themselves.

teile.einleitung: A tsunami is a series of huge sea waves, usually set off by an undersea earthquake. On the open sea it is hardly noticeable, but at the coast it can grow into an enormous wall of water. Tsunamis are among the most dangerous natural disasters.
wichtigste: The Japanese word tsunami means harbour wave.
A tsunami is most often set off by an undersea earthquake.
In the deep ocean a tsunami can travel about as fast as an aeroplane.
One warning sign is when the sea suddenly draws back a long way.
On 26 December 2004 a devastating tsunami occurred in the Indian Ocean.
Tsunamis can also happen on lakes, for example in 563 on Lake Geneva.
When there is a tsunami warning, you must flee to higher ground at once.

abschnitte.text: The word **tsunami** comes from Japanese and means harbour wave. In the past, fishermen came back to a destroyed harbour even though they had noticed nothing on the open sea. Unlike normal waves made by the wind, a tsunami moves the water from the seabed to the surface. It usually consists of several waves that arrive minutes to an hour apart. The first wave is not always the biggest.

A tsunami is most often set off by an **undersea earthquake**. The seabed suddenly lifts or drops, often at a subduction zone, where one plate sinks beneath another. The whole column of water above moves with it and spreads out as a wave. Volcanic eruptions, rockfalls and underwater landslides can also set off tsunamis. Very rarely, the impact of a meteorite can be the cause.

In the deep ocean a tsunami races along at 700 to 800 kilometres per hour, about as fast as an aeroplane. There the wave is often less than a metre high, and ships hardly feel anything. Only when the water becomes shallower near the coast does the wave slow down and pile up, sometimes to more than ten metres. Often the sea suddenly draws back a long way beforehand and the seabed is exposed. This **warning sign** means: get away from the beach at once and up to higher ground!

On 26 December 2004 a huge undersea earthquake with a magnitude of about 9.1 shook the seabed off the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It set off a tsunami that hit the coasts of many countries around the **Indian Ocean**, including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Thailand. More than 200,000 people died, among them tourists from Switzerland. In 2011 a tsunami devastated the east coast of Japan and led to the accident at the Fukushima nuclear power station.

Tsunamis can also form on lakes. In the year 563 a mountain collapsed in the Rhône Valley near the fortress of Tauredunum, and the debris set off a huge flood wave on **Lake Geneva**. It flooded the shores and caused great damage even in Geneva. The earthquake of 1601 in Central Switzerland also set off large waves on **Lake Lucerne**. Today researchers study the deposits on the lake bed to assess such dangers better.

After 2004 a **tsunami early warning system** was also set up in the Indian Ocean, as had long existed in the Pacific. Measuring buoys and pressure sensors on the seabed detect unusual waves. Because earthquake waves are much faster than the tsunami, there is often some time for a warning. On coasts at risk, signs show the escape route to higher places.

begriffe.erklaerung: Japanese for harbour wave, a series of huge waves, usually after an undersea earthquake.
Earthquake whose centre lies below the seabed.
Network of measuring devices that warns of a danger before it arrives.
Place where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.

gewusst: The highest tsunami wave ever observed was set off by a rockfall in Lituya Bay in Alaska in 1958 and surged more than 500 metres up a slope.
A tsunami can cross a whole ocean in less than a day.
The undersea earthquake of 2004 was so strong that it made the whole Earth vibrate slightly.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Stocker is a Swiss climate physicist at the University of Bern. He is one of the internationally known climate researchers and led part of the fifth world climate report.
wichtigste: Thomas Stocker was born on 1 July 1959.
He studied environmental physics at ETH Zurich.
From 1993 he led the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics in Bern.
From 2008 to 2015 he was co-chair of Working Group I of the IPCC.
In 2017 he received the Marcel Benoist Prize.
Among other things, he researched the bipolar seesaw.

abschnitte.text: **Thomas Stocker** was born on **1 July 1959**. He studied **environmental physics** at **ETH Zurich** and completed a doctorate in **1987**. After that he did research in London, Montreal and New York, among other places. In **1993** he became a professor at the Physics Institute of the **University of Bern**. There he led the Division of **Climate and Environmental Physics**, which is known for its work on **ice cores**.

abschnitte.titel: Work for the world climate council
abschnitte.text: The **IPCC**, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, sums up what is known about the climate in large reports. From **2008 to 2015** Stocker was **co-chair of Working Group I**, together with a Chinese colleague. This group deals with the scientific basis. Its report for the Fifth Assessment Report came out in **2013**. In 2015 the Federal Council nominated him to chair the IPCC. However, the South Korean economist **Hoesung Lee** was elected.

Stocker researched how the northern and southern hemispheres are connected. If the ocean current that brings warmth into the **North Atlantic** weakens, the north cools down. At the same time the south slowly warms up. This pattern is called the **bipolar seesaw**. Ice cores from **Greenland** and **Antarctica** show it.

In **2017** Stocker received the **Marcel Benoist Prize**. It is considered the most important science prize in Switzerland. In 2026 he received the **Alfred Wegener Medal** of the European Geosciences Union. It is named after the German polar researcher **Alfred Wegener**, who founded the theory of continental drift.

gewusst: Ice cores contain tiny trapped air bubbles that show what the air was made of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
When the IPCC report he co-led came out in 2013, Stocker was 54 years old.

teile.einleitung: Radar interferometry, or InSAR for short, is a measuring method using radar satellites. Two radar images of the same area are compared, and in this way the tiniest movements of the ground can be seen. This makes it possible to watch earthquakes, volcanoes and landslide slopes from space.
wichtigste: InSAR compares the phase of the reflected radar wave between two images.
One full colour cycle in an interferogram equals a shift of half a wavelength.
Radar satellites send out their own microwaves and measure even at night and through clouds.
A single measurement only records the movement in the satellite's line of sight.
Persistent scatterers are points such as buildings or rocks that reflect steadily for a long time.
Snow often destroys coherence, which is why winter images in the Alps are difficult.
At best, InSAR records movements of a few millimetres a year.

abschnitte.text: A radar satellite sends **microwaves** to the Earth and receives the echo. Because it brings its own radiation, it does not need sunlight. That is why it can measure even **at night**, and microwaves pass through **clouds**. In **SAR**, **synthetic aperture** radar, the movement of the satellite is used. Many images along its path are calculated together as if there were a very long antenna. This gives sharp pictures.

A radar wave has a **phase**, which means you know at what point in its vibration it comes back. In InSAR, the phase of two images taken at different times is compared. If the ground has moved, the wave travels a little longer or shorter. The result is an **interferogram** with coloured stripes called **fringes**.

The wave travels to the ground and back again. That is why one full colour cycle equals a shift of **half a wavelength**. With a wavelength of 5.6 centimetres, that is 2.8 centimetres per stripe. So three full stripes mean 8.4 centimetres. However, a single image only measures the movement in the **satellite's line of sight**. To get the whole movement, images from different directions are needed.

For long time series, **persistent scatterers** are used. These are points such as buildings, bridges or rocks that reflect the radar steadily over a long time. With many images, movements of a few **millimetres a year** can be detected in this way. It becomes difficult when the surface changes a lot. A **snow cover** changes the reflection, and the **coherence** is lost. That is why winter images in the Alps are often unusable.

In 2000, the **Shuttle Radar Topography Mission** used a Space Shuttle to measure almost the whole land area of the Earth. This produced a worldwide **elevation model**. Today experts use InSAR to watch how the ground shifts in earthquakes or how volcanoes swell. In Switzerland the method helps to monitor **landslide slopes** and rock glaciers in the Alps. Settling of buildings can also be detected.

gewusst: In the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, a 60-metre mast stuck out of the Space Shuttle, with a second antenna at its end.
From hundreds of kilometres up, InSAR can tell that an area has risen by a few millimetres.

teile.einleitung: Air is not nothing: it has weight and presses down on everything below it. This pressure is called air pressure. It affects the weather, the wind and even when water boils.
wichtigste: Air pressure is caused by the **weight of the air** above us.
At sea level it is on average around **1,013 hectopascals**.
Weather services such as MeteoSwiss give it in **hectopascals** (hPa).
Near the ground, it falls by around 1 hPa for about every 8 metres of height.
At a height of about 5,500 metres, it is only half as great.
Air flows from high to low pressure, and this creates **wind**.

abschnitte.text: Above every place on Earth there is a huge **column of air** that reaches up to the edge of the atmosphere. The air in it has weight. It presses down on the ground and on us. This is **air pressure**. We do not feel it, because it acts equally strongly from all sides and our bodies push back against it.

Air pressure is measured in **pascals**. Because the numbers are very large, **hectopascals** are used. Hecto means 100, so 1,013 hPa equals **101,300 pascals**. In the past people said **millibars**; the number is the same. **Standard pressure** at sea level is 1,013.25 hPa. The actual value varies with the weather. It is measured with a **barometer**.

The higher you climb, the less air there is above you. That is why air pressure falls. At low altitudes it drops by about 1 hPa for around every 8 metres, and more slowly higher up. At a height of about **5,500 metres**, it is only half as great as at sea level. If you take the train from Interlaken up to the **Jungfraujoch**, the pressure falls clearly. Many people feel this in their ears.

Air pressure is not the same everywhere. There are areas with high pressure, the **highs**, and areas with low pressure, the **lows**. Air evens out such differences. It flows from high to low pressure, and this creates **wind**. The bigger the difference, the stronger it blows. A high often brings fine weather, a low more likely clouds and rain.

At sea level, water boils at 100 °C. On a high mountain, the air pressure is lower. Then water particles can turn into gas more easily, and water boils earlier. On the **Jungfraujoch** it boils below 90 °C. That is why pasta or eggs take longer to cook at high altitude.

gewusst: On every square centimetre of our skin, the air presses about as hard as a weight of one kilogram.
On the summit of Mount Everest, the air pressure is only about a third of the value at sea level.

teile.einleitung: Igneous rocks form from hot molten rock that cools down and becomes solid. In German they are therefore also called “solidification rocks”. Whether they solidify deep inside the Earth or at the surface decides what they look like.
wichtigste: Igneous rocks form from solidified **magma** or solidified **lava**.
**Intrusive rocks** solidify slowly in the Earth's crust, for example granite.
**Extrusive rocks** solidify quickly at the surface, for example basalt.
Slow cooling produces large, clearly visible crystals.
**Obsidian** is volcanic glass, and **pumice** can float on water.
Gabbro and basalt have the same make-up.

abschnitte.text: Deep inside the Earth there is molten rock: **magma**. When it cools, it becomes solid and crystals form. This produces **igneous rocks**. Together with sedimentary rocks and metamorphic rocks, they are one of the three large groups of rock. They are grouped according to where they solidified.

**Intrusive rocks**, also called **plutonic rocks**, solidify deep in the Earth's crust. There the melt cools very slowly, often over thousands of years. The crystals have plenty of time to grow and become large. That is why you can see the individual grains clearly in **granite**. Granite is also found in the Swiss Alps, for example in the Gotthard area.

**Extrusive rocks**, also called **volcanic rocks**, form from lava that flows out during volcanic eruptions. They cool quickly, so their crystals are usually very small. The most common extrusive rock is dark **basalt**. **Andesite** is a grey extrusive rock named after the **Andes** in South America. It is found in many volcanoes there.

If lava cools extremely quickly, no crystals can form at all. Then volcanic glass forms: black **obsidian**. It has sharp edges when broken and was used for blades in the Stone Age. **Pumice** forms from lava full of gas that froths up during an eruption. It is full of holes and so light that it can float on water.

Rocks that look completely different can form from the same melt. **Gabbro** and **basalt** have the same chemical make-up. Gabbro solidifies slowly deep down and is coarse-grained. Basalt solidifies quickly at the surface and is fine-grained. In a similar way, granite deep down and **rhyolite** at the surface belong together.

gewusst: Pumice is still used today to remove hard skin from feet.
The ocean floor is made largely of basalt, with gabbro underneath.

teile.einleitung: A lake is not equally warm everywhere. Often warm water lies on top and cold water below. At certain times the water mixes. This **lake circulation** is very important for life in the lake.
wichtigste: Fresh water is densest at about 4 °C.
Dimictic lakes mix completely twice a year.
Meromictic lakes never or only very rarely mix their deep water.
The northern basin of Lake Lugano did not mix completely for decades.
Mixing brings oxygen down into the depths and nutrients up to the top.
Under the ice, water at around 0 °C lies at the top and water at about 4 °C at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: Most substances get denser and denser as they cool. Water is different: **fresh water** is densest at about **4 °C**. Even colder water becomes lighter again. That is why water at about 4 °C collects at the bottom of deep lakes. In a **frozen lake**, water at around 0 °C lies at the top, directly under the ice, while at the bottom it is about 4 °C warm. This is how fish can survive at the bottom in winter.

In summer the sun warms the surface. Warm, light water then lies above cold, heavy water. The lake is **stratified**. In autumn the surface water cools down, becomes **denser** and **sinks**. This is the **autumn turnover**. Wind helps until the whole lake is mixed.

Lakes that mix completely **twice a year**, in spring and autumn, are called **dimictic**. In mild climates there are **warm monomictic** lakes: they circulate **once a year, in winter**, because they never freeze over. Lakes whose deep water **never or only very rarely** mixes are called **meromictic**.

Complete mixing brings **oxygen** from the air down into the depths. At the same time, **nutrients** come up from the bottom to where algae need them in the light. If there is no mixing for a long time, there can be too little oxygen deep down. Then hardly any fish or other animals can live there.

The **northern basin of Lake Lugano** is known for not having mixed completely for **decades**. Its deep water therefore contained hardly any oxygen. Other deep lakes in Switzerland do not mix right down to the bottom every year either. With warmer winters, complete mixing is becoming rarer, because the surface water cools down less.

gewusst: Because water is heaviest at 4 °C, deep lakes freeze from the top down and never from the bottom up.
Only a very cold winter can supply the deep water of a large lake with oxygen again.

teile.einleitung: Radiative forcing is a measure used in climate research. It describes how strongly a factor such as carbon dioxide or aerosols changes the Earth's energy balance.
wichtigste: Radiative forcing is given in watts per square metre.
A positive forcing warms the Earth, a negative one cools it.
For CO2, approximately ΔF = 5.35 · ln(C/C0).
Doubling CO2 gives around 3.7 W/m².
Human-made aerosols have a cooling effect overall.
According to the IPCC, the total human-made forcing in 2019 was around 2.7 W/m².

abschnitte.text: The Earth receives energy from the Sun and gives off heat radiation into space. When the two are the same size, the **radiation balance** is even. **Radiative forcing** tells you how strongly a factor shifts this balance. It is measured in **watts per square metre** (W/m²). A **positive** forcing means that more energy comes in than goes out, which warms the Earth. A **negative** forcing has a cooling effect.

For carbon dioxide there is an approximate formula: **ΔF = 5.35 · ln(C/C0)**. Here C is the new and C0 the original concentration, and ln is the natural logarithm. With a **doubling**, C/C0 = 2 and ln 2 ≈ 0.693. This gives around **3.7 W/m²**. A rise from 280 to 420 ppm, with ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405, gives around **2.2 W/m²**.

Forcing grows **logarithmically** with the concentration. This means that what counts is the ratio, not the difference. Going from 280 to 560 ppm has about the same effect as going from 560 to 1,120 ppm. The reason is that the most important **absorption bands** of CO2 are already saturated in their middle. Only at their edges does the effect keep growing.

**Aerosols** are particles floating in the air, for example sulphate. They scatter sunlight back into space and make clouds brighter. That is why the forcing from human-made aerosols is **negative** overall. Volcanoes have a similar effect: after the eruption of **Pinatubo** in 1991, sulphate droplets formed in the stratosphere. The average temperature fell temporarily by around **0.5 °C**.

The **IPCC**, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, adds all the factors together. In its sixth report it gives a best estimate of **2.72 W/m²** for 2019 compared with 1750. This includes warming greenhouse gases and cooling aerosols. So the aerosols hide part of the warming caused by the greenhouse gases.

gewusst: The cooling after Pinatubo lasted about one to two years, after which the particles had disappeared from the stratosphere.
A forcing of a few watts per square metre seems small, but it affects the whole surface of the Earth day and night.

teile.einleitung: A moraine is debris that a glacier carries along and leaves behind somewhere. Moraines still show us today how big the glaciers used to be. In Switzerland they are found in the Alps and all over the Swiss Plateau.
wichtigste: Moraines are made of rock debris carried by a glacier.
Lateral moraines lie at the edge, medial moraines in the middle of the ice.
The terminal moraine shows how far the glacier once reached.
The ground moraine forms under the glacier.
Moraine material is mixed up without any order.
Lakes often form behind terminal moraines.

abschnitte.text: A glacier flows slowly down the valley and takes rock with it. Stones fall onto the ice from the valley slopes, and underneath, the glacier tears material from the ground. Everything it carries along and deposits is called **moraine**. Moraine material is **mixed up without any order**: big boulders, gravel, sand and loam lie jumbled together. A river, on the other hand, sorts its material by size.

At the edge of the glacier, the debris from the slopes collects into a long ridge, the **lateral moraine**. When two glaciers flow together, their inner lateral moraines join. This creates a dark stripe in the middle of the ice, the **medial moraine**. On large glaciers such as the Aletsch Glacier you can see such stripes from far away.

In front of its snout, the glacier pushes debris up into a ridge, the **terminal moraine**. It marks how far the ice once reached. Meltwater often collects behind a terminal moraine, because the ridge acts like a dam. This is how **lakes** form. Under the ice, rock is ground into fine and coarse material. When the ice melts, this layer stays behind as **ground moraine** and covers the valley floor.

During the ice ages, glaciers covered almost the whole Swiss Plateau. Many lines of hills and lakes there are traces of this. In the **Zurich Oberland**, for example, there are **drumlins**. These are long, streamlined hills of ground moraine material that the glacier shaped underneath itself. Their long direction shows where the ice flowed. In front of many Alpine glaciers you can also see fresh ridges with hardly any plants on them, from the time around **1850**, when the **Little Ice Age** ended.

When a glacier melts, its lateral moraines are left behind as steep slopes. In the past the ice supported these slopes. Now the loose material is unprotected. In rain or thawing weather it can slide down as **rockfall** or as a **debris flow**. That is why such slopes in the Alps are monitored, and hiking paths are sometimes moved.

gewusst: Large boulders that glaciers have carried a long way are called erratics.
Drumlins still reveal the direction in which long-vanished glaciers flowed.
Many lakes on the Swiss Plateau are dammed by moraine ridges.

teile.einleitung: A dripstone cave is a cave in which stone icicles grow from the ceiling and the floor. They form from limestone that the water brings with it and they grow very slowly. In Switzerland you can visit such caves, for example the Höllgrotten in the canton of Zug.
wichtigste: Dripstone caves usually form in limestone.
Water dissolves lime from the rock and deposits it again in the cave.
Dripstones grow very slowly, often only millimetres in many years.
In caves it is roughly equally cool and damp all year round.
The Höllgrotten near Baar are in the canton of Zug.
The Hölloch in the Muota Valley is one of the longest caves in the world.
You must not touch dripstones, because the grease from your skin disturbs their growth.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up a little **carbon dioxide** in the soil and becomes slightly acidic. This lets it dissolve **lime** from the rock. When this water drips into a cave, it gives off part of the gas into the air. Then a tiny bit of lime is left behind. Drop by drop, a dripstone grows like this over a very long time.

Dripstones that hang down from the ceiling are called **stalactites**. The stones that grow upwards from the floor are called **stalagmites**. When the two meet, a **column** forms. A memory aid: stalactites hold on tight to the ceiling. Sometimes thin straws, curtains or small pools of lime also form.

The **Höllgrotten** lie near Baar in the canton of Zug and are open to visitors. There you can see many beautiful dripstones. The **Hölloch** in the Muota Valley in the canton of Schwyz is more than 200 kilometres long and is one of the longest caves in the world. It has been explored by **cavers** for many decades. They wear a helmet and a lamp and draw exact plans of the passages.

abschnitte.titel: Life and climate in the cave
abschnitte.text: Deep inside the mountain you notice little of the weather outside. That is why it is roughly **equally cool** in caves all year round. The air is usually damp. **Bats** like to hibernate in caves, because it is quiet, dark and frost-free there. Visitors should not disturb them.

If you visit a dripstone cave, take a **warm jacket** and sturdy shoes, even in summer. The ground can be wet and slippery. You must **not touch** the dripstones. The grease from your skin stays on the stone, and no new lime can be deposited there. That way the stones stay beautiful for everyone.

gewusst: A broken dripstone often needs thousands of years to grow as big again.
Because dripstones grow in layers, researchers can learn from them about the climate of earlier times.
